description: Double displacement precipitation; calcium hydroxide in water reacts with iron(III) chloride to yield soluble calcium chloride and insoluble iron(III) hydroxide precipitate; performed at room temperature in aqueous solution; no catalyst; employed for removal or recovery of iron(III) as a hydroxide.

Alkaline saponification (hydrolysis) of a carbamate; purpose is to obtain the sodium salt of dimethylcarbamate; key transformation: methyl N,N‑dimethylcarbamate + NaOH → sodium dimethylcarbamate + methanol; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1‑2 M), temperature 50‑70 °C, stirring until complete; product isolated by evaporation of water and drying the solid salt.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) reaction: aqueous thallium(I) chloride reacts with silver nitrate, precipitating insoluble silver chloride and forming soluble thallium(I) nitrate. Purpose is to separate silver as a precipitate or to synthesize thallium nitrate. Key transformation: Cl⁻ + Ag⁺ → AgCl↓, Tl⁺ + NO₃⁻ → TlNO₃ (aq). Performed in water at room temperature with gentle stirring; no catalyst; the precipitate is filtered off.

Double‑displacement precipitation: Aqueous sodium phosphate reacts with praseodymium(III) chloride; Pr³⁺ combines with PO₄³⁻ to form insoluble praseodymium(III) phosphate precipitate, while Na⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to remain in solution as sodium chloride. Conducted in water at room temperature with stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling (aryl‑alkyl C‑C bond formation). Purpose: construct 3‑phenyl‑1‑chloropropane by coupling phenyl from phenylboronic acid with the iodo‑propyl fragment. Key steps: oxidative addition of Pd(0) into the C–I bond of 1‑chloro‑3‑iodopropane, transmetalation with phenyl‑B(OH)₂, reductive elimination to give the C(sp²)–C(sp³) bond; KI and boric acid are formed as by‑products. Typical conditions: Pd(OAc)₂ (≈5 mol %), triphenylphosphine, base such as K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃, mixed solvent (dioxane/water or THF/water), 80–100 °C under inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated oxime. Purpose: saturate the C=C bond of acrolein oxime while preserving the oxime, affording propanal oxime. Key transformation: H₂ addition across the double bond on a Pd/C surface, converting CH₂=CH–CH=NOH to CH₃‑CH₂‑CH=NOH. Conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), 10 % Pd on carbon, protic solvent (ethanol or methanol), 25–50 °C, atmospheric or mild pressure.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) between NaOH and barium silicate. Purpose: convert insoluble barium silicate into soluble sodium silicate and barium hydroxide. Key transformation: ion exchange producing Na₂SiO₃ (or NaSiO₃) and Ba(OH)₂. Conditions: excess NaOH in water, heating to 60–80 °C to aid dissolution; no catalyst required.

Aqueous cation‑exchange (double‑displacement) between sodium carbonate and potassium phosphate tribasic. Purpose: swap Na⁺ and K⁺ ions to give potassium carbonate and sodium phosphate, useful for reagent preparation. Key transformation: formation of K₂CO₃ and Na₃PO₄ from the starting salts. Conditions: dissolve both salts in water, stir at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; reaction proceeds spontaneously, no catalyst needed.

Iodination of alcohol with phosphorus triiodide; primary alcohol reacts with PI₃ (often generated in situ from red phosphorus and I₂) to give the corresponding alkyl iodide and phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃). SN2 pathway. Conducted in dry ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt; anhydrous conditions are essential.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; methoxide ion from sodium methoxide attacks 2‑ethylhexanoate, displacing ethoxide and forming methyl 2‑ethylhexanoate. The reaction is reversible; using excess methanol (or removal of ethanol) drives it to completion. Typical conditions: methanol as solvent, catalytic or stoichiometric NaOMe (10–20 mol %), reflux (≈65 °C) for 1–4 h under nitrogen; the mixture is then neutralized and the product isolated by extraction or distillation.

Acid-base neutralization. Produces bismuth sulfate from hydroxide via sulfuric acid protonation. Sulfuric acid’s H+ neutralizes hydroxide, yielding water and sulfate salt. Stability of Bi2(SO4)3 in solution determines reaction conditions. Water as solvent.

Ethanolysis (transesterification) of cyclohexyl acetate; ethanol replaces the cyclohexoxy group, yielding cyclohexanol and ethyl acetate; acid catalyst such as H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH (or base catalyst) is used; reaction run under reflux in excess ethanol, which serves as both reagent and solvent; removal of the by‑product alcohol drives the reaction forward.

Aldehyde reduction – sodium borohydride delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of 2‑methylbutanal, reducing it to the primary alcohol 2‑methylbutanol. Performed in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is quenched with water after completion.

Strong oxidative conversion of para‑xylene to terephthalic acid using potassium permanganate. Purpose: industrial synthesis of terephthalic acid for polyester manufacturing by oxidizing both methyl groups to carboxyl groups. Key transformation: oxidation of each –CH₃ to –CO₂H, reduction of Mn(VII) to MnO₂ precipitate, water formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (KMnO₄ in NaOH), reflux or autoclave at 150–200 °C, followed by acidification to isolate terephthalic acid; MnO₂ is filtered off.

Double displacement / complex formation reaction; combines calcium fluoride with silicon tetrafluoride to produce calcium hexafluorosilicate (CaSiF6). The key transformation is the coordination of six fluoride ligands to silicon and incorporation of calcium as the counter‑cation. Typically carried out anhydrous at elevated temperatures (150‑300 °C) in a sealed vessel or molten fluoride melt; no solvent is used, and an inert atmosphere (dry nitrogen or argon) is required to avoid moisture.

Hydrolysis (hydration) of zirconium oxide to zirconium hydroxide. Purpose: generate Zr(OH)₄ (or related hydroxide) from ZrO₂ for further processing or precipitation. Key transformation: addition of H₂O to the oxide lattice forming zirconium hydroxide. Conditions: aqueous suspension of ZrO₂, elevated temperature (80–120 °C) or hydrothermal treatment, neutral to mildly basic pH; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an alkyl‑benzyl amine (reductive N‑C bond cleavage). N‑benzylethanamine is hydrogenated over Pd/C (or Raney Ni) in ethanol or methanol under H₂ pressure (10–50 bar) at 25–80 °C, producing ethylamine and toluene; used for N‑benzyl deprotection.

Redox/halogen-induced decomposition; purpose is to generate nitrogen gas and precipitate insoluble silver chloride; chlorine oxidizes azide anion releasing N2 while Ag+ forms AgCl; typically carried out in a dry inert solvent such as acetonitrile or directly as a solid‑state reaction at low temperature; no catalyst required.

Direct oxidative fluorination (combination reaction); synthesizes rhenium heptafluoride by reacting elemental rhenium with fluorine gas; Re + 3.5 F₂ → ReF₇; performed in the gas phase with excess F₂ at 200–400 °C in a fluorination apparatus (e.g., nickel or Mo reactor); no solvent or catalyst is used.

Combustion (oxidation) of 1,3‑butadiene; purpose is complete oxidation to CO2 and H2O with release of heat; the hydrocarbon is fully oxidized by excess O2 yielding carbon dioxide and water; performed in open flame or furnace with abundant oxygen at temperatures above 800 °C; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Dehydrative condensation to form an acid anhydride; purpose is synthesis of isobutyryl anhydride from isobutyric acid; two acid molecules lose water, which is absorbed by phosphorus pentoxide, forming the anhydride; carried out under anhydrous conditions with excess P2O5, refluxing in a dry non‑polar solvent such as toluene or benzene, under nitrogen.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis; purpose is conversion of 1,3‑dibromobutane to 1,3‑butanediol; hydroxide ions replace bromide on both carbon atoms, producing the diol and sodium bromide; conducted in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) with reflux (80–100 °C), often in a water/ethanol mixture; no additional catalyst required.

Carbodiimide‑mediated condensation (acid anhydride formation); purpose is preparation of benzoic anhydride from benzoic acid; DIC activates the acid to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate that couples with a second acid molecule, releasing N,N‑diisopropylurea; performed in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; the by‑product precipitates and can be filtered.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acetylation of amine); purpose is protection of one amino group of putrescine as an amide; acetyl chloride reacts with the primary amine to give N‑acetylputrescine and HCl, which is scavenged by a base; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane or THF with triethylamine or pyridine at 0 °C to rt; inert atmosphere is advisable.

Type: Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling. Purpose: Form a C–C bond between a heteroaryl bromide and an arylboronic acid to install a phenyl group onto selenophene. Key transformation: Pd‑catalyzed transmetalation and reductive elimination couple 2‑bromoselenophene with phenylboronic acid, yielding 2‑phenylselenophene and KBr (from base). Typical conditions: Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(dppf)Cl₂ (2–5 mol %), base such as K₂CO₃ (2 equiv), solvent mixture of dioxane/H₂O or toluene/H₂O, 80–100 °C, nitrogen atmosphere, 4–12 h.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of methyl carbamimidate hydrochloride with NaOH to produce N‑methylurea, sodium chloride and water. Hydroxide attacks the C=N bond of the amidine, converting it to a carbonyl (urea) and releasing chloride as NaCl. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature to 50 °C; excess NaOH ensures complete conversion.

Mitsunobu esterification: conversion of benzoic acid to tert‑butyl benzoate using tert‑butyl alcohol, triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate. The reaction forms an ester with inversion of configuration (irrelevant for acids). Typical conditions are anhydrous THF or CH₂Cl₂, 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, and the reagents act as both oxidant and activating agent. By‑ are triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazine‑1,2‑dicarboxylate.

Carbothermic reduction of copper(II) oxide; purpose is to obtain metallic copper from its oxide ore; CuO is reduced to Cu while carbon is oxidized to CO₂; requires high temperature (≈900–1000 °C) in a furnace; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Grignard addition to an ester: phenylmagnesium bromide attacks methyl p‑nitrobenzoate, giving a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses after work‑up to the ketone p‑nitrobenzophenone and methanol. Conducted in dry ether or THF, usually at –78 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous acid work‑up to protonate the alkoxide. The reaction installs a second aryl group onto the carbonyl carbon, yielding a diaryl ketone.

Sulfonyl chloride aminolysis: ammonia nucleophilically substitutes the chloride of p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride to give p‑toluenesulfonamide, with generation of hydrogen chloride. Commonly performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile, often in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the HCl, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Redox halogenation of a metal oxide: solid vanadium(II) oxide is chlorinated by dry Cl2 gas to give vanadium(II) chloride and O2; performed at elevated temperatures (≈300–500 °C) in a sealed tube under inert atmosphere, gas‑solid reaction, no solvent or catalyst required.

Acyl chloride formation from anhydride: phosphorus pentachloride converts phthalic anhydride into phthaloyl chloride (the di‑acid chloride). The reaction proceeds via chlorination of the carbonyl oxygens, releasing POCl₃ and HCl as by‑products. Typical conditions are reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, under anhydrous atmosphere.

Selective reduction of an acid chloride to an aldehyde: sodium borohydride reduces acetyl chloride to acetaldehyde while generating sodium chloride and sodium metaborate. The reaction is run in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often under nitrogen, and is quenched carefully to avoid over‑reduction to the alcohol.

Epoxide ring opening by amine (aminolysis): methylamine attacks the less‑substituted carbon of styrene oxide, opening the ring to afford N‑methylphenylethanolamine (a β‑amino alcohol). The reaction proceeds in a polar protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol, typically at room temperature, and may be aided by a mild base to neutralize the generated HCl if the amine is used as its hydrochloride salt.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation). Reaction of the basic nucleobase 2,6-diaminopurine with acidic sodium bisulfate to give the water‑soluble sulfate salt. Typically performed in aqueous solution (often water or water/ethanol) at room temperature with gentle stirring. No catalyst required.

Stork enolate alkylation of a β‑keto ester. Ethyl acetoacetate is deprotonated by sodium ethoxide to form the enolate, which is alkylated with methyl iodide to give ethyl 2‑methylacetoacetate, NaI and ethanol. Conducted in refluxing ethanol (or anhydrous ethanol) with NaOEt generated in situ, methyl iodide added at 0 °C to rt. Provides a carbon‑carbon bond‑forming step for substituted acetoacetates.

Strong‑base induced β‑elimination (E2) of 2‑chloroethylbenzene with potassium tert‑butoxide. KOzylic hydrogen, eliminating HCl to give 2‑chlorostyrene (phenyl‑CH=CH‑Cl) and potassium chloride. Purpose: to convert a saturated haloalkyl side chain into a vinyl chloride derivative useful for polymerization or further functionalization. Typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent (THF, DME, or DMF), 0 °C to reflux temperature, 1–2 equiv KOtBu, inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic epoxide ring‑opening (alkylation). The nitrogen of 2‑methyl‑5‑nitro‑1H‑imidazole attacks propylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to afford secnidazole, a β‑hydroxy‑alkylated imidazole. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO with a base (e.g., NaH, K₂CO₃) at 0 °C to reflux; often under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of ethyl p‑hydroxybenzoate with methanol to give methyl p‑hydroxybenzoate (methylparaben) and ethanol; usually catalyzed by a mineral acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or a basic catalyst (NaOMe) under reflux; methanol acts as both solvent and reactant.

Hydrolysis (acid–base reaction); aluminum hydride reacts violently with water to give aluminum hydroxide precipitate and hydrogen gas; AlH3 + 3 H2O → Al(OH)3 + 3 H2; performed in aqueous medium, often under cooling due to exotherm, no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution. Hydroxide ion replaces the bromide of 3‑(bromomethyl)pyridine to give 3‑(hydroxymethyl)pyridine and NaBr. Usually carried out in aqueous NaOH or NaOH/ethanol solution, heated gently (50–80 °C) or refluxed. No catalyst needed.

O‑methylation of phenol (electrophilic alkylation). Dimethyl sulfate transfers a methyl group to the remaining phenolic OH of 4‑ethylcatechol, producing 4‑ethylguaiacol. Performed in the presence of a base such as NaOH, K₂CO₃ or pyridine, in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF) at 0–25 °C; reaction is typically quenched with ice water. No catalyst beyond the base.

Metathesis/precipitation (binary chalcogenide synthesis). Arsenic trichloride reacts with sodium selenide to form arsenic triselenide (As₂Se₃) and sodium chloride as by‑product. Conducted under inert atmosphere, often in sealed quartz tubes or high‑temperature melt (200–400 °C). No solvent or catalyst is required; the product precipitates on cooling.

Redox reduction of thallium(I) salt. Sodium borohydride reduces thallium(I) sulfate to metallic thallium, liberating hydrogen gas and oxidizing borohydride to boric acid while sodium sulfate remains in solution. Typically performed in aqueous medium at 0–5 °C to control H₂ evolution, with slow addition of NaBH₄. No additional catalyst.

Solid‑state chalcogen exchange (metathesis). Elemental tellurium replaces sulfur in antimony(III) sulfide to give antimony(III) telluride, a thermoelectric semiconductor, with elemental sulfur as the by‑product. Conducted at 600–800 °C in an evacuated quartz tube or under inert gas; no solvent, often sealed to prevent oxidation.

High‑temperature oxidation (redox) of chromium(III) oxide to chromium(IV) oxide. Molecular oxygen transfers electrons to Cr₂O₃, forming the metastable CrO₂ phase. Typically performed at 800–1000 °C in a flowing O₂ atmosphere (or high‑pressure O₂). No solvent; the reaction is conducted in a ceramic or quartz reactor.

Oxime formation (condensation of aldehyde with hydroxylamine). The aldehyde carbonyl of 2,4‑dihydroxybenzaldehyde is transformed into its oxime, releasing water. Usually carried out in ethanol or methanol (often with a small amount of aqueous buffer, pH 4–6) at 0 °C to rt; no catalyst is needed, though mild acid can accelerate the reaction.

Dehydrative cyclization (anhydride formation). Phorus(V) oxide acts as a strong dehydrating agent, removing water from benzene‑1,2,4‑tricarboxylic acid to afford trimellitic anhydride. The reaction is heated to 150–200 °C, often in the absence of solvent or with a non‑reactive medium such as carbon tetrachloride; P₂O₅ is removed after completion.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive conversion of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol). Salicylaldehyde is reduced by H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst such as 5 % Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 25–50 °C, in ethanol, methanol or THF as solvent. The product is salicyl alcohol.

Neutralization of arsenic pentoxide with ammonium hydroxide to give ammonium arsenate; As2O5 + 6 NH4OH → 2 (NH4)3AsO4 + 3 H2O; performed in water at room temperature or slight warming; no catalyst required.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation followed by intramolecular condensation to synthesize rubiadin (an anthraquinone). Phthalic anhydride supplies an acyl group that electrophilically attacks 2‑methyl‑1,3‑dihydroxybenzene in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The reaction proceeds at 0–50 °C then reflux, often in carbon disulfide, nitrobenzene or dichloromethane, with water eliminated during cyclization to give rubiadin.

Redox single‑displacement (metal reduction of a halide); copper metal reduces vanadium tetrachloride to elemental vanadium while being oxidized to copper(II) chloride; requires heating of the solid reagents under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (e.g., sealed tube or melt) to facilitate electron transfer.

Esterification (Fischer esterification); purpose: convert a carboxylic acid to its methyl ester. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl of 2‑bromobutanoic acid, followed by loss of water to give methyl 2‑bromobutyrate. Typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of a strong Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH); removal of water drives the equilibrium. Common solvent: methanol itself; sometimes toluene is used as a Dean‑Stark trap.

Base‑promoted dehydrofluorination (E2 elimination) of a perfluorinated alkane; KOH abstracts a fluorine/hydrogen to generate 2,3,3,3‑tetrafluoropropene, potassium fluoride and water. Typically carried out with aqueous or alcoholic KOH, heated.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitro arene; purpose: reduce the nitro group to an amine while leaving the ester intact. Key transformation: H₂ adds across the NO₂ group, converting it to NH₂ and producing two molecules of water. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol, or THF) at 25–80 °C. Reaction is usually carried out under an inert atmosphere.

Acid-base protonation reaction to regenerate dimethyl phosphoric acid from its sodium salt. Purpose is to convert a salt to a free acid. Transformation is the exchange of Na+ with H+. Typically performed in aqueous solution with excess HCl at room temperature.

Photochemical [2+2] cycloaddition of tetrachloroethylene; purpose: dimerize the C=C units to form a cyclobutane ring. Key transformation: two C₂Cl₄ molecules undergo a concerted cycloaddition forming octachlorocyclobutane (C₄Cl₈). Typical conditions: UV irradiation (λ ≈ 300 nm) in an inert, non‑absorbing solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or neat liquid, often at room temperature. No catalyst is required; sometimes a sensitizer (e.g., benzophenone) is added to increase efficiency.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution. Sodium acetate functions as a nucleophile, replacing chloride to form allyl acetate. Usually conducted in aprotic solvents or under phase-transfer conditions. May require heat or catalytic assistance.

General type: Double displacement reaction. Purpose: Ion exchange between salts. Key transformations: Exchange of tetrafluoroborate and nitrate ions to form new salts. Typical reaction conditions: Room temperature in aqueous solution. Common solvents: Water.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination (Friedel‑Crafts halogenation); purpose: introduce chlorine substituents onto the aromatic ring of toluene. Key transformation: Cl₂, activated by AlCl₃, generates the electrophilic Cl⁺ that substitutes at the ortho and para positions relative to the methyl group, yielding ortho‑ and para‑chlorotoluene and HCl as a by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1 equiv) in a non‑protic, non‑coordinating solvent such as CS₂, CCl₄, or CH₂Cl₂; temperature 0 °C to 25 °C to control regioselectivity; reaction performed under nitrogen.

Electrophilic nitration of cinnamic acid using nitronium tetrafluoroborate; purpose: install a nitro group onto the aromatic ring of cinnamic acid. Key transformation: the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) attacks the benzenoid ring, forming nitrocinnamic acid; BF₄⁻ acts as a non‑nucleophilic counter‑ion, and the process generates BF₃ and HF as side products. Typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C to 0 °C → room temperature) in a dry, non‑coordinating solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; reaction is usually carried out under an inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Type: SN2 nucleophilic substitution (Williamson ether synthesis). Purpose: form an aryl ether from phenoxide. Key transformation: phenoxide oxygen attacks the ethyl carbon of ethyl trifluoromethanesulfonate, displacing CF3SO3− to give ethyl phenyl ether and NaOTf. Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, acetone) at 0 °C to rt; sodium phenoxide generated in situ or used as salt; no additional catalyst required.

Type: redox (metallothermic reduction) reaction. Purpose: reduce boron trichloride to elemental boron while oxidizing zinc to zinc chloride. Key transformation: zinc metal donates electrons to BCl3, forming ZnCl2 and depositing boron metal. Typical conditions: high temperature (often above 400 °C) under inert atmosphere; reaction may be carried out in a sealed tube or molten salt medium; no external catalyst.

Type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation). Purpose: acylate morpholine to afford an N‑propionyl amide. Key transformation: the nitrogen lone pair of morpholine attacks the carbonyl carbon of propionyl chloride, releasing chloride as HCl and forming N‑propionylmorpholine. Typical conditions: aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt; a base (triethylamine, pyridine, or NaHCO3) is added to scavenger HCl; no catalyst needed.

Type: acid‑catalyzed ring opening of an oxetane (hydrohalogenation). Purpose: convert the four‑membered cyclic ether into a chloro‑alcohol. Key transformation: protonation of the oxetane oxygen followed by nucleophilic attack of chloride at the most substituted carbon, opening the ring to give 3‑chloro‑1‑propanol. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl or HCl gas in a miscible solvent (water, MeOH); reflux or gentle heating; no additional catalyst.

This is a hydrolysis reaction where ytterbium tribromide reacts with water to form ytterbium hydroxide and hydrogen bromide. It typically occurs in aqueous solution without requiring additional catalysts. The reaction is spontaneous upon exposure to moisture, releasing HBr gas.

Radical redox reaction of chlorine monoxide with nitric oxide; ClO oxidizes NO to NO2 while being reduced to a chlorine atom radical. Important in atmospheric ozone chemistry, occurs in the gas phase under typical stratospheric conditions, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Condensation of carbon disulfide with a primary amine to give a thiourea derivative, with loss of hydrogen sulfide; typically carried out under reflux in ethanol or THF, sometimes with a base; H2S gas evolves.

Direct fluorination (combination) of zinc to produce zinc fluoride; purpose is preparation of ZnF2; key transformation Zn(0) → Zn(II) with two fluorine atoms added; usually carried out by exposing powdered zinc to F2 gas at 150‑300 °C in a sealed quartz tube or flow reactor, sometimes with a dilute F2/Ar mixture; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Metathesis/neutralization reaction; arsenic tribromide reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to yield insoluble arsenic trihydroxide and soluble sodium bromide; usually carried out in water or dilute NaOH solution at ambient temperature; stirring facilitates precipitation.

Acid–base neutralization of yttrium oxide with aqueous sulfuric acid; purpose is to convert the refractory oxide into soluble yttrium sulfate. The oxide O2‑ is protonated while sulfate anion replaces oxide, producing Y2(SO4)3 and water. Typically performed in water with excess 1–2 M H2SO4, heated to 80–120 °C under stirring until the solid dissolves; no catalyst required.

Type: transesterification (ester exchange). Purpose: convert a methyl ester to the corresponding ethyl ester. Key transformation: ethanol attacks the carbonyl carbon of methyl decanoate, displacing methanol and forming ethyl decanoate. Typical conditions: excess ethanol, reflux temperature; acid catalyst (p‑toluenesulfonic acid, H2SO4) or base catalyst (NaOMe, K2CO3); removal of methanol drives equilibrium; solvent often the excess alcohol itself.

Type: oxidative cleavage of an internal alkyne (strong oxidant). Purpose: break the C≡C bond to yield carboxylic acids. Key transformation: KMnO4 (hot, aqueous, usually alkaline) adds across the triple bond, leading to complete oxidation of each carbon to a carboxyl group, producing ethanoic acid and propanoic acid from 2‑pentyne. Typical conditions: aqueous KMnO4 solution, heating to reflux, basic medium (NaOH); after reaction, acid work‑up (HCl) to precipitate MnO2 and isolate acids.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of a β‑hydroxy ester; produces an α,β‑unsaturated ester; key transformation: loss of water from ethyl 3‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoate to form ethyl 2‑methylprop‑2‑enoate; conditions: catalytic p‑TsOH or H₂SO₄, heating (80–120 °C) in toluene or similar solvent.

Redox halogenation: direct chlorination of titanium dihydride yields titanium tetrachloride and hydrogen gas; gas‑phase reaction performed at 300–400 °C under inert atmosphere, no solvent, chlorine gas as reagent.

Reduction reaction; converts phosphorus trichloride to phosphine; involves hydrogen gas as a reductant; requires elevated temperature and pressure; may use a transition-metal catalyst (e.g., Ni or Pt-based).

Gallium hydroxide reacts with hydrochloric acid in an acid-base neutralization reaction to form gallium chloride and water. The hydroxide ion from gallium hydroxide reacts with hydrogen ions from hydrochloric acid, producing water, while gallium and chloride ions combine. This reaction is used to synthesize gallium chloride. Typical conditions involve aqueous solutions at room temperature.

Metal‑acid reaction (single‑displacement/acid‑base); thulium metal dissolves in acetic acid, forming thulium(III) acetate and releasing hydrogen gas. Performed in aqueous or glacial acetic acid, often under reflux or with gentle heating; inert atmosphere may be used to avoid oxidation of the metal.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation: dicyandiamide reacts with 4‑chlorophenylhydrazine in refluxing aqueous HCl to cyclize into cycloguanil hydrochloride (a cyclic guanidine); typical conditions are excess HCl, heating 80–100 °C in water, product isolated as the HCl salt.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination: nitrobenzene undergoes meta‑chlorination with Cl₂ in the presence of a Lewis‑acid catalyst (FeCl₃ or AlCl₃) to give 3‑chloro‑nitrobenzene and HCl; usually carried out in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., CCl₄) at 0–50 °C with catalytic Lewis acid.

Precipitation (salt metathesis); purpose is to isolate samarium(III) carbonate; key transformation is the exchange of SO₄²⁻ and CO₃²⁻ ions between Sm₂(SO₄)₃ and Na₂CO₃, precipitating Sm₂(CO₃)₃ while Na₂SO₄ remains soluble; typically carried out in water with gentle heating and stirring, followed by filtration of the solid; water is the solvent.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of the alkene; ozone adds across the double bond of trans‑anethole and fragments it to produce p‑methoxybenzaldehyde and formaldehyde; carried out in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane at –78 °C, followed by a reductive work‑up (Zn/AcOH) or oxidative work‑up (H₂O₂) to afford the aldehydes; no metal catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement precipitation: aqueous potassium carbonate reacts with strontium bromide, exchanging ions to precipitate insoluble strontium carbonate while forming soluble potassium bromide; conducted in water at room temperature, product filtered and washed.

Acid displacement (salt metathesis) to regenerate the free acid; purpose is recovery of lactic acid and formation of soluble strontium chloride. Strontium lactate is protonated by hydrochloric acid, yielding lactic acid and SrCl₂ in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium at 0–25 °C; excess HCl ensures complete conversion.

Electrophilic addition of bromine to an alkene; anti‑addition across the C=C bond of ethylene to give 1,2‑dibromoethane. Reaction proceeds via a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate. Usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, dichloromethane or chloroform, without catalyst. Stoichiometric Br2 (1 equiv) is added dropwise until the violet color disappears.

Acid‑base salt hydrolysis: calcium lactate is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid, liberating two equivalents of lactic acid and forming calcium chloride; performed in water, often with gentle heating to drive off the free acid.
Direct oxidation; forms uranium dioxide, a common nuclear fuel oxide. Solid uranium reacts with dry O2 gas at 500‑800 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation/deoxygenation: 9,10‑phenanthrenedione is reduced under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with palladium on carbon to remove the carbonyl groups and afford phenanthrene; typical solvent is ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature ambient to reflux, catalyst filtered off after reaction.

Halide metathesis (solid‑state double displacement). Exchange of iodide and fluoride ligands to form aluminum fluoride, which has a very high lattice energy, and lutetium(III) iodide. Typically carried out by mixing the two solid halides and heating to 500–800 °C under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen); no solvent is used.

Hydride reduction of an epoxide with lithium borohydride; nucleophilic attack of BH4⁻ on ethylene oxide opens the ring to give ethanol, with borane and lithium ethoxide as by‑products. Conducted in dry THF at 0 °C to room temperature, then quenched with water.

Coordination complex formation; synthesis of a cobalt(III) bis(dioxime) chloride‑pyridine complex used as a catalyst or analytical reagent. Key transformation is chelation of 2,3‑butanedione dioxime to CoCl₂ in basic pyridine medium, displacing chloride and forming the octahedral complex. Typical conditions: reflux of cobalt(II) chloride, 2,3‑butanedione dioxime and pyridine in ethanol/water with NaOH as base, under inert atmosphere. Common solvents/catalysts: ethanol or methanol, pyridine acts as both ligand and solvent; NaOH provides deprotonation.

Acid–base proton transfer (deprotonation of ammonia). Phenyl lithium, a strong Brønsted base, abstracts a proton from ammonia, yielding benzene and lithium amide. Conducted in dry ether (e.g., THF) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert gas to avoid moisture.

Salt formation (protonation of a heterocycle). Pyridine is protonated by p‑toluenesulfonic acid to give pyridinium p‑toluenesulfonate. Usually performed in anhydrous organic solvent such as dichloromethane or ethanol at room temperature; the reaction proceeds quantitatively.

Isopropyl pentanoate + water → pentanoic acid + isopropanol  
General type: acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (acidic hydrolysis). Purpose is to cleave the ester into the corresponding carboxylic acid and alcohol. Key transformation: carbonyl C=O of the ester becomes a carboxylic acid; the isopropoxy group is released as isopropanol. Typical conditions: reflux in a mixture of water and a strong acid (e.g., 1–6 M HCl or H₂SO₄) for 2–6 h; excess water drives the reaction forward. Common solvent: water with a miscible organic co‑solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or toluene to dissolve the ester.

Acid‑catalysed transesterification. Glycerol attacks the carbonyl of propyl acetate, transferring the acetate group to glycerol (forming glycerol monoacetate) and releasing propanol. Catalyzed by a mineral acid (e.g., 1–5 % H₂SO₄), reflux in excess glycerol or a suitable high‑boiling solvent (e.g., toluene); removal of propanol drives the equilibrium to product.

Diazotization of 2,5‑dichloroaniline: general type diazotization to form an aryl diazonium salt; purpose is to generate a reactive diazonium intermediate for subsequent substitution; key transformation is conversion of the –NH2 group to –N₂⁺Cl⁻; typically carried out in cold (0‑5 °C) aqueous hydrochloric acid with sodium nitrite added slowly; solvent is water/HCl, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base salt metathesis (acid dissolution of a metal tungstate). Concentrated nitric acid protonates the tungstate anion, producing tungstic acid (H₂WO₄) and soluble strontium nitrate. Performed in aqueous HNO₃, often with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to ensure complete dissolution.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis. The cyclic acetal 1,3‑dioxolane‑2‑methanol is protonated by aqueous H₂SO₄, water attacks the acetal carbon and the ring opens, giving the free aldehyde (glyceraldehyde) and liberating ethylene glycol. Typical conditions: dilute sulfuric acid, aqueous medium, reflux (80‑100 °C). No special solvent other than water; the reaction is driven to completion by excess water.

Redox acid‑metal reaction; sodium metal is oxidized to Na⁺ while sulfuric acid is reduced, producing sodium sulfate and hydrogen gas. Performed in dilute H₂SO₄ at ambient temperature, often under inert atmosphere due to vigorous H₂ evolution.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S_NAr) on a pyridine halide. Sodium hydrosulfide (NaSH) provides HS⁻, which attacks the electron‑deficient C‑2 of 2‑chloropyridine, displacing chloride to give 2‑mercaptopyridine. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often heated to 80‑120 °C for several hours. The by‑product NaCl precipitates and can be filtered off.

Organolithium alkylation (Wurtztype coupling). n‑Butyllithium acts as a nucleophile toward propyl bromide, forming a new C‑C bond and yielding n‑heptane; lithium bromide is generated as the inorganic salt. Reaction is carried out at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous ether or THF under nitrogen or argon to prevent moisture attack on the organolithium reagent. After addition, the mixture is warmed to room temperature and quenched.

Acid–base neutralization of the acidic oxide boron trioxide with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium metaborate (NaBO2) and water; usually performed by mixing B2O3 and NaOH in water and heating to 150–250 °C to drive the reaction to completion, water serves as the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Partial hydrolysis of a nitrile to the primary amide using aqueous ammonia; 2‑fluoroacetonitrile reacts with NH₃ (aq) to produce 2‑fluoroacetamide. Typically carried out by heating the nitrile in a dilute aqueous NH₃ solution (≈5–10 % NH₃) at reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h; the conditions are milder than acidic hydrolysis, limiting conversion to the amide rather than the acid.

Acid chloride formation (chlorination) of 2‑methylbenzoic acid using phosphorus pentachloride. Purpose: convert the carboxylic acid into a more reactive acid chloride for subsequent acylation reactions. Key transformation: COOH → COCl with formation of POCl₃ and HCl as gaseous by‑products. Typical conditions: addition of PCl₅ to the acid in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature, then reflux under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Halide exchange (metathesis) on an organotin halide. Triethyl‑tin‑chloride reacts with sodium bromide, swapping the halide ligands to give triethyl‑tin‑bromide and sodium chloride. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or THF, often with gentle heating (40‑60 °C) to accelerate exchange. The inorganic NaCl precipitates and can be removed by filtration.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (Fischer‑type). Phenol attacks the carbonyl carbon of methyl 4‑fluorobenzoate under the action of concentrated H₂SO₄, displacing methanol and forming phenyl 4‑fluorobenzoate. Reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (toluene or xylenes) with removal of methanol by azeotropic distillation drives the equilibrium. Typical conditions: 1–2 equiv H₂SO₄, 120‑130 °C, several hours; product isolated after aqueous work‑up and purification.

This is a carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling (condensation) reaction used to acetylate the amino group of glycine. The carboxyl of acetic acid is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is then attacked by the amine of glycine to give N‑acetylglycine and dicyclohexylurea as the by‑product. The reaction is typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP to accelerate acyl transfer. No additional catalyst is required beyond DCC.

Acyl chloride esterification (acylation of alcohol); purpose is to prepare the acetate ester more efficiently than Fischer esterification. 3‑Octanol attacks acetyl chloride, releasing HCl and forming octan‑3‑yl acetate. Performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl. Reaction is usually fast and does not require heating.

This is a sulfide exchange/precipitation reaction that converts arsenic pentoxide to arsenic pentasulfide using ammonium sulfide as the sulfiding agent. In aqueous solution the arsenic(V) oxide reacts with sulfide ions, replacing oxygen with sulfur to precipitate As₂S₅ while releasing ammonia and water. The reaction is usually carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of As₂O₅ and (NH₄)₂S and heating gently (≈70–80 °C) with stirring; the solid As₂S₅ is isolated by filtration. Water acts as the solvent; no catalyst is needed.

This is a nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of an acyl chloride with a secondary alcohol to form sec‑butyl acetate. The hydroxyl of sec‑butanol attacks the carbonyl carbon of acetyl chloride, displacing chloride as hydrogen chloride. The reaction is typically run in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature, with pyridine (or triethylamine) serving as an HCl scavenger. No additional catalyst is required.

This is a base‑catalyzed transesterification where sodium ethoxide exchanges the alkoxy group of methyl butyrate for an ethoxy group, giving ethyl butyrate and sodium methoxide. The reaction is performed in excess ethanol (or ethyl ethanoate) as solvent, with catalytic or stoichiometric sodium ethoxide, and heated under reflux to drive equilibrium toward product; removal of methanol (by distillation) helps shift the reaction. No special catalyst beyond the alkoxide base is needed.

This is a peracid epoxidation of an alkene. Performic acid adds an oxygen atom across the carbon–carbon double bond of styrene, producing styrene oxide while being reduced to formic acid. The reaction is usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often under inert atmosphere; no metal catalyst is required, though a buffer may be used to control acidity.

Type: selective reduction of a Weinreb amide to an aldehyde. Purpose: generate an aldehyde from an amide without over‑reduction. Key transformation: DIBAL‑H delivers hydride to the carbonyl of N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to acetaldehyde and N‑methoxy‑N‑methylamine. Typical conditions: 1 equiv DIBAL‑H, −78 °C to −20 °C in dry THF or toluene under nitrogen, followed by careful aqueous quench. No additional catalyst required.

Thermal disproportionation of mercurous iodide. Upon heating, mercurous iodide splits into mercuric iodide and elemental mercury. Conducted by heating the solid to about 200 °C in a sealed tube or under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst.

This is a borane‑mediated reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol. BH₃·THF complexes add to the carbonyl of 2‑butanone to form a borate ester intermediate, which upon oxidative work‑up (e.g., H₂O₂/NaOH) yields sec‑butanol. The reaction is carried out in dry tetrahydrofuran at 0 °C to room temperature, with stoichiometric BH₃; the oxidation step is performed after removal of THF. No additional catalyst is needed.

Type: strong hydride reduction of a silyl ester. Purpose: convert a protected benzoate (triethylsilyl benzoate) into the corresponding primary alcohol. Key transformation: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, reducing the ester to benzyl alcohol and cleaving the Si–O bond to give triethylsilanol. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; reagent added portionwise to a suspension of LiAlH4. No additional catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to isolate insoluble lead(II) iodide from aqueous solution; key ion exchange: Pb²⁺ pairs with I⁻ to form PbI₂ solid while NH₄⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to remain in solution as NH₄NO₃; performed in water at ambient temperature, no special catalyst.

Type: carbodiimide‑mediated Steglich esterification. Purpose: synthesize the alkyl ester octyl gallate from gallic acid. Key transformation: DCC activates the carboxylic acid of gallic acid to an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is attacked by 1‑octanol; DMAP catalyzes acyl transfer, yielding the ester and precipitating dicyclohexylurea. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane (or THF), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; reaction stirred until DCC is consumed, then filtration to remove urea.

Type: aldehyde‑amine/thiol cyclocondensation forming a thiazolidine ring. Purpose: generate a protected cysteine analogue (1,3‑thiazolidine). Key transformation: formaldehyde reacts with the amine and thiol groups of cysteamine (present as the HCl salt) to form a five‑membered thiazolidine ring, releasing HCl and water as by‑products. Typical conditions: aqueous or methanolic solution, mildly acidic to neutral pH, ambient temperature or gentle reflux; the reaction proceeds spontaneously without added catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitro group; converts 5‑nitro‑1,2‑benzisoxazole to 5‑amino‑1,2‑benzisoxazole with loss of water. Typically run with H₂ (1–5 atm) and 5–10 % Pd/C in ethanol or methanol at 25‑60 °C. The nitro functionality is reduced to an amine while the isoxazole ring remains intact.

Acidic redox oxidation–reduction: sulfite ions reduce permanganate to Mn²⁺ while being oxidized to sulfate; permanganate serves as oxidant in hot acidic solution. Carried out in aqueous sulfuric acid, heated; no external catalyst required.

Hydrolytic cleavage of a phosphorothioate ester; water attacks the phosphorus center, breaking P‑S and P‑O bonds to afford 2‑(diethylamino)ethanethiol and ethyl methylphosphonic acid. Performed in aqueous medium, optionally with mild acid or base, at ambient or gently elevated temperature.

Type: halide‑alkoxide metathesis (preparation of a metal alkoxide). Purpose: synthesize vanadium(V) tri‑isopropoxide oxide, a precursors for vanadium oxide materials. Key transformation: V(O)Cl3 reacts with three equivalents of sodium isopropoxide; each NaOPr i replaces a chloride, forming V(O)(OiPr)3 and NaCl as solid by‑product. Typical conditions: dry, oxygen‑free solvent such as THF or toluene, low to ambient temperature under nitrogen; stoichiometric NaOiPr added slowly to a suspension of V(O)Cl3; reaction stirred until Cl⁻ is fully consumed; solid NaCl filtered off.

Catalytic hydrogenation: reduction of the aldehyde group of 2‑ethylbutanal to the primary alcohol 2‑ethylbutanol using H₂ gas over Pd/C. Typically performed in ethanol or methanol (or ethyl acetate) at 1–5 atm H₂, 25–50 °C.

Nitric‑acid oxidation: converts benzoin (α‑hydroxy‑ketone) to benzil (1,2‑diketone) by oxidizing the secondary alcohol to a carbonyl. Usually carried out with conc. HNO₃ at 0–25 °C, often in acetic acid or water; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate). The potassium carboxylate attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide and forming methyl 3‑methylbutanoate (a methyl ester). Useful for converting a carboxylate salt into its methyl ester for further manipulation or purification. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often at room temperature to gentle reflux, using excess MeI. No catalyst is required; KI is formed as a by‑product.

SN2 alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of a thiolate; purpose is to prepare a thioether (methyl phenyl sulfide). The benzenethiolate anion attacks the methyl carbon of iodomethane, displacing iodide. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, THF) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; sodium iodide formed as by‑product.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution: acetate anion from lithium acetate displaces chloride of 1‑propyl chloride to give propyl acetate and LiCl. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or DMSO, often with mild heating (50–80 °C); no catalyst needed.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of elemental aluminum in oxygen to form aluminum oxide (Al2O3); the reaction proceeds upon heating aluminum powder or foil in air or pure O2 at >1000 °C, no solvent or catalyst is involved.

Protonolysis (acidolysis) of a metal alkyl with hydrogen bromide; analogous to the HCl reaction, producing gallium tribromide and methane. Carried out in dry diethyl ether or THF at low temperature (–78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; HBr gas is introduced into the solution. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization and precipitation; oxalic acid reacts with praseodymium(III) hydroxide in aqueous solution to form insoluble praseodymium oxalate precipitate and water; performed at ambient temperature with stirring in water; no catalyst required.

Jones oxidation; oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using chromium(VI) reagent. The aldehyde is treated with Jones reagent (a mixture of CrO₃ and H₂SO₄ in acetone), converting it to 2‑methoxyacetic acid. Reaction is typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in acetone as solvent, with aqueous acidic conditions to maintain Cr(VI) in solution. No extra catalyst beyond the chromium species.

Benzoin condensation (umpolung) catalyzed by thiamine hydrochloride; thiamine generates an acyl‑carbanion equivalent from benzaldehyde which attacks a second benzaldehyde molecule, forming benzoin. Conducted in ethanol or aqueous buffer at room temperature using catalytic thiamine·HCl.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl 4‑fluorobenzoate; NaOH aqueous solution (1–2 M) refluxes with the ester (often in MeOH/H₂O) for several hours, then the mixture is acidified (HCl) to precipitate 4‑fluorobenzoic acid.
Acid‑base metathesis: silver acetate reacts with iodic acid to produce silver iodate precipitate and acetic acid. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Oxidation; conversion of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. Chromic acid (generated from CrO₃/H₂SO₄) oxidizes 1‑propanol, removing two hydrogens to give propanal and water. Typically performed in aqueous sulfuric acid at 0‑25 °C, often using acetone as co‑solvent; the reaction is exothermic and requires careful temperature control.

Direct synthesis (combination) of zinc chloride; elemental zinc reacts exothermically with chlorine gas to give ZnCl2. Usually performed by exposing zinc metal to a stream of Cl2 at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature; reaction is performed in the gas phase, no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of cyclopropane‑1,1‑diol to yield cyclopropanone. Loss of a water molecule forms the strained three‑membered ketone. Usually carried out with a mild Brønsted acid (e.g., p‑TsOH or dilute H₂SO₄) at 40–80 °C, often in a dry organic solvent such as dichloromethane; the acid acts as catalyst.

Chlorination (oxidative combination) of aluminum monochloride; gaseous AlCl reacts with chlorine gas at high temperature (≈400–600 °C) to give aluminum trichloride (AlCl₃). The reaction proceeds in a flow reactor or sealed tube under an inert carrier gas. AlCl₃ formed is a key Lewis acid used in Friedel‑Crafts catalysis and other electrophilic aromatic substitutions.

Type: halogen exchange/oxidative fluorination; purpose: generate cyanogen fluoride (FCN); key transformation: fluorine gas oxidizes cyanide ion to FCN while being reduced to fluoride forming NaF; typical conditions: low temperature (often 0‑25 °C), inert atmosphere, dry solvent such as liquid HF, anhydrous acetonitrile or dichloromethane; no catalyst required.

Selective oxidation of an allylic primary alcohol to an α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde using manganese dioxide. MnO₂ serves as a mild oxidant that removes only the hydroxyl hydrogen without affecting the C=C bond. Reaction is typically carried out at room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or diethyl ether, with excess activated MnO₂.

Type: carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling (peptide bond formation); purpose: synthesize N‑lauroylsarcosine, a fatty‑acid amide surfactant; key transformation: DCC activates lauric acid to an O‑acylurea, DMAP catalyzes nucleophilic attack by the sarcosine amino group to give the amide; by‑product is dicyclohexylurea; typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, dry dichloromethane or DMF, inert nitrogen atmosphere; catalysts: catalytic DMAP, stoichiometric DCC.

Metathesis/acid–base exchange in aqueous solution; lead(II) thiocyanate reacts with nitric acid, replacing the thiocyanate anion with nitrate to give soluble lead(II) nitrate and thiocyanic acid; performed at ambient temperature using water as the medium.

Type: aminolysis of a carbonate (transesterification) to form a carbamate; purpose: prepare N‑hexyl carbamate (urethane); key transformation: hexylamine attacks diethyl carbonate, displaces ethanol and forms the N‑hexyl carbamate; typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous solvent such as toluene, THF or the amine used neat; removal of ethanol (e.g., by distillation) drives the reaction; no additional catalyst required.

Type: acid‑mediated decomposition/metathesis of a metal oxalate; purpose: convert insoluble yttrium oxalate to soluble yttrium trichloride; key transformation: protonation of oxalate releases CO₂ and H₂O, while Y³⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to form YCl₃; typical conditions: aqueous HCl, gentle heating (50‑80 °C) to ensure complete dissolution; performed in water, no additional catalyst.

Ammonia‑lyase (aspartase) reaction; non‑oxidative deamination of L‑aspartic acid. The enzyme L‑aspartase catalyzes the elimination of ammonia from L‑aspartic acid to give fumaric acid. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution (often Tris or phosphate buffer, pH 7.5–8.5) at 25–37 °C, and may require Mg²⁺ or Mn²⁺ as a metal cofactor for optimal activity. No external oxidant or reductant is needed; the transformation is a simple elimination.

Type: Fischer esterification; purpose: produce hexadecyl acetate (a fragrance/solvent ester); key transformation: condensation of hexadecanol with acetic acid, eliminating water to form the ester; typical conditions: reflux with catalytic amount of strong Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH), often in excess acetic acid or an azeotrope‑forming solvent such as toluene; water is removed by azeotropic distillation or a Dean‑Stark trap.

Combination/redox synthesis: elemental chlorine reacts with metallic lithium to form lithium chloride. Lithium is oxidized to Li⁺ and chlorine reduced to Cl⁻, yielding LiCl as a solid salt. Typically carried out in a dry, inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at elevated temperature; often performed in a sealed tube or under vacuum with no solvent, sometimes in dry ether to control the exotherm.

Combustion/solid‑state synthesis of lithium ruthenate: citric acid serves as a fuel, while lithium nitrate provides both lithium and an oxidizing nitrate. Upon heating, the mixture undergoes rapid combustion, releasing CO₂, H₂O, and NO₂ and leaving behind lithium ruthenate as the inorganic product. Conducted in an open crucible or furnace at 800–900 °C in air; no additional solvent needed. Used to prepare Li₂RuO₃ or related Li‑Ru oxides for battery cathodes.

Ester hydrolysis of methyl tetradecanoate; converts the methyl ester into myristic acid and methanol; typically performed by refluxing the ester in aqueous acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or aqueous base (e.g., NaOH) followed by acid work‑up; solvent water or water/MeOH; catalyst acid or base.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis: ethyl acetoacetate reacts with water to give acetoacetic (acetylacetic) acid and ethanol. The carbonyl carbon of the ester is attacked by water, followed by proton transfers and cleavage of the C–O ethoxy bond. Usually performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) under reflux (80–100 °C). Solvent can be water alone or a water‑organic mixture such as water/THF Base‑catalyzed (saponification) conditions are also common, followed by acid.

Acid‑base neutralization of ytterbium hydroxide with nitric acid; purpose is to dissolve the hydroxide and generate soluble Yb(NO3)3. OH– from Yb(OH)3 reacts with H⁺ from HNO3 to give water, and Yb³⁺ is coordinated by nitrate ions. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle warming; water is the medium and no catalyst is required.

Type: Hydride reduction of alkyl halide to alkane. Purpose: replace the iodine with hydrogen, yielding the saturated hydrocarbon. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers a hydride to the carbon bearing iodine, displacing I⁻ and forming a C–H bond; subsequent work‑up gives heptane, Al(OH)₃ and LiI. Typical conditions: dry ethereal solvent (THF, diethyl ether), anhydrous atmosphere (N₂), 0 °C to reflux, careful quench with aqueous acid or water after completion.

Acid‑base neutralization of a metal oxide: mercurous oxide (Hg₂O) reacts with sulfuric acid to form mercurous sulfate (Hg₂SO₄) and water. The basic oxide is protonated, and the sulfate anion pairs with Hg₂²⁺. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or gentle heating, with H₂SO₄. No special solvent beyond water is required.

N‑acetylation (acylation) of methacrylamide: acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to the nitrogen of methacrylamide, producing N‑acetyl‑methacrylamide and acetic acid as by‑product. Reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the amide nitrogen on the anhydride carbonyl. Commonly performed in pyridine or triethylamine as a base/solvent at 0 °C to room temperature; alternative solvents include dichloromethane with catalytic DMAP. Reaction is mild and gives high yields.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 1,1,2,2‑tetrabromoene: molecular hydrogen adds across the carbon–carbon double bond, converting the alkene to the saturated 1,1,2,2‑tetrabromoethane. Requires a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as palladium on carbon (Pd/C), Raney nickel, or platinum oxide, under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at room temperature to 50 °C. Solvent typically ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate. Purpose is to remove unsaturation while retaining bromine substituents.

The reaction involves chlorination of an alkane via free radical halogenation. It is a substitution reaction where chlorine replaces a hydrogen atom in pentane. Initiated by UV light or heat, the mechanism proceeds through radical intermediates. Chlorine gas and pentane react under these conditions, typically in the absence of a solvent, producing 1-chloropentane and hydrogen chloride.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange; replaces the acetate anion of the imidazolium salt with nitrate and generates silver acetate. Typically carried out in aqueous or polar aprotic solvent (e.g., water or MeCN) at room temperature; the insoluble Ag acetate precipitates and is filtered off. No catalyst required.

Oxidative N‑hydroxylation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes acetamidine hydrochloride to N‑hydroxyacetimidine while liberating HCl and water. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 7–9) at 0–25 °C, often with a mild base to neutralize the released HCl. No additional catalyst is usually needed.

Electrophilic addition of halogen; iodine adds across the C=C bond of prop‑1‑ene to give the vicinal 1,2‑diiodopropane. Performed in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at room temperature; the reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Oxidation of primary alcohol to aldehyde. Uses chromium(VI) in acidic medium (sodium dichromate/sulfuric acid) as strong oxidizing agent. Reaction requires temperature control to prevent over-oxidation to carboxylic acid. Fluorine substituent is inert under these conditions, not influencing oxidation pathway. Selectivity achieved by controlling equivalents of oxidant or via distillation of product.

neodymium metal reacts with hydrochloric acid in a single displacement reaction to form neodymium(iii) chloride and hydrogen gas. neodymium is oxidized from 0 to +3, while hydrogen ions (h+) are reduced to h2. this reaction occurs in aqueous hcl, typically at room temperature or with mild heating. no catalyst is required.

Dehydrative chlorination (acid chloride formation); phosphorus pentachloride converts 4‑bromobutyric acid into the corresponding acid chloride (4‑bromobutyryl chloride) with evolution of HCl and formation of POCl₃ as by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous, aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or toluene) under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C to rt. No additional catalyst is required.

Williamson ether synthesis (phenolic O‑methylation); methyl p‑toluenesulfonate acts as a methylating agent for the phenolic hydroxyl of kaempferol in the presence of potassium carbonate, giving kaempferide and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone, reflux under inert atmosphere; K₂CO₃ serves as base, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1) of tert‑butyl alcohol using heated phosphoric acid; performed at 140‑180 °C, water is eliminated to afford isobutylene; typically carried out in a batch reactor or short‑path distillation with the acid acting as both catalyst and medium.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of one hydroxyl group of (2S)‑propane‑1,2‑diol with chloride to give 1‑chloro‑2‑propanol and water. Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) in acidic medium. Typical conditions: conc. HCl (excess) at 0‑100 °C, aqueous phase, reaction time from minutes to a few hours depending on temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed ester, methyl decanoate + water → decanoic acid + methanol. Purpose: obtain the free fatty acid and methanol. Key transformation: ester bond cleavage, RCOOCH₃ → RCOOH + CH₃OH. Typical conditions: reflux with dilute aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl or H₂SO₄) at 80‑100 °C. Solvent: excess water or water/organic co‑solvent; acid acts as catalyst.

Nucleophilic alkylation (SN2) of allylamine by methyl iodide; purpose is to methylate the primary amine to give N‑methyl allylamine while generating HI as by‑product. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or MeCN) at 0 – 25 °C, often with an added base such as Na₂CO₃ or excess amine to neutralize the formed HI.

Aminolysis (ester‑amide exchange) of methyl benzoate with ethylamine; nucleophilic attack of ethylamine on the ester carbonyl displaces methanol, forming N‑ethylbenzamide and methanol; reaction is run with excess ethylamine (liquid or gas) at reflux (≈120 °C) either solvent‑free or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF); removal of methanol drives the equilibrium to completion.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation) of sodium chlorate; redox process that converts chlorate ions to chloride ions and releases molecular oxygen. Performed by heating solid NaClO₃ strongly (≈250–300 °C), in the presence of a catalyst like MnO₂ to lower the onset temperature. No solvent required; reaction occurs in the solid state.

Amidation (condensation) of propiolic acid with ammonia; forms propiolamide and water by direct nucleophilic attack of NH₃ on the carboxyl carbon followed by dehydration. Usually conducted by bubbling gaseous NH₃ through neat acid or a solution in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., toluene) under reflux, or by first converting the acid to an acid chloride (SOCl₂) then reacting with NH₃ at 0 – 25 °C.

SN2 substitution of 2‑(iodomethyl)oxolane with acetate ion; acetate displaces iodide to give 2‑(acetoxymethyl)oxane. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone at 0 – 50 °C. Sodium acetate provides the nucleophile; the formed NaI remains in solution and may be removed by aqueous work‑up.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of 1,4‑dichlorobenzene; nitration introduces a nitro group at the ortho position relative to one chlorine to afford 1,4‑dichloro‑2‑nitrobenzene, with water as the only by‑product. Performed with a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ (mixed acid) at 0 – 50 °C, typically without an external solvent (the substrate acts as solvent) and with careful temperature control to avoid over‑nitration.

Acid‑base proton transfer between acetic acid and potassium nitrite; generates nitrous acid (HNO₂) and potassium acetate. Carried out in aqueous solution at low temperature (0 – °C) to stabilize the transient HNO₂, often under inert atmosphere to prevent its rapid decomposition. No additional catalysts required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 phenoxide alkylation); purpose is to convert 2,6‑dimethylphenol into its methyl ether. Potassium carbonate deprotonates the phenol to give a phenoxide ion, which attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide to form 2,6‑dimethyl anisole and KI. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or DMSO at 50‑80 °C; solid K₂CO₃ serves as the base, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolytic cleavage) of octyl octanoate; purpose is to split the ester into its constituent 1‑octanol and octanoic acid. Key transformation: cleavage of the ester C‑O bond with addition of water, yielding the alcohol and the acid. Typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., 1–2 M HCl or H2SO4), heating at reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours; solvent may be a mixture of water and a water‑miscible organic solvent such as THF or dioxane.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage of an alkene); purpose is to break the exocyclic double bond of 3‑methylenecyclobutane into carbonyl fragments. Ozone adds across the C=C to give an ozonide, which upon reductive work‑up (e.g., dimethyl sulfide or Zn/AcOH) yields formaldehyde from the terminal CH₂ and cyclobutanone from the ring carbon. Conditions: O₃ bubbled through a solution in CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by the chosen work‑up; inert atmosphere optional.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; hydrogen peroxide converts the (2E)-3-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)prop‑2‑enal to the corresponding (E)-3-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)prop‑2‑enoic acid, releasing water; commonly carried out in aqueous or alcoholic medium with a catalytic amount of a metal catalyst such as Na₂WO₄ orO₅·H₂O, at 0‑25 °C to 60 °C.

High‑temperature solid‑state of a metal chalcogenide purpose is to convert lead(II) selenide into leadII) oxide and selenium dioxide. Molecular oxygen oxidizes PbSe, producing PbO and volatile SeO₂. Typical conditions: heating the solid mixture in a furnace under flowing air or O₂ at 300‑600 °C; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Oxidation (hydrogen‑peroxide oxidation of a sulfoxide); upgrades the sulfoxide to the corresponding sulfone. Performed with aqueous H₂O₂ (1–2 equiv) in the presence of a mild acid or a catalytic amount of tungstate or molybdate, at ambient temperature in water or mixed water/acetone; water is formed as the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Hydrolysis/acid‑base reaction of carbonyl sulfide with ammonia; purpose is to ammonium thiocyanate and water. Ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon of O=C=S, followed by proton transfers that give SCN⁻ and NH₄⁺, which combine to form NH₄SCN; water is released. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with excess NH₃; water is the solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) neutralization; purpose is to produce cesium sulfate and liberate ammonia gas from ammonium sulfate. Hydroxide ions from CsOH neutralize NH₄⁺, forming water and releasing NH₃, while Cs⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to give Cs₂SO₄. Performed in aqueous solution at room to ~50 °C; water is the reaction medium.

Oxidative deamination; sodium hypochlorite oxidizes the β‑amino acid (3‑aminopropionic acid, β‑alanine) to the corresponding α‑keto acid (3‑oxopropanoic acid) while releasing ammonia. The reaction proceeds in aqueous NaOCl (household bleach) at 0‑5 °C, pH adjusted to about 9 with NaOH to limit over‑oxidation; the mixture is usually buffered with phosphate and stirred under mild stirring.

Acid‑base exchange; strontium acetate reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce strontium chloride and free acetic acid. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with mild heating to ensure complete ion exchange. No catalyst needed; water serves as the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of cyclohexyl acetate; water (often supplied with H₂SO₄) cleaves the ester to give cyclohexanol and acetic acid; conducted by refluxing the ester in aqueous sulfuric acid or a water‑acid mixture at 80–100 °C; the reaction is driven to completion by excess water and heat.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of anthracene to anthracene‑9,10‑dione (anthraquinone). Anthracene is dissolved in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform and bubbled with ozone at –78 °C to –20 °C. After completion, the reaction mixture is treated with a reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH) or oxidative work‑up (e.g., H₂O₂) to afford the quinone dione. The key transformation is cleavage of the 9,10‑double bond forming two carbonyl groups.

Metathesis/neutralization; aqueous sodium hydroxide reacts with tricalcium phosphate to dissolve the phosphate as trisodium phosphate while precipitating calcium hydroxide. The process is carried out in water at ambient to slightly elevated temperature (20‑50 °C) with vigorous stirring; the solid Ca(OH)₂ can be filtered off, leaving Na₃PO₄ in solution.

Hydrolytic deamination; guanine undergoes aqueous hydrolysis, cleaving the exocyclic amine as ammonia and converting the heterocycle to xanthine. The reaction is facilitated by heating in water (often 80‑100 °C) and may be accelerated by acidic (pH ≈ 4‑5) or basic (pH ≈ 9‑10) conditions; no external catalyst is required.

Peracid oxidation (ene reaction) of α‑terpinene with meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid forming the endoperoxide ascaridole; by‑product m‑chlorobenzoic acid is recovered. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane under inert atmosphere, using stoichiometric m‑CPBA.

Oxidation of a primary benzylic alcohol to the corresponding carboxylate using sodium chlorite. Benzyl alcohol is converted to sodium benzoate with formation of NaCl and water. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 4–5) at ambient temperature, often with catalytic TEMPO; solvent is water or water/acetone mixture.

Hydrolysis of ethyl chloroformate to ethanol, carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride. Water attacks the carbonyl carbon displacing chloride, then the intermediate decomposes to CO₂. Performed in aqueous solution, mild heating (0–50 °C); solvent is water or a water/organic co‑solvent.

N‑chlorination of succinimide with chlorine gas to give N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) and HCl. Reaction is a halogenation on nitrogen, used to prepare NCS as a chlorinating reagent. Carried out in anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., chloroform or carbon tetrachloride) at 0–5 °C under inert atmosphere, with chlorine bubbled through the solution.

Type: metal‑dithiocarbamate precipitation (salt metathesis). Purpose: synthesis of silver diethyldithiocarbamate, often used as a reagent or for analytical precipitation. Key transformation: carbon disulfide reacts with diethylamine in basic medium (NaOH) to form the diethyl dithiocarbamate anion, which then complexes Ag⁺ from AgNO₃ to give the insoluble silver dithiocarbamate, releasing water and NaNO. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, NaOH added to generate the dithiocarbamate, temperature 0 °C to reflux as needed, then AgNO₃ solution added; stir until precipitation completes. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no additional catalyst required.

Type: acid‑base proton transfer (salt exchange). Purpose: conversion of triethylammonium acetate to triethylammonium chloride while liberating acetic acid; useful for preparing the chloride salt or adjusting buffer composition. Key transformation: HCl protonates the acetate anion, forming acetic acid, while the chloride anion pairs with the triethylammonium cation. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stoichiometric amounts, vigorous stirring. Common solvent/catalyst: water; reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); converts insoluble titanium(IV) hydroxide into soluble titanium(IV) sulfate for analytical or synthetic use; hydroxide groups are protonated, yielding titanium(IV) sulfate and water; carried out by stirring Ti(OH)₄ in aqueous concentrated sulfuric acid, often with gentle heating (50‑80 °C); water is the solvent.

Acid–base neutralization of a metal oxide with hydroiodic acid; the oxide is dissolved by aqueous HI, producing soluble scandium(III) iodide and water; commonly carried out by stirring the oxide in excess aqueous HI at room temperature to reflux, using water as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Type: acid dissolution / double‑replacement (acid–base) reaction. Purpose: extraction of oxalic acid from calcium oxalate, with simultaneous formation of soluble calcium chloride. Key transformation: calcium oxalate reacts with excess HCl, the oxalate anion is protonated to oxalic acid, and Ca²⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give CaCl₂. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (conc. 6‑12 M), heating to 60–100 °C to promote dissolution, stirring until solid disappears. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst needed.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation. Silver nitrate exchanges anions with cyclohexylamine hydrochloride, forming insoluble silver chloride precipitate and soluble cyclohexylammonium nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution, often at 0–25 °C to maximize AgCl precipitation; no catalyst needed.

Type: anion‑metathesis (acid–salt exchange). Purpose: preparation of magnesium perchlorate and generation of tetrafluoroboric acid; may be used when a non‑aqueous perchlorate source is required. Key transformation: Mg²⁺ exchanges its BF₄⁻ ligands for ClO₄⁻ from perchloric acid, yielding Mg(ClO₄)₂ and free HBF₄. Typical conditions: anhydrous, non‑protic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, low temperature (0–25 °C) to avoid decomposition, inert atmosphere (N₂). Common solvent/catalyst: dry MeCN; no additional catalyst, but careful exclusion of water.

Type: Ullmann homocoupling (copper‑mediated reductive aryl‑aryl coupling). Purpose: synthesis of 1,1′‑binaphthyl, a building block for chiral ligands and organic materials. Key transformation: copper metal inserts into the C–Br bond of 1‑bromonaphthalene, generating a copper‑aryl intermediate that undergoes reductive elimination to couple two naphthyl units. Typical conditions: copper powder (1–2 equiv), high temperature (200–250 °C), polar aprotic solvent such as N,N‑dimethylformamide (DMF) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), often under nitrogen atmosphere; sometimes a base (K₂CO₃) is added to improve yield. No additional ligands are mandatory, though modern variants may employ catalytic Cu(I) salts with ligands.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis an alkyl halide under basic conditions. Purpose: conversion of sodium 3‑chloropropanoate to sodium 3‑hydroxypropanoate (sodium β‑hydroxypropionate), useful in polymer precursors or as a building block. Key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the carbon bearing the chloride, displacing Cl⁻ and forming the 3‑hydroxypropanoate anion; Na⁺ remains as counter‑ion, producing NaCl as by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution (1–2 equiv), reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h, then cooling and crystallization or isolation of the product. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis; protonation of sulfite to sulfurous acid and formation of soluble silver perchlorate; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst, water as solvent; purpose is salt exchange.

Single‑displacement redox (metal reduction) reaction; sodium metal reduces aluminum(III) iodide to elemental aluminum while forming sodium iodide. Key transformation: AlI3 + 3 Na → Al (solid) + 3 NaI. Typically conducted in molten state or high‑temperature inert atmosphere (e.g., in a sealed tube) because both reagents are solids; no solvent; no catalyst. (If conditions are not well established, description may be uncertain.)

Fischer esterification; converts 2‑methoxybenzoic acid to its methyl ester; key transformation is condensation of carboxylic acid with methanol releasing water; typically refluxed with catalytic sulfuric or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; removal of water (Dean–Stark) shifts equilibrium; common solvent is toluene or excess methanol.

Aldehyde hydration (gem‑diol formation); benzaldehyde adds water under dilute phosphoric acid to give phenylmethanediol equilibrium mixture; reaction proceeds at room temperature in aqueous acid; no catalyst beyond acid; water is both reactant and solvent.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: replace the silver ion with copper(II) to generate copper(II) benzoate and insoluble silver chloride. Key transformation: Ag⁺ exchanges with Cu²⁺, yielding Cu(C₆H₅COO)₂ in solution and a white precipitate of AgCl. Usually performed in water at room temperature or with mild heating; no catalyst required.

Radical halogen exchange; iodine reacts with dichlorofluoromethane to replace a chlorine atom, yielding iodine monochloride and chlorofluoroiodomethane; typically initiated by UV light or heat; carried out in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride; purpose is synthesis of organoiodide.

Halogen‑silane exchange (chlorination of trimethylsilane); chlorine gas attacks the Si–H bond of trimethylsilane, producing trimethylsilyl chloride and hydrogen chloride; performed under dry, inert atmosphere, often in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0–25 °C; no catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (O‑methylation); potassium carbonate deprotonates the phenolic OH of 6‑hydroxy‑7‑methoxy‑2H‑1‑benzopyran‑2‑one, which then attacks methyl iodide to give 6,7‑dimethoxy‑2H‑1‑benzopyran‑2‑one; typical conditions are reflux in acetone or DMF with K2CO3; by‑product KI formed.

0.ytic hydrogenolysis of a benzyl phenyl carbonate using H2 and Pd/C; purpose is to cleave the carbonate protecting group to liberate benzyl alcohol and phenol. Key transformation: carbonate O–C bond reduction to give two phenolic alcohols. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, 5 % Pd on carbon (0.05–0.1 eq), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, 25–60 °C, with stirring until gas uptake ceases.

Type: Strong reduction of an ester with lithium aluminium hydride. Purpose: Convert the ester carbonyl into a primary alcohol and release the alkoxy fragment as ethanol. Key transformation: C=O of ethyl 2‑methylbutanoate is reduced to CH2OH, forming 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol; the ethoxy group is protonated to give ethanol. Typical conditions: Anhydrous ether (dry THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C addition followed by reflux; excess LiAlH4 is used, then quenched cautiously with water or a dilute acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of ethylene glycol with methyl bromide to form 2‑methoxyethanol and HBr. The primary hydroxyl attacks the methyl carbon, displacingide. Usually performed in an aprotic polar solvent (acetone or DMF) with an inorganic base (K2CO3, NaHCO3, or NaOH) to scavenge HBr; temperature 40–80 °C under reflux; reaction is moisture‑sensitive and often run under nitrogen.

Electrophilic chlorination of theophylline at C‑8 using sodium N‑chloro‑p‑toluenesulfonamide (a mild chlorinating agent). The N‑Cl bond delivers Cl⁺ to the C‑8 position, giving 8‑chlorotheophylline; p‑toluenesulfonic acid is generated as by‑product. Typical conditions: dissolve theophylline in anhydrous acetonitrile or dimethylformamide, add the chlorinating reagent at 0 °C to room temperature, stir 1–3 h; no metal catalyst required.

Selenium dioxide oxidation of anthracene to anthracene‑9‑boxaldehyde; SeO₂ acts as an oxidant delivering oxygen to the benzylic (9‑position) carbon, producing the aldehyde and elemental selenium precipitate. Commonly carried out in refluxing 1,4‑dioxane, toluene, or ethanol (0.5–1 M) at 80–120 °C for several hours; sometimes a catalytic amount of acetic acid is added to improve solubility. The reaction is a classic SeO₂‑mediated allylic/benzylic oxidation.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification): acetyl 2‑hydroxypropanoate is cleaved by aqueous NaOH, converting the acetyl ester into sodium acetate while the 2‑hydroxypropanoate portion becomes sodium lactate; typical condition is NaOH (1–2 equiv) in water (or water/ethanol) under reflux, followed by neutralization.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation between potassium carbonate and barium sulfite forming insoluble barium carbonate and soluble potassium sulfite. Reaction is carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at ambient temperature with stirring; the BaCO₃ precipitate is filtered and washed. No special catalyst or heating is required.

Acid‑base dissolution of zinc phosphate; purpose is to convert insoluble zinc phosphate into soluble zinc sulfate and to liberate phosphoric acid. The solid Zn₃(PO₄)₂ is treated with aqueous sulfuric acid (conc. or 1‑6 M) and heated gently (50‑80 °C) to ensure complete reaction: Zn₃(PO₄)₂ + 3 H₂SO₄ → 3 ZnSO₄ + 2 H₃PO₄. The mixture remains aqueous; the zinc sulfate stays in solution, and phosphoric acid can be isolated by evaporation or further processing.
