Sulfide formation (solid‑state synthesis); tungsten metal combines with sulfur vapor to afford tungsten disulfide (WS₂), a layered semiconductor material; produced by heating tungsten with sulfur vapor at 700–900 °C in an inert (argon) atmosphere, often in a sealed quartz tube; no solvent.

Direct combination (halogenation) synthesis; elemental titanium reacts with iodine vapor to form titanium(IV) iodide (TiI₄); requires heating titanium (200–400 °C) under a stream of iodine in an inert atmosphere (argon); no solvent or catalyst is needed, product sublimes and is collected by condensation.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling (DCC coupling) of acetic acid with tert‑butylamine; activates the carboxyl group to form an O‑acylurea intermediate that is attacked by the amine, giving N‑tert‑butylacetamide and dicyclohexylurea as the by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or DMF, at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; DCC is the coupling reagent/catalyst.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride (hydrohalogenation) to 1‑heptene; follows Markovnikov regioselectivity, adding H to the terminal carbon and Cl to the adjacent carbon to afford 2‑chloroheptane (commonly named 1,2‑chloroheptane). Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic HCl at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no additional catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of a benzylic alcohol to a benzoic acid using hydrogen peroxide in basic aqueous medium. Type: base‑mediated oxidation. Purpose: converts 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzyl alcohol into the corresponding carboxylic acid. Key transformation: primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid via H₂O₂/NaOH. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), 30 % H₂O₂ added dropwise at 0 °C then warmed to 50–80 °C; reaction time 1–4 h. Common solvent: water, often with a co‑solvent such as THF or MeCN.

Base‑mediated C‑alkylation of a β‑diketone; purpose is to install a methyl group at the α‑position relative to one carbonyl. The 1,3‑cyclohexanedione is first deprotonated to form the enolate (commonly using NaH, K₂CO₃ or NaOEt) and then reacts with methyl iodide via an SN2 pathway, giving 5‑methyl‑1,3‑cyclohexanedione and HI. Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or THF, ambient to reflux temperature, inert atmosphere; the base neutralizes the generated HI.

Catalytic hydrogenation of acetylene to ethane. Type: heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenation (alkyne → alkane). Purpose: fully reduce the triple bond. Key transformation: C≡C → C–C with addition of two equivalents of H₂. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–10 atm, catalyst Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni; temperature 0–50 °C; solvent ethanol or methanol. Reaction proceeds rapidly under mild conditions.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) of zinc fluoride with sodium hydroxide, precipitating zinc hydroxide and forming sodium fluoride in solution; performed in aqueous NaOH at room temperature; purpose is conversion of the fluoride to the corresponding hydroxide or removal of fluoride ions.

Condensation of imidazole with carbonyl fluoride to give 1,1′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) with release of HF. Type: dehydration/condensation reaction forming a carbamoyl linkage. Purpose: preparation of CDI, a common coupling reagent. Key transformation: carbonyl fluoride + 2 imidazole → CDI + 2 HF. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; by‑product HF is scavenged by a base (e.g., pyridine). No additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of a metal halide; aqueous scand(III) iodide reacts with water, partially reverting to insoluble scandium(III) hydroxide and regenerating hydroiodic acid; usually observed when an aqueous solution of the iodide is diluted or heated, leading to precipitation of the hydroxide; water is the medium, no catalyst.

Oxidative homocoupling of quinoline to 2,2′‑biquinoline mediated by copper(II) acetate under oxygen. Type: metal‑catalyzed oxidative C–C coupling. Purpose: synthesize biquinoline ligands. Key transformation: two quinoline units join at the 2‑positions, Cu(OAc)₂ is reduced to Cu(OAc) (Cu(I)). Typical conditions: quinoline (excess) with Cu(OAc)₂ (10–20 mol %), reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene, DMF or DMSO, under an O₂ atmosphere (balloon or flow), temperature 120–150 °C, 12–24 h. No extra ligand usually required.

Hydrogenolysis of 2‑azidopyridine to 2‑aminopyridine using palladium on carbon. Type: catalytic hydrogen reduction of azide. Purpose: convert azide functional group to primary amine. Key transformation: –N₃ → –NH₂ with H₂. Typical conditions: Pd/C (5 wt %), H₂ 1 atm (or 10 psi), solvent methanol or ethanol, ambient temperature or gentle warming (20–40 °C), reaction time 1–3 h. Product isolated by filtration of catalyst and concentration.

Type: Redox (sulfite reduction of ferricyanide). Purpose: convert ferricyanide to ferrocyanide. Key transformation: sulfite ion (SO₃²⁻) reduces Fe(III) in K₃[Fe(CN)₆] to Fe(II) in K₄[Fe(CN)₆]; sulfite is oxidized to sulfate (SO₄²⁻). Typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, neutral to slightly acidic pH; no catalyst required.

Phenolic acetylation (esterification). The phenolic hydroxyl of 2,5‑dichlorophenol attacks acetic anhydride, substituting an acetate group to give 2,5‑dichlorophenyl acetate and acetic acid as by‑product. Usually performed neat with acetic anhydride or in pyridine/CH₂Cl₂ as solvent, optionally catalyzed by DMAP or pyridine, and heated to reflux (≈80‑110 °C) for 1‑2 h.

Acid‑base addition of CO₂ to rubidium hydride forming rubidium formate. Type: salt formation / hydride insertion into CO₂. Purpose: generate the metal formate salt. Key transformation: RbH + CO₂ → RbOCHO. Typical conditions: performed in dry THF or ether under inert atmosphere (argon), low temperature (0 °C) to control exotherm, then warmed to room temperature; solid product isolated by evaporation of solvent. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of calcium carbonate with gluconic acid forming calcium gluconate, carbon dioxide and water; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; CO₂ evolution drives the reaction forward; no catalyst required; stirring and gentle heating improve dissolution of the carbonate.

Acid–base double displacement; aqueous HCl protonates strontium chromate, converting the chromate to chromic acid (H2CrO4) and forming soluble strontium chloride; typically performed in water at ambient to mild heating, no catalyst required.
Halogenation; yields uranium tetrachloride, a precursor for uranium chemistry. Uranium metal is passed through dry Cl2 gas at 300‑400 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst.

Dehydrative phosphorylation (nucleoph substitution) of ethanol with phosphorus oxychloride to afford triethyl phosphate and gaseous HCl; typically carried out under reflux in an aprotic solvent (e.g., pyridine or dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of ethyl p‑hydroxybenzoate with aqueous HCl to regenerate p‑hydroduct p‑hydroxybenzoic acid and ethanol; typical conditions are reflux in a mixture of water and a strong acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) for several hours; solvent is water or aqueous ethanol.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of allyl bromide with sodium acetate to form allyl acetate and sodium bromide. Usually run in acetone, DMF, or ethanol at reflux or 50–80 °C; acetate ion serves as nucleophile, no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of an alkoxysilane to a silanol; methylethoxysilane reacts with water (often in a biphasic water/organic mixture or neat water) at ambient or mild heat to give methylsilanol and ethanol, cleaving the Si–OEt bond without added catalyst.

Gem-diol formation (hydration) of acetaldehyde; reversible addition of water across the carbonyl to give 1,1‑ethanediol; generally proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; equilibrium can be shifted toward the diol with excess water or mild acid/base catalyst; water is both reagent and solvent.

Oxidation of fluorene to fluorenone using peroxyacetic acid (a peracid); proceeds via peracid-mediated insertion of an oxygen atom at the benzylic position; commonly conducted in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, no additional catalyst needed.

SN2 cyanation of a primary alkyl bromide with sodium cyanide to afford propanenitrile; performed in aqueous or polar aprotic solvent (e.g., water, ethanol, or DMF) at 50–80 °C; excess NaCN improves yield; sodium bromide is formed; no catalyst required.

Cyanohydrin formation; addition of hydrogen cyanide to 2‑methylbutanal generates 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylbutanenitrile. The carbonyl carbon receives a cyanide ion (CN⁻) while the oxygen is protonated to give an OH group. Conducted at 0–25 °C in aqueous or alcoholic solvent (e.g., water or ethanol) using NaCN/HCl or dilute HCN gas; the reaction is base‑ or mildly acidic to maintain cyanide nucleophilicity and is typically stopped when completion is indicated by TLC.

Oxidation of phenylglyoxal with hydrogen peroxide to phenylglyoxylic acid; aldehyde oxidized to carboxylic acid; commonly performed in aqueous 30 % H₂O₂ with a catalytic amount of FeSO₄ or tungstate under mildly acidic conditions (pH 2‑3) at 0‑25 °C.

Acid–base reaction of erbium(III) carbonate with acetic acid, yielding erbium(III) acetate with evolution of carbon dioxide and water; performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution with gentle heating to drive off CO2; no catalyst required.

Acid–base reaction (salt metathesis); protonation of sulfide ion releases hydrogen sulfide gas; K2S dissolved in water reacts with aqueous HCl to give aqueous KCl and H2S gas; performed at ambient temperature, typically in aqueous solution, no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium sulfite. Heating ammonium sulfite (≈100–150 °C) causes it to break down to ammonia, sulfur dioxide and water: (NH₄)₂SO₃ → 2 NH₃ ↑ + SO₂ ↑ + H₂O. The reaction is carried out in a dry flask or under inert gas; no solvent or catalyst is needed. Useful for generating SO₂ gas or removing sulfite residues.

Electrophilic aromatic alkylation (Friedel‑Crafts alkylation) of phenol with isobutylene to give 2,6‑di‑tert‑butylphenol; catalyzed by a strong Lewis or Brønsted acid (e.g., AlCl₃, H₂SO₄, or HF·BF₃), typically in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as nitrobenzene or chloroform at 0–50 °C.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid (chromium(VI) oxidation); phenylacetaldehyde is oxidized by potassium dichromate in concentrated H₂SO₄ to phenylacetic acid, producing Cr³⁺ (as chromium(III) sulfate) and water; performed under reflux in aqueous sulfuric acid, typically with the aldehyde added portionwise to control exotherm.

Acid‑base (salt metathesis/neutralization); purpose: generate the sodium carboxylate and free ammonia; key transformation: ammonium hexanoate + NaOH → sodium hexanoate + NH₃↑ + H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, stoichiometric amounts; common solvent: water; no catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration using nitronium tetrafluoroborate; biphenyl is treated with NO₂⁺ BF₄⁻ in anhydrous dichloromethane or nitromethane at 0 °C to room temperature. The nitronium ion adds to the aromatic ring, yielding nitrobiphenyl; boron trifluoride and hydrogen fluoride are generated as by‑products. Reaction performed under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an α‑bromo acid with silver nitrite; purpose is to convert 2‑bromoacetic acid into the corresponding α‑nitroacid. The nitrite ion attacks the carbon bearing bromine, displacing Br⁻ which precipitates as AgBr, driving the equilibrium. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or ethanol; silver nitrite serves both nucleophile and precipitating agent, no additional catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of zinc chlorate; purpose is to generate oxygen gas and zinc chloride. Upon strong heating (≈250–300 °C) the solid Zn(ClO₃)₂ breaks down to ZnCl₂ and 3 O₂. The reaction is performed in the absence of solvent, often in a quartz tube or furnace under an inert atmosphere to collect the liberated O₂; no catalyst is needed.

Salt formation (Lewis acid–base reaction); LiF reacts with BF₃ to generate the tetrafluoroborate salt LiBF₄. Usually performed under anhydrous conditions in aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile, dichloromethane or THF; no catalyst required.

Acid‑promoted protonolysis of a Si–C bond; tert‑butyl(trimethyl)silane reacts with hydrogen chloride, cleaving the Si–C bond to release isobutane (2‑methylpropane) and generating chlorotrimethylsilane. Usually carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to rt, using gaseous or aqueous HCl.

Acid–base neutralization forming a salt; purpose is to generate the ionic solid ethanolammonium formate. Formic acid protonates the amine group of ethanolamine, giving the ethanolammonium cation and formate anion. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in a protic solvent such as water or ethanol; no catalyst is needed.

Thermal decomposition of a perchlorate salt; heating rubidium perchlorate induces loss of oxygen to give rubidium chloride and O2 gas. The reaction requires high temperature (≈400–500 °C) in a sealed or flow‑through vessel; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Oxidation of 1H‑benzotriazole with peracetic acid; purpose is to install an N‑oxide functionality on the benzotriazole ring. Peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the nitrogen, yielding benzotriazole N‑oxide and acetic acid as by‑product. Typically carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent like dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature; the peracid itself acts as the oxidant, no additional catalyst required.

Copper‑catalyzed cyanation (SN2′/allylic substitution) of 1‑bromo‑2‑methylprop‑1‑ene; purpose is to convert the allylic bromide into methacrylonitrile. CuCN supplies cyanide ion, which attacks the allylic carbon, displacing bromide and forming the nitrile group. Reaction is performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, generally heated to 80–100 °C under inert atmosphere. Copper(I) cyanide serves both as cyanide source and as Lewis‑acid promoter; no further catalyst is required.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation; purpose is to introduce a sulfonic acid group onto benzene to form benzenesulfonic acid. The sulfur trioxide acts as the electrophile, attacking the aromatic ring in an EAS mechanism. Typical conditions: reaction performed at 0‑50 °C, often in fuming sulfuric acid (oleum) or neat SO₃; no additional solvent required. The mixture is quenched with water to precipitate the sulfonic acid.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction; aqueous sodium bromide reacts with lead(II) nitrate yielding insoluble lead(II) bromide precipitate and soluble sodium nitrate; employed to isolate PbBr₂ or to remove bromide ions; performed by mixing aqueous solutions at room temperature with stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed; no catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction. Ammonium nitrate forms as a byproduct while copper arsenate precipitates from aqueous solutions of the reactants. No catalyst or specific conditions required beyond mixing the salts.

High‑temperature metallothermic reduction (redox) of V₂O₅ with lithium metal; purpose is to produce metallic vanadium and lithium oxide; Li reduces V⁵⁺ to V⁰ while being oxidized to Li₂O; conducted under inert atmosphere (Ar or N₂) at 1000 °C or higher; solid‑state reaction, typically in a sealed crucible; no catalyst, solid reagents only.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev oxidation) of the C=C bond in acrylamide; converts the alkene to an epoxide (glycidamide) while the peroxyacetic acid is reduced to acetic acid; reaction proceeds via a concerted transfer of an oxygen atom; usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0‑25 °C; stoichiometric peroxyacetic acid, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base deprotonation (alkoxide formation); sodium hydroxide abstracts a proton from ethanol, yielding sodium ethoxide and water; serves to generate the nucleophilic ethoxide ion for further reactions; performed in anhydrous ethanol or other polar aprotic solvent; mild heating may be applied, but no catalyst is needed.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction between ammonium hydroxide and manganese(II) sulfate; manganese(II) is converted to insoluble Mn(OH)₂ precipitate while ammonium sulfate remains dissolved; used to remove Mn²⁺ from solution or to prepare Mn(OH)₂; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; simple stirring, no catalyst.

Lithium‑halogen exchange followed by carboxylation (n‑BuLi mediated organolithium formation); n‑BuLi converts 1‑bromo‑2‑ethoxybenzene to the corresponding aryllithium, which then adds CO₂ to give the lithium carboxylate that on acidic work‑up affords 2‑ethoxybenzoic acid; typical conditions: dry THF, -78 °C to 0 °C under inert gas (N₂ or Ar); quench with dilute acid; no additional catalyst.

Jones oxidation (chromium(VI) oxidation) of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid. 2‑Methylbutanal is converted to 2‑methylbutanoic acid by treatment with a solution of CrO₃ in dilute H₂SO₄ (Jones reagent) in acetone, typically at 0 °C to room temperature. The reaction is quenched with isopropanol or methanol and the acid isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (anhydride amidation). Used to synthesize N‑propylbenzamide. n‑Propylamine attacks one carbonyl of benzoyl anhydride, displacing benzoate which picks up a proton to give benzoic acid. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; often a base (e.g., triethylamine) is added to neutralize the generated acid and improve yield.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of benzylic C–N bonds; used to remove benzyl protecting groups from nitrogen atoms. Hydrogen gas and 10 % Pd/C reduce 1,4‑dibenzylpiperazine, cleaving the N‑CH₂Ph linkages to give piperazine and toluene. Typical conditions: H₂ (1–3 atm) in ethanol or methanol at rt to reflux; Pd/C as catalyst, inert atmosphere.

Intramolecular dehydration cyclization of creatine to cyclocreatine; forms a cyclic amidine ring with loss of one molecule of water. Usually carried out under acidic or thermal dehydration conditions (e.g., concentrated HCl or heating at 150–200 °C), sometimes with a Dean–Stark trap to remove water. Solvent can be aqueous acid or refluxing toluene; no external catalyst required.

Carbodiimide‑mediated cyclization of 2‑aminobenzoic acid to a benzoxazin‑2,4‑dione; 1,1′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) activates the carboxyl group, releasing two equivalents of imidazole and allowing the ortho‑amine to attack, forming the cyclic 2H‑1,3‑benzoxazine‑2,4‑dione. Conducted in dry aprotic solvents such as THF, DMF or dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; CDI is the reagent/coupling agent.

Simple acid–base proton transfer; sodium tert‑butoxide deprotonates imidazole, generating sodium imidazolate and tert‑butanol. Performed in aprotic solvents (THF, DMF, DMSO) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed α‑iodination of acetone (electrophilic halogenation). Iodine in the presence of aqueous HCl generates electrophilic I⁺, which substitutes the α‑hydrogen of acetone to give 1‑iodopropan‑2‑one and hydrogen iodide as by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl/I₂ mixture, sometimes with a polar solvent (acetone itself) as both reactant and medium.

Strong‑base‑induced E2 dehydrofluorination of 2‑fluorobutane; potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen, eliminating HF to afford 2‑butene, while the base is protonated to tert‑butanol and the fluoride ion forms KF. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to rt; no metal catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of disilene to disilane; disilene reacts with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) in the presence of a transition‑metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ or Wilkinson’s catalyst, often in an inert solvent like ether or THF at 20‑100 °C, adding hydrogen across the Si=Si bond to give Si₂H₆; purpose is to saturate the silicon double bond.

Titanium tetrachloride‑catalyzed polyene cyclization of geranylgeraniol to sclareol; a Lewis‑acid mediated cationic cyclization that converts the linear diterpene into the bicyclic diterpene sclareol. Typically run under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform, at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen atmosphere. TiCl₄ (0.1–1 equiv) is added dropwise, the mixture is stirred, then quenched with aqueous NaHCO₃; the product is isolated by extraction and chromatography.

Catalytic hydrogenation (azide reduction); hydrogen gas over palladium on carbon converts the azide group of methyl 2‑azidopropanoate to a primary amine, preserving the methyl ester to give methyl 2‑aminopropanoate. Common conditions: H2 (1–3 atm), 5–10 % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, rt to 50 °C.
Single displacement reaction; extraction of elemental molybdenum via metallic reduction; highly exothermic, performed at high temperatures (e.g., molten state); solvent-free conditions.

DMTMM‑mediated esterification of caffeic acid with phenethyl alcohol to give caffeic‑phenethyl ester. The triazine‑based coupling reagent activates the carboxylic acid, allowing nucleophilic attack by the alcohol under mild, neutral conditions. Usually performed in a mixed solvent (e.g., acetonitrile/water or DMF) at room temperature for 1–4 h. No additional base is required; after completion the mixture is diluted, extracted, and the ester is purified by chromatography.

Hofmann elimination of tributyl(ethyl)ammonium bromide with aqueous sodium hydroxide to produce ethene, tributylamine and sodium bromide. Strong base abstracts a β‑hydrogen from the ethyl group, yielding the least substituted alkene (ethene) and the tertiary amine. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (≈1 M) at elevated temperature (80–120 °C) for several hours. After cooling, the organic amine is extracted, while inorganic salts remain in the aqueous layer.

General type: dehydration of an oxime to a nitrile (oxime‑to‑nitrile conversion). Purpose: generate the aromatic nitrile from the corresponding oxime. Key transformation: removal of water from the oxime, forming a C≡N triple bond to give 2‑methoxybenzonitrile. Typical conditions: strong dehydrating agents such as phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃), phosphorus pentoxide (P₂O₅), or thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, toluene) at 0 °C to reflux, often in the presence of a base (triethylamine) to neutralize generated HCl. Alternative milder conditions use ZnCl₂ with acetic acid.

Acid–base neutralization of gallium(III) hydroxide with hydrofluoric acid; hydroxide is replaced by fluoride to give gallium(III) fluoride and water; carried out in aqueous HF solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization between hydrobromic acid and benzyltrimethylammonium hydroxide to afford benzyltrimethylammonium bromide and water. Simple proton transfer reaction performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature. The resulting quaternary ammonium bromide can be isolated by evaporation of the solvent or by precipitation with an anti‑solvent such as ethanol.

Chlorination of zirconium phosphide with chlorine gas to give phosphorus trichloride and zirconium tetrachloride. This redox halogenation oxidizes the phosphide to PCl₃ while converting Zr to ZrCl₄. Typically carried out in a sealed reactor at elevated temperature (200–300 °C) under a flow of Cl₂; gaseous products are condensed, and the metal chloride is collected as a solid or by sublimation. Inert‑gas handling is required due to the corrosive nature of Cl₂ and the.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation of cadmium hydroxide from cadmium bromide and ammonium hydroxide. Cadmium ions react with OH⁻ to form insoluble Cd(OH)₂, while NH₄⁺ pairs with Br⁻ to give soluble NH₄Br. Performed at room temperature in water; the cadmium hydroxide precipitate is filtered, washed, and dried, and the ammonium bromide remains in the filtrate.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis of a tertiary alkyl halide (SN1). Sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes tert‑ tert‑butyl carbocation that captures water to give tert‑butyl alcohol; NaI is the salt by‑product. Conducted in aqueous ethanol or water, often refluxed to ensure complete conversion.

Reductive conversion of nitrobenzene to aniline using hydrazine as the reductant. Reaction type: nitro‑group reduction (hydrazine reduction). Purpose: synthesis of aniline from a nitro aromatic. Key transformation: –NO₂ group is reduced to –NH₂ while hydrazine is oxidized to N₂ and H₂O. Typical conditions: reflux in ethanol or water, often with a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Cu, or Fe to accelerate the reduction. Common solvent: ethanol or aqueous ethanol.

Direct combination (synthesis) oxidation‑reduction; elemental vanadium reacts with fluorine gas to form vanadium(III) fluoride (V + 3/2 F2 → VF3); typically carried out in an inert, dry reactor at controlled temperature (often 200–400 °C) to limit higher oxidation states; no solvent, fluorine gas is the reagent.

Acid‑mediated decomposition of calcium bisulfite to release sulfur dioxide. Reaction type: acid‑base reaction with gas evolution (SO₂). Purpose: generate SO₂ gas and form calcium sulfate as a by‑product. Key transformation: bisulfite ion is protonated, yielding SO₂ and water; calcium combines with sulfate to give CaSO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no heating required. Solvent: water.

Strong oxidative oxidation of an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding benzoic acid; KMnO₄ in alkaline aqueous solution oxidizes the aldehyde carbon of 2,4‑dimethoxybenzaldehyde to a carboxyl group, yielding 2,4‑dimethoxybenzoic acid; reaction run under reflux (≈80–100 °C) with NaOH or K₂CO₃ as base, followed by acid work‑up (HCl) to precipitate the acid; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement (precipitation) reaction; potassium fumarate exchanges cations with calcium chloride to give insoluble calcium fumarate and soluble potassium chloride. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; the calcium salt precipitates and is filtered off.

Hydrolysis of 2‑aminopropanamide to 2‑aminopropanoic acid (alanine) with release of ammonia. Reaction type: amide hydrolysis (acidic or basic). Purpose: convert an amide into the corresponding α‑amino acid. Key transformation: cleavage of the C(=O)–NH₂ bond, yielding a carboxylic acid and NH₃. Typical conditions: heating in aqueous HCl (acidic) or NaOH (basic) followed by neutralization. Solvent: water.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of methyl hexanoate to sodium hexanoate and methanol. Hydroxide ion attacks the ester carbonyl, forming the carboxylate salt and methanol. Performed in aqueous NaOH (or NaOH in methanol/water) at reflux; after completion the mixture may be acidified to isolate the free acid if desired. No additional catalyst is needed.

Chlorination of molybdenum disilicide to give silicon tetrachloride and molybdenum pentachloride. Reaction type: high‑temperature gas‑solid halogenation. Purpose: synthesis of SiCl₄ and MoCl₅ from a refractory silicide. Key transformation: Si–Mo bonds are broken; silicon is converted to SiCl₄ and molybdenum to MoCl₅. Typical conditions: Cl₂ gas passed over MoSi₂ at 500–800 °C in a sealed reactor or flow tube, under inert atmosphere. No solvent (gas‑solid reaction).

Reduction of pyridine N‑oxide to pyridine with lithium aluminum hydride. Reaction type: N‑oxide reduction (deoxygenation). Purpose: regenerate the parent heterocycle from its N‑oxide. Key transformation: the N–O bond is cleaved; O is removed as water while LiAlH₄ supplies hydride. Typical conditions: LiAlH₄ in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen or argon. Common solvent: dry ether (THF or Et₂O).

Acid-catalyzed methanolysis (esterification) of prop-2-ynamide; purpose is to convert the amide into methyl prop-2-ynoate and release ammonia; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl of the amide followed by elimination of NH3; typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol with catalytic sulfuric acid (1–5 %); methanol serves as both reagent and solvent.

Acid–salt metathesis (double displacement); used to exchange anions between silver nitrate and nitrous acid, producing soluble silver nitrite and nitric acid; key transformation: Ag⁺ swaps from NO₃⁻ to NO₂⁻ while H⁺ swaps from NO₂⁻ to NO₃⁻; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Acid–base double displacement producing an oxidizing acid; calcium bromate reacts with sulfuric acid to generate bromic acid and precipitate calcium sulfate; key transformation: BrO₃⁻ pairs with H⁺ to form HBrO₃ while Ca²⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to form CaSO₄(s); usually carried out in water with stirring, often at mild heating to ensure complete reaction and precipitation; no catalyst needed; CaSO₄ precipitates and is filtered off.

Direct chlorination (oxidative halogenation) of a metal‑arsenide; cadmium arsenide is exposed to chlorine gas, yielding arsenic trichloride and cadmium chloride; key transformation: each As atom is oxidized to AsCl₃ and each Cd atom forms CdCl₂; reaction is conducted in the gas phase or in a sealed tube, typically at elevated temperature (150–300 °C) under an inert atmosphere to prevent side reactions; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Precipitation/sulfide generation for cadmium sulfide synthesis; thioacetamide decomposes under heat in aqueous solution to release sulfide ion, which reacts with cadmium chloride to form insoluble CdS while producing acetamide and HCl; key transformation: CH₃C(S)NH₂ → CH₃CONH₂ + S²⁻ (as H₂S under acidic conditions) then Cd²⁺ + S²⁻ → CdS(s); performed in water (often with gentle heating 60–80 °C) and sometimes buffered to pH ≈ 7–8; no external catalyst required.

Acid-catalyzed ring-opening of an epoxide. Hydrogen chloride opens the glycidol epoxide to form 2-chloro-1-propanol. Typically occurs under mild acidic conditions in aqueous solution. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of chloride at the less hindered epoxide carbon.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution forming an isopropyl chloroformate; sodium isopropoxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of phosgene, displacing one chloride and forming isopropyl chloroformate while generating sodium chloride; key transformation: COCl₂ + NaOCH(CH₃)₂ → ClCOOCH(CH₃)₂ + NaCl; carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dry THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst, but low temperature helps control side reactions.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is anion exchange to isolate insoluble silver bromide. In aqueous solution at room temperature, AgSCN reacts with KBr forming a white AgBr precipitate and soluble KSCN; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Bechamp reduction of a nitro group; used to transform 3‑nitrobenzyl alcohol into 3‑aminobenzyl alcohol; elemental iron reduces the nitro group to an amine while being oxidized to Fe³⁺, which complexes chloride from HCl to give FeCl₃; the reaction also produces water; carried out in aqueous hydrochloric acid, usually refluxing (60‑100 °C) with excess iron powder; the mixture is a simple aqueous HCl solution, no organic solvent required.

Acid–base double displacement (precipitation) reaction; sulfuric acid protonates lead acetate, forming insoluble lead(II) sulfate precipitate and releasing acetic acid; performed in aqueous solution, typically at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Selective aldehyde reduction with sodium borohydride; purpose is to convert the aldehydic C‑1 of 2‑deoxy‑D‑glucose to a primary alcohol, yielding 2‑deoxy‑D‑sorbitol (a sugar alcohol); key transformation is hydride delivery to the carbonyl carbon forming a new C‑H bond; commonly performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, often under nitrogen; no additional catalyst is needed.

Thermal decarboxylative decomposition; heating mesoxalic acid causes loss of one carbon dioxide molecule, forming oxalic acid. The reaction proceeds via cleavage of the central carbonyl–carbon bond. Usually performed by heating the solid or aqueous solution of mesoxalic acid to 150–250 °C, often under reduced pressure to drive off CO₂. No additional reagents or catalysts are required.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; hydrochloric acid generates nitrous acid from sodium nitrite, which nitrosates 2‑methylpiperidine hydrochloride to give N‑nitroso‑2‑methylpiperidine; carried out in cold aqueous HCl (0‑5 °C) to control side reactions; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑induced decomposition/precipitation of a metal oxo‑salt; concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with sodium niobate, producing niobium(V) oxide (Nb₂O₅) as a solid and sodium sulfate in water; usually heated under reflux; no additional catalyst.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction in solution; copper(II) nitrate exchanges anions with sodium tetrafluoroborate to afford copper(II) tetrafluoroborate and sodium nitrate; conducted in aqueous or polar organic solvent (e.g., water or methanol) at room temperature; no catalyst.

Acid chlorination of a refractory oxide; gaseous or aqueous hydrogen chloride reacts with hafnium dioxide at elevated temperature to give volatile hafnium tetrachloride and water; performed in a dry HCl stream or hot concentrated HCl (≈250 °C); no catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an isocyanate; methyl isocyanate reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide and methylamine hydrochloride; carried out at moderate temperature in water/HCl solution; no additional catalyst.

Type: Chlorination / silyl chloride synthesis. Purpose: Generate trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) in situ for silylation reactions. Key transformations: Oxalyl chloride reacts with trimethylsilanol, releasing CO and CO₂ gases and HCl while substituting the hydroxyl group with chlorine to give TMSCl. Conditions: Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere. Solvent/catalyst: Anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform; no added catalyst required.

Type: Base‑promoted ether formation (Williamson ether synthesis) via SN2 substitution. Purpose: Couple two 3‑chloro‑1‑propanol units to afford a diol ether. Key transformations: Hydroxide deprotonates 3‑chloro‑1‑propanol to generate an alkoxide, which displaces chloride on a second molecule, forming 3,3′‑dihydroxydipropyl ether and NaCl; water is a by‑product. Conditions: Reflux in aqueous NaOH, often with ethanol or water as the reaction medium; reaction time 1–4 h. Solvent/catalyst: Aqueous NaOH (base); no additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation; indium(III) sulfate solution is added to sodium phosphate solution, forming insoluble indium(III) phosphate precipitate and sodium sulfate in the filtrate; carried out in water, often at neutral to slightly acidic pH to control phosphate speciation, ambient temperature, stirring; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic addition of HBr to the alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑butene (Markovnikov addition) producing 2‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or CCl₄ at 0 °C to rt, no catalyst needed.

Hydrolytic decarboxylation of a cyclic carbonate. Water attacks the carbonyl of glycerol carbonate, opening the ring; subsequent collapse releases CO₂ and regenerates glycerol. Carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) at 80–120 °C; sometimes a solid acid catalyst such as Amberlyst‑15 is used. Purpose: recycle glycerol carbonate back to glycerol while generating carbon dioxide.

Type: Oxidative conversion of a benzylic‑type methyl group to an aldehyde (Oxone oxidation). Purpose: Transform 2‑methylthiophene into 2‑thiophenecarboxaldehyde. Key transformations: Potassium peroxymonosulfate (Oxone) oxidizes the methyl substituent to a formyl group, producing 2‑thiophenecarboxaldehyde, hydrogen peroxide, and potassium bisulfate as by‑products. Conditions: Aqueous media at 0 °C to ambient temperature, typically pH‑controlled (often buffered). Solvent/catalyst: Water; Oxone (KHSO₅) serves as the oxidant, no separate catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and precipitate lanthanum carbonate from soluble salts; La2(SO4)3(aq) + 3 Na2CO3(aq) → La2(CO3)3(s) + 3 Na2SO4(aq); typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; the carbonate precipitate is filtered; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Type: Oxidative coupling of thiols to disulfides (iodine oxidation). Purpose: Convert sodium methyl mercaptan (NaSMe) to dimethyl disulfide. Key transformations: I₂ oxidizes the thiolate to a thiyl radical/intermediate, which dimerizes to Me–S–S–Me, while I₂ is reduced to NaI. Conditions: Room temperature, often in anhydrous organic solvent. Solvent/catalyst: Dichloromethane, ether, or THF; iodine itself acts as the oxidant, no further catalyst.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide with a strong nitrogen nucleophile. Purpose: Synthesize allylamine from allyl bromide. Key transformations: Sodium amide (NaNH₂) deprotonates to give NH₂⁻, which attacks allyl bromide, displacing Br⁻ to form allylamine; NaBr is formed as a salt. Conditions: Conducted in liquid ammonia at –33 °C to –78 °C to keep NaNH₂ soluble and suppress side reactions; reaction typically proceeds quickly (minutes). Solvent/catalyst: Anhydrous liquid NH₃; NaNH₂ provides the nucleophile, no external catalyst.

Esterification. Dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) activates the carboxylic acid group of p-aminobenzoic acid for ester bond formation with 2-diethylaminoethanol. The reaction produces dicyclohexylurea as a byproduct. Commonly conducted in aprotic solvents like dichloromethane at room temperature.

Base‑promoted alkaline hydrolysis (cleavage) of an N‑nitrosamine; converts the N‑nitroso group into a secondary amine while generating nitrite ion. Typically carried out in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (50–80 °C) with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to the corresponding primary amine (reductive amination) forming a β‑amino alcohol. Usually performed with H₂ (1–5 atm) over a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C or Pt‑O₂, in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, methanol, or water) at 50–100 °C.

Acid‑base neutralisation to give the disodium salt of etidronic acid (sodium etidronate). Simple salt formation by adding two equivalents of NaOH to an aqueous solution of the acid, stirring at ambient temperature; water is the sole solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of the C=C double bond in oleic acid to produce the fully saturated fatty acid stearic acid. Performed with H₂ (3–10 atm) over a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni) in a solvent mixture of alcohol/water or neat oil, at 50–150 °C.

N‑acetylation of 2‑piperidone; purpose is to protect or modify the lactam nitrogen; key transformation is formation of an amide bond between the nitrogen and an acetyl group, producing 1‑acetylpiperidin‑2‑one and acetic acid; commonly performed by refluxing 2‑piperidone with excess acetic anhydride in anhydrous pyridine or CH₂Cl₂, sometimes catalyzed by DMAP; the solvent is an aprotic organic solvent and pyridine may act as base.

Catalytic hydrogenation of vinylcyclopentane to ethylcyclopentane, reducing the terminal alkene to a saturated alkane. Typical conditions involve H (1–5 atm) with Pd/C, Pt, or Ni catalyst in an alcohol solvent (ethanol or isopropanol) at 25–100 °C.

Acid–base neutralization; lactic acid is deprotonated by sodium bicarbonate, producing sodium lactate, water, and releasing CO₂ gas. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; aqueous NaCl exchanges anions with cupric acetate to give copper(II) chloride and sodium acetate. Performed in water or dilute aqueous solution; simple mixing at room temperature suffices; no catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); NaOH attacks the carbonyl of methyl acrylate, cleaving the ester to generate sodium acrylate and methanol. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with methanol as co‑solvent) under reflux or gentle heating; aqueous/ethanol solvent, no additional catalyst.

Oxidative coupling of thiols; N‑bromosuccinimide oxidizes two thiophenol molecules, forming diphenyl disulfide while producing HBr and succinimide as by‑products. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride as solvent, ambient temperature, inert atmosphere; NBS acts as the oxidant, no metal catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution using a Grignard reagent; phenylmagnesium bromide adds to benzoyl chloride, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to give benzophenone after aqueous work‑up. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in ether or THF, usually at 0 °C to room temperature; Pd catalyst not involved, the Grignard reagent supplies the nucleophile.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; phenylboronic acid couples with 3‑iodopyridine in the presence of Pd(PPh₃)₄ and K₂CO₃ base, yielding 3‑phenylpyridine and potassium iodide as salt by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as dioxane/water or DMF, heating to 80–100 °C under nitrogen or argon; the palladium complex and carbonate base are essential for the transformation.

Electrophilic addition of sulfuric acid to an alkene; purpose: generate ethyl hydrogen sulfate, a precursor to ethyl sulfate or ethanol; key transformation: protonation of ethylene followed by nucleophilic attack of bisulfate (CH2=CH2 + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂OSO₃H); typical conditions: 0‑20 °C to suppress polymerization, using concentrated (≈98 %) sulfuric acid; solvent: often the acid itself acts as solvent, occasionally inert solvent (e.g., chloroform) is used for work‑up.

Ullmann‑type oxidative homocoupling; copper powder mediates the coupling of two 4‑iodophenol molecules to form the C–C bond of 4,4′‑dihydroxybiphenyl. Conducted by heating the aryl iodide with powdered copper (often 2–5 equiv) at 150–200 °C in a polar high‑boiling solvent such as DMF, NMP, or quinoline; a base (K2CO3) may be added to deprotonate the phenol. Provides a straightforward method for synthesizing symmetric diaryl diols.

Ester aminolysis (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose: convert ester to amide. Key transformation: ammonia attacks carbonyl of methyl 3‑methylbutanoate, displaces methoxy group as methanol, yielding 3‑methylbutanamide. Typical conditions: excess liquid or gaseous NH₃, reflux (≈80‑100 °C) for several hours in a sealed tube; solvent may be liquid ammonia or water/ethanol mixture; no catalyst required.

Acid‑metal displacement (single‑replacement) of zinc by phosphoric acid, producing hydrogen gas and zinc phosphate; conducted in aqueous H₃PO₄ solution, usually heated to reflux (≈60‑100 °C) to promote metal dissolution; water is the solvent and no added catalyst is needed.

Direct fluorination (radical halogenation) of benzene with elemental fluorine, yielding hexafluorobenzene and HF; performed in the gas phase at low temperature (‑78 to 0 °C) or in a nickel‑lined reactor, often with excess F₂ and an inert carrier gas; no separate catalyst besides the reactor material.

Hydrolysis of a metal nitride: terbium nitride reacts with water to form terbium(III) hydroxide and ammonia gas; carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature or mild heating (≈20‑80 °C); no catalyst required.

Reaction type: SN2 nucleophilic substitution (cyanation) using copper(I) cyanide. Purpose: introduce a nitrile group onto a primary carbon. Key transformation: CuCN transfers a cyanide anion to 1‑iodobutane, yielding butanenitrile and precipitating CuI. Typical conditions: CuCNoften as a slurry) in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, reflux under nitrogen. Copper(I) cyanide can act both as cyanide source and catalyst; stoichiometric amounts are common.

Oxidation (peracid oxidation); converts thioether to sulfoxide using m‑chloroperoxybenzoic acid, which transfers an oxygen atom to sulfur, producing 2‑methyl‑2‑(methylsulfinyl)propane and m‑chlorobenzoic acid; usually carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (solid‑state) of sodium arsenite, where two equivalents decompose on heating to give arsenic(III) oxide (As₂O₃) and sodium oxide; conducted by heating the solid above ~300 °C under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Metathesis/acid‑base reaction between hydrofluoric acid and mercury(II) acetate, producing insoluble mercury(II) fluoride precipitate and acetic acid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring to aid precipitation; no additional catalyst required.

Gas‑phase/solution precipitation reaction; used to trap Hg^2+ as insoluble mercury(II) sulfide by bubbling H₂S through a solution of mercuric bromide. HgBr₂ + H₂S → HgS (black precipitate) + 2 HBr (released to solution or gas phase). Typically performed in aqueous acidic medium at room temperature; water solvent, H₂S supplied as gas; no catalyst.

Alkali dissolution of an amphoteric oxide; forms sodium gallate (a metallo‑oxo complex) and water; Ga₂O₃ + 2 NaOH → 2 NaGaO₂ + H₂O (often written as Na₃GaO₃ depending on stoichiometry); performed in aqueous NaOH solution, usually heated to 60–90 °C to ensure complete reaction; no external catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange cations and generate insoluble strontium sulfate which precipitates while producing soluble ammonium nitrate; key transformation: Sr(NO3)2 + (NH4)2SO4 → SrSO4(s) + 2 NH4NO3; typical condition: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a trivalent phosphorus compound by a peracid; purpose is to convert tris(dimethylamino)phosphine to hexamethylosphoramide (HMPA) while reducing m‑chloroperbenzoic acid to m‑chlorobenzoic acid; key transformation: P(NMe2)3 + m‑ClC6H4CO3H → O=P(NMe2)3 + m‑ClC6H4CO2H; typical conditions: inert atmosphere, low temperature (0 °C to room temperature), dropwise addition of the peracid in an aprotic solvent such as dry dichloromethane; no additional catalyst.

Double displacement (neutralization/precipitation) reaction; purpose is to replace the beryllium halide with hydroxide, forming insoluble beryllium hydroxide; key transformation: BeI2 + 2 NaOH → Be(OH)2(s) + 2 NaI; typical condition: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: exchange cations to convert soluble silver benzoate into insoluble silver carbonate while forming soluble sodium benzoate. Key transformation: Ag⁺ swaps with Na⁺ producing Ag₂CO₃ precipitate and NaC₆H₅CO₂. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no special catalyst needed. Water is the solvent; the reaction proceeds spontaneously.

Oxidation (dehydrogenation) of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using copper(II) oxide as the oxidant; purpose is to obtain 2‑methylbutanal while reducing CuO to metallic copper; key transformation: CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2OH + CuO → CH3CH2CH(CH3)CHO + H2O + Cu; typical condition: heating (reflux) of the alcohol with solid CuO, often in a high‑boiling inert solvent as quinoline or without solvent under a nitrogen stream; no additional catalyst.

Metallothermic reduction (single‑displacement redox) of antimony(III) chloride by sodium metal; purpose is to produce elemental antimony and sodium chloride; key transformation: SbCl3 + 3 Na → Sb + 3 NaCl; typical condition: dry, oxygen‑free environment, low temperature (often –78 °C to 0 °C) in a polartic solvent such as dry THF or liquid ammonia; sodium metal is the reducing agent, no additional catalyst.

Peroxide‑acid formation (acid–peroxide reaction); purpose is to generate peroxynitric acid, a strong oxidizing agent; key transformation: H2O2 + HNO3 → HOONO2 + H2O; typical condition: cold (0–5 °C), dilute solutions water to control exotherm; aqueous medium, no catalyst required.

General type: O‑silylation (formation of a silyl ether). Purpose: protect the phenolic hydroxyl group. Key transformation: phenol O–H is replaced by O–SiMe₃, generating trimethylsilyl phenyl ether and trifluoromethanesulfonic acid as a by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, inert atmosphere; stoometric trimethylsilyl triflate, no additional catalyst needed.

General type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2 halide exchange). Purpose: convert an alkyl mesylate into the corresponding bromide. Key transformation: bromide ion displaces the mesylate leaving group on isopropyl mesylate, affording 2‑bromopropane and potassium methanesulfonate. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone, excess KBr, reflux or ambient temperature; the insoluble potassium methanesulfonate precipitates driving the reaction forward.

General type: Electrophilic aromatic bromination (halogenation). Purpose: introduce a bromine substituent onto the indole nucleus of N,N‑dimethyltryptamine. Key transformation: Br₂ adds to the 5‑position of the indole ring, producing 5‑bromo‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine and hydrogen bromide as a by‑product. Typical conditions: acetic acid as solvent (or a mixture of acetic acid/DCE), 0 °C to room temperature, stoichiometric bromine; no metal catalyst required.

Acid metal dissolution; AlSb reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, typically concentrated HCl under reflux, to convert the intermetallic into soluble aluminum chloride and antimony trichloride while liberating hydrogen gas. Key transformation: Al–Sb bonds broken, formation of AlCl3, SbCl3, H2. No special catalyst; water is solvent.

Ozonolysis with reductive work‑up; cleaves the vinyl group of 3,4‑dimethoxystyrene to afford 3,4‑dimethoxybenzaldehyde and formaldehyde. Ozone is bubbled through a solution of the alkene in dichloromethane at –78 °C, followed by treatment with dimethyl sulfide to reduce the ozonide to the aldehydes.

General type: Syn‑dihydroxylation (oxidation) of an alkene. Purpose: convert 1‑pentene into the corresponding vicinal diol. Key transformation: catalytic OsO₄ adds across the C=C bond to give a cyclic osmate ester, which is hydrolyzed to 1,2‑pentanediol; N‑methylmorpholine N‑oxide (NMO) re‑oxidizes Os(VI) back to Os(VIII) to make the process catalytic. Typical conditions: 0.5–5 mol % OsO₄, 1–2 equiv NMO, t‑BuOH/H₂O (1:1) or acetone/H₂O mixture, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere.

General type: Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1/E2 elimination). Purpose: form the nitroalkene from a β‑nitro alcohol. Key transformation: loss of water from 2‑nitroethanol to give nitroethene, with sulfuric acid acting as both catalyst and dehydrating agent. Typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄, heating to 70–100 °C, often performed neat or with a small amount of an inert solvent such as toluene; reaction time ranges from minutes to a few hours.

Oxidation of nitroso groups to nitro groups; nitric acid serves as a strong oxidizing agent converting hexahydro‑1,3,5‑trinitroso‑1,3,5‑triazine to the corresponding trinitro‑triazine derivative. Reaction is carried out under controlled low‑temperature acidic conditions, often with reflux, and does not require additional catalyst.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed) of methyl 2,2‑difluoroacetate; cleavage of the C–O ester bond to afford 2,2‑difluoroacetic acid and methanol; typically reflux in aqueous HCl or NaOH (followed by acid work‑up), solvent water or water/THF, no special catalyst beyond acid/base.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); para‑chlorination of biphenyl to afford 4‑chlorobiphenyl; a hydrogen atom on the aromatic ring is substituted by chlorine and HCl is produced; uses Cl₂ in the presence of catalytic FeCl₃ as a Lewis acid; performed in a non‑protic, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C under an inert atmosphere.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation). Purpose: remove the chloro substituent from 2‑chloroacetophenone to afford acetophenone. Key transformation: Pd/C catalyzes cleavage of the C–Cl bond under H₂, producing acetophenone and HCl. Typical conditions: Pd on carbon (5–10 % wt), hydrogen pressure 1–5 atm, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, ambient temperature; reaction run under inert gas with H₂ sparge.

Buchwald‑Hartwig amination; palladium‑catalyzed C‑N cross‑coupling of an aryl bromide with piperazine to install a 4‑nitrophenyl group on the nitrogen; base (triethylamine) neutralizes the HBr formed; typically performed under inert atmosphere at 80‑120 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene, dioxane or DMF with triphenylphosphine as ligand and Pd(OAc)₂ as catalyst.

Copper‑mediated reduction of an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol; NaBH₄ reduces 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde, while CuCl₂ is reduced to CuCl, often enhancing selectivity; carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt; sodium chloride is a benign by‑product.

Neutralization with sodium carbonate; purpose is to liberate the free amine while generating CO2; key transformation octan‑1‑amine·HCl + Na2CO3 → octan‑1‑amine + NaCl + CO2↑ + H2O; typically carried out in water with slight heating to evolve CO2; water is the solvent; carbonate acts as a weak base and also buffers the mixture.

Conversion of allyl alcohol to allyl chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); purpose is to replace a hydroxyl group with chloride to obtain a reactive alkyl chloride; the reaction proceeds via formation of an intermediate chlorosulfite which collapses, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases; usually conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature; pyridine or a tertiary amine acts as an HCl scavenger; by‑products are gaseous SO₂ and HCl.

Acetylation (acylation) of a secondary alcohol using acetic anhydride; the alcohol attacks the anhydride carbonyl to form hexan‑2‑yl acetate and acetic acid usually conducted at 0  to rt in an inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the acid.

Acid–base neutralization of iodic acid with sodium carbonate; carbonate deprotonates HIO₃ forming sodium iodate, while CO₂ and H₂O are released as gases; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ring‑opening) of tetrahydrofuran to 1,4‑butanediol; water adds across the C–O bond, regenerating the diol. Usually carried out in dilute aqueous H₂SO₄ (1–5 M) at 80–120 °C under reflux.

Nitrosation reaction; purpose is to synthesize the N‑nitroso compound N‑nitrosodiethanolamine. The secondary amine diethanolamine reacts with the nitrosating agent dinitrogen trioxide (generated in situ from nitrous acid) to form an N‑N=O linkage, with water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions are aqueous acidic medium (often HCl/NaNO2) at 05 °C to control the exotherm and avoid over‑nitrosation. Water is the common solvent; the reaction may be performed in an ice bath with careful addition of the nitrosating species.

Oxime formation (condensation of hydroxylamine with a carbonyl); purpose is to prepare the corresponding chloro‑oxime. Hydroxylamine adds to the carbonyl carbon of 2‑chloro‑1‑phenylethanone, followed by elimination of water to give N‑(2‑chloro‑1‑phenylethylidene)hydroxylamine. The reaction is usually carried out in an alcohol solvent such as ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of weak acid (p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or under neutral conditions, at reflux or ambient temperature, and the mixture is worked up to isolate the oxime.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile to a primary amine; 2,2-difluoroacetonitrile is reduced by H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni, Pd/C, or Pt) to give 2,2-difluoroethylamine. Reactions are carried out in ethanol or methanol at 50–150 °C under 1–5 atm H₂ pressure.

Acid‑base salt formation; purpose is to convert the free base bendamustine into its more water‑soluble hydrochloride salt for pharmaceutical formulation. Bendamustine is dissolved in a suitable solvent (e.g., ethanol or a water/ethanol mixture) and treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid at room temperature, resulting in precipitation or solution of bendamustine hydrochloride. No additional catalysts are required; the reaction is typically performed at 0–25 °C with stirring until complete salt formation is confirmed.

Electrophilic aromatic sulfonation; purpose is to introduce a sulfonic acid group para to the ethyl substituent on the benzene ring, yielding 4‑ethylbenzenesulfonic acid. Ethylbenzene is treated with fuming (oleum) sulfuric acid, which provides sulfonating species (SO₃/H₂SO₄). The reaction conducted at elevated temperature (80–150 °C) under reflux in the sulfuric acid medium. After cooling, the mixture is poured onto ice and the product is isolated by neutralization and extraction. No external catalyst is needed; the acid itself acts as both solvent and electrophile source.

Esterification via acyl transfer using butyric anhydride and ethanol; the anhydride donates a butyryl group to ethanol forming ethyl butyrate while the remaining acyl fragment becomes butyric acid; usually refluxed in excess ethanol or a non‑protic solvent (e.g., toluene) and may be catalyzed by a trace of acid (H₂SO₄) to accelerate the reaction; by‑product acid can be removed by azeotropic distillation.

Type: Hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of a phosphoric mixed anhydride. Purpose: Convert theylated phosphite into the corresponding dimethyl phosphate. Key transformation: Water attacks the acyl phosphorus center, breaking the P–OAc bond to give dimethyl phosphate and acetic acid. Typical conditions: Aqueous NaOH (0.1–1 M) or dilute HCl at 25–50 °C for 1–2 h; after completion, neutralize and isolate dimethyl phosphate. No additional catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of an acyl chloride back to the carboxylic acid; purpose is to obtain the acid after a prior activation step; key transformation is 2‑ethylhexanoyl chloride + H2O → 2‑ethylhexanoic acid + HCl; typical conditions: slow addition of the acyl chloride to ice‑cold water or dilute aqueous NaHCO3 at 0–25 °C; the mixture is stirred until gas evolution ceases; the organic layer is separated, washed with brine, and the aqueous phase is acidified if needed to isolate the acid.

Hydrolysis of phosphorus oxychloride; purpose is to convert POCl₃ into phosphoric acid while generating hydrogen chloride gas. POCl₃ is added dropwise to cold water (often an ice bath) under vigorous stirring to control the exotherm. The reaction proceeds rapidly, producing phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) in solution and three equivalents of HCl, which evolve as gas and dissolve in the aqueous phase. The process is performed in a fume hood; no additional catalysts are required.

Base‑catalyzed aldol (Claisen‑Schmidt) condensation between 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzaldehyde and 4‑hydroxyacetophenone, followed by dehydration to generate the diaryl ketone Tapinarof. Typical conditions use a mild inorganic base (e.g., NaOH or KOH) in ethanol or methanol, refluxing until completion, then work‑up and purification.

Acid‑base protonation reaction. Sodium bromite (NaBrO2) reacts with concentrated H2SO4 in aqueous solution, forming bromous acid (HBrO2) and sodium bisulfate (NaHSO4). Performed at ambient temperature with stirring.

Oxidation of ethyl methyl sulfide to the sulfone (1‑methylsulfonylethane) using peracetic acid; type: peracid oxidation (sulfur oxidation to sulfone); key transformation: R‑S‑R′ → R‑SO₂‑R′; typical conditions: peracetic acid (1.2–2 equiv) in dichloromethane at 0 °C to 25 °C, often with a small amount of acetic acid as co‑solvent; reaction is run under inert atmosphere.

Redox reduction of osmium tetroxide with sulfite; purpose is to convert toxic OsO₄ to the less soluble OsO₂ while oxidizing sulfite to sulfate; OsO₄ + Na₂SO₃ → OsO₂ + Na₂SO₄ + H₂O; carried out in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C, often under slightly basic conditions; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

General type: keto‑enol tautomerization of a furanone. Purpose: interconvert hydroxy‑furanone tautomers to reach the more stable or desired form, often affecting odor or reactivity. Key transformation: migration of a hydrogen atom from the hydroxyl group to the adjacent carbon, shifting the double bond and converting a 3‑hydroxy‑2‑furanone to a 2‑hydroxy‑5‑furanone. Typical conditions: mild heating (30‑80 °C) or catalytic amounts of acid (p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (pyridine, NaHCO₃) in polar protic/aprotic solvents such as water, ethanol, or dichloromethane. No special catalyst required.

General type: substitution of an alcohol by a halide using phosphorus pentachloride. Purpose: convert 2‑octanol into the corresponding secondary alkyl chloride for further functionalization. Key transformation: PCl₅ reacts with the hydroxyl group to generate POCl₃ and HCl, while the chlorine from PCl₅ replaces the –OH, forming 2‑chloro‑octane. Typical conditions: anhydrous environment, 0 °C to reflux, in dry dichloromethane, carbon tetrachloride, or chloroform; inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). No additional catalyst needed.

Enzymatic oxidative deamination of L‑isoleucine; purpose is to generate the corresponding α‑keto acid while reducing NAD+; key transformation is removal of the amino group as NH3 and oxidation of the α‑carbon, producing 3‑methyl‑2‑oxopentanoic acid, NADH and NH3; performed in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C with the enzyme (e.g., L‑isoleucine dehydrogenase) and NAD+ as cofactor; no additional solvents or catalysts required beyond the enzyme.

General type: electrophilic aromatic chlorination (halogenation) of phthalonitrile. Purpose: synthesize tetrachlorophthalonitrile (chlorothalonil), a widely used fungicide. Key transformation: four equivalents of Cl₂ substitute for hydrogen atoms on the aromatic ring, producing C₆Cl₄(CN)₂ and releasing four equivalents of HCl. Typical conditions: Cl₂ gas passed over the substrate at 60‑120 °C in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃; solvents may include carbon tetrachloride, nitrobenzene, or chlorobenzene. Reaction often performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere.

Hydration of phosphorus pentoxide. Addition of water to solid P₂O₅ (exothermic) forms phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄). The reaction proceeds spontaneously at ambient temperature; it is usually performed in a glass vessel under a fume hood to control heat release.

General type: thermal decomposition of an ammonium formate salt (acid–base dissociation). Purpose: liberate the parent amine and acid from their salt form. Key transformation: ethylammonium formate undergoes proton transfer and breakdown upon heating, yielding free ethylamine and formic acid. Typical conditions: gentle heating (50‑100 °C) in aqueous or alcoholic solution; no catalyst required. The reaction is driven by removal of volatile formic acid or by applying reduced pressure.

General type: sulfonylation of an alcohol to form an alkyl triflate (trifluoromethanesulfonate ester). Purpose: activate the alcohol as a good leaving group for subsequent substitution or cross‑coupling reactions. Key transformation: trifluoromethanesulfonic anhydride transfers a Tf to the oxygen of 1‑propanol, generating propyl‑OTf and one equivalent of triflic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, dry dichloromethane or chloroform as solvent, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize the generated TfOH. Reactions are conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂).

General type: high‑temperature solid‑gas fluorination (redox) of a metal oxide. Purpose: produce scandium fluoride, a refractory fluoride material, and release oxygen gas. Key transformation: fluorine gas oxidizes scandium from Sc₂O₃ to ScF₃, while oxygen atoms are liberated as O₂. Stoichiometry: 6 F₂ +  Sc₂O₃ → 4 ScF₃ + 3 O₂. Typical conditions: fluorine flow at 400‑800 °C, often in a sealed quartz or nickel reactor; no solvent, inert carrier gas (Ar) may be used to control fluorine concentration. No catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition of methanol to phenyl isocyanate to form a carbamate (methyl phenylcarbamate); purpose is synthesis of a urethane protecting group; key transformation is O‑H attack on the electrophilic carbon of the isocyanate, followed by proton transfer to give the methyl phenylcarbamate; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere in solvents such as dichloromethane, THF or toluene; catalyst is often unnecessary but a catalytic base (e.g., triethylamine or DMAP) can accelerate the reaction.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using silver oxide (Ag2O); 3‑methyl‑2‑butanol is converted to 3‑methyl‑2‑butanone with the reduction of Ag2O to metallic silver. Reaction proceeds at room temperature or slight heating in an aqueous or alcoholic medium, often with stirring, and does not require additional reagents.

Metathesis / acid‑base exchange (regeneration of the acid). Lithium methanesulfonate is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid; the proton transfers to the methanesulfonate anion to give methanesulfonic acid, while lithium chloride remains in solution. Performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

Acid chloride formation / sulfonyl chloride synthesis; conversion of a sulfonate salt to the corresponding sulfonyl chloride using thionyl chloride. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic substitution where the sulfonate oxygen attacks SOCl₂, releasing CO and SO₂ gases and forming NaCl. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; excess SOCl₂ is distilled off.

Double displacement (metathesis) and precipitation; reaction of oxalic acid with aqueous nickel(II) sulfate exchanges the anions to give sparingly soluble nickel(II) oxalate precipitate and soluble sulfuric acid. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; the mixture is stirred, the NiC₂O₄ solid is filtered and washed. No special catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of potassium ethyl carbonate; purpose is to generate potassium carbonate, carbon dioxide and ethanol; key transformation cleavage of the ethyl carbonate to carbonate ion plus CO₂ and ethanol; typical conditions: heating solid to 150‑200 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction); converts the para‑nitro group of 4‑nitrophenol to an amino group, yielding 4‑aminophenol. Conduct under H2 (1‑5 atm) with Pd/C, Pt, or Raney Ni in ethanol or methanol at 25‑50 °C.

Direct fluorination (oxidative halogenation). Elemental fluorine reacts with solid boron nitride to produce gaseous boron trifluoride and nitrogen trifluoride. Requires vigorous fluorination conditions: F₂ gas flow at 200‑500 °C, often in a quartz reactor; no solvent, sometimes a fluorine‑resistant metal catalyst (e.g., nickel) may be used to promote initiation.

Acid‑base (proton transfer) deprotonation; sodium amide, a strong base, abstracts the acidic N‑H proton of imidazole, yielding sodium imidazolate and ammonia gas. Usually carried out in dry liquid ammonia or THF under nitrogen at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) to avoid moisture; the ammonia can be removed by gas venting.

Electrophilic nitration of 4‑chloropyridine; introduces a nitro group ortho to the chlorine to give 4‑chloro‑3‑nitropyridine while forming water; conducted with a mixed acid (conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄) at 0–5 °C; the acid mixture serves as solvent and the reaction is quenched with ice.

Redox (reduction–oxidation) reduction of lead(IV) oxide; carbon monoxide reduces lead tetroxide (Pb₃O₄) to lead(II) oxide (PbO) while being oxidized to carbon dioxide. Performed by heating a mixture of solid Pb₃O₄ and CO gas in a tube furnace at 300–500 °C; no solvent or catalyst is needed, and the reaction is conducted in a flow of CO or CO/N₂.

Acid‑catalyzed epoxide ring opening (hydrolysis); protonation of the 1,2‑epoxy‑octane oxygen activates the epoxide toward nucleophilic attack by water, giving octane‑1,2‑diol (typically trans‑diol). Conducted in aqueous dilute acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, pH ≈ 1–2) at 25–60 °C, often in a water–acetone or THF mixture to improve solubility. No additional catalyst is required beyond the acid.

Oxidative chlorination; chlorine gas oxidizes molybdenum(IV) chloride (MoCl₄) to molybdenum(V) chloride (MoCl₅). The reaction is carried out in a dry, inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at room temperature to 150 °C, often in a sealed glass tube or Schlenk flask; excess Cl₂ is vented after completion. No solvent is typically used, but if a solvent is required, dry carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane can be employed.

Acid–metal redox: zinc metal reduces hydrazoic acid to give hydrogen gas and zinc azide; a straightforward redox/acid–base reaction carried out in aqueous solution (often cold, inert atmosphere) to avoid azide detonation; no catalyst required.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative coupling (carbonylation) of 4‑ethoxyiodobenzene with carbon monoxide and ethanol to form ethyl 4‑ethoxybenzoate; tri‑tert‑butylphosphine and triethylamine act as ligand and base, Pd(OAc)2 as catalyst; performed under CO pressure (≈1–5 atm) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or toluene at 80–120 °C; hydrogen iodide is generated as a by‑product.

Aqueous ester hydrolysis of centrophenoxine (meclofenoxate) yielding 2‑(dimethylamino)ethanol and 4‑chlorophenoxyacetic acid; typically done in water or aqueous buffer, often with mild heating (reflux) and either acid or base catalysis; no special catalyst needed.

Acidification of sodium perrhenate with sulfuric acid; acid‑base conversion to perrhenic acid (HReO4) and sodium sulfate; typically conducted in aqueous solution using concentrated H2SO4, sometimes with gentle heating; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous dysprosium(III) nitrate is treated with sodium hydroxide, yielding insoluble dysprosium(III) hydroxide as a solid precipitate and soluble sodium nitrate. Performed in water at ambient temperature, often with excess NaOH and vigorous stirring; the solid is filtered and washed.

Hydrolysis of dimethylacetoxysilane to the corresponding silanol; water cleaves the Si–OAc bond, forming dimethylsilanol and acetic acid. Usually carried out at ambient temperature in a mixture of THF/H₂O or MeCN/H₂O; can be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed but often proceeds without added catalyst.

Two‑step amidation via acid chloride; 5‑methyl‑1H‑pyrazole‑3‑carboxylic acid is first converted to the acid chloride with thionyl chloride, then treated with ammonia to give the amide. Key transformations: (a) formation of R‑COCl (SOCl₂, 0 °C → rt, CH₂Cl₂ or pyridine), (b) nucleophilic attack of NH₃ (gas or aqueous) on the acyl chloride to afford 5‑methyl‑1H‑pyrazole‑3‑carboxamide, releasing HCl and SO₂. Conditions: SOCl₂ added dropwise at 0 °C, stirred 1 h, solvent removed, residue dissolved in dry, cooled, and NH₃ introduced at 0 °C to rt. No metal catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (hydrogen reduction) of an aromatic aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Molecular hydrogen reduces the C=O of vanillin to a CH₂OH group, giving vanillyl alcohol. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, solvent like ethanol or methanol, temperature ranging from 0 °C to 50 °C. Reaction proceeds until complete consumption of aldehyde (monitored by TLC or GC).

Phosphorylation of 4‑hydroxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine using phosphorus oxychloride in pyridine to give psilocybin; pyridine serves as solvent and HCl scavenger; reaction run under anhydrous conditions at 0 °C to room temperature, producing hydrogen chloride as by‑product.

Ester hydrolysis (neutral or acid/base-catalyzed). Converts the ethyl ester of 3‑hydroxyvaleric acid into the free acid and ethanol. Typically performed in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (NaOH) with reflux for 1–4 h; water acts as solvent and nucleophile; after base hydrolysis, acidification yields the product.

Hydroamination of an alkene. Rhodium on alumina catalyzes the addition of methylamine across ethylene to give N‑methylethylamine, a secondary amine. Reactions are usually run under inert atmosphere at 80–150 °C, often neat or in a high‑boiling hydrocarbon (toluene); Rh/Al₂O₃ provides the active site and no additional solvent is required.

redox oxidation; iodine is oxidized to iodate by acidic permanganate, manganese reduced to Mn(II) sulfate; used in analytical chemistry to generate iodate or consume excess iodine; carried out in aqueous sulfuric acid, often with reflux or gentle heating; water is the solvent, KMnO4 acts as oxidant, no other catalyst.

Cleavage of a Se–Se bond by a Grignard reagent. Phenylmagnesium bromide attacks diphenyl diselenide, producing diphenyl selenide and phenylselenol. Conducted in anhydrous THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; the Grignard reagent acts as nucleophile and reductant, and the reaction is quenched with aqueous NH₄Cl to isolate the products.

Transesterification. Methanol exchanges with the ethoxy group of 2‑fluoroethyl 2‑fluoroacetate, yielding 2‑fluoroethanol and methyl 2‑fluoroacetate. Usually performed with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (NaOMe) at reflux in excess methanol; the reaction proceeds to equilibrium, and removal of excess methanol drives conversion.

Acid‑base complexation (metal citrate formation). Citric acid reacts with bismuth oxide to form bismuth citrate and water. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating (60–80 °C) to improve dissolution; the mixture is kept under stirring until gas evolution ceases, yielding the soluble bismuth citrate complex.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation). The phenolic proton of picric acid is deprotonated by methoxide, yielding the sodium picrate salt and methanol. Typically carried out in methanol or aqueous methanol at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Aerobic oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; isobutyraldehyde is converted into isobutyric acid in the presence of molecular oxygen and a metal catalyst (e.g., Cu/TEMPO, Co‑Mn‑Br, or Pd); typically run in acetonitrile or water/tert‑butanol mixture at 30–80 °C under an O₂ balloon or pressure; a base such as NaOH may be added to facilitate deprotonation.

Haloform (iodoform) reaction. Acetaldehyde undergoes base‑promoted oxidation with iodine in aqueous NaOH, giving iodoform (CHI₃) and sodium acetate. Reaction is performed in water, often at 0 °C to room temperature, with excess NaOH and I₂; no metal catalyst needed.

Catalytic reductive amination (transfer hydrogenation). Phenylacetaldehyde is reduced and aminated in the presence of palladium on carbon and ammonium formate, which serves as a hydrogen donor, producing phenethylamine, CO₂ and H₂O. Conducted in ethanol or methanol under reflux; Pd/C is the catalyst.

Azo coupling (diazo electrophilic substitution). The diazonium salt of p‑nitrobenzenediazonium chloride couples with the activated aromatic ring of N‑ethyl‑2‑methylaniline to form the azo dye Disperse Orange 3, with HCl generated as a by‑product. Performed in cold (0–5 °C) aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH) to keep the diazonium ion stable; no additional catalyst required.

Direct combination of gases to form dioxygen difluoride (O₂F₂). Molecular oxygen reacts with fluorine under cryogenic conditions (typically –196 °C) in an inert matrix or condensed phase to give the highly reactive O₂F₂. No solvent or catalyst; the reaction must be kept at very low temperature to avoid explosive decomposition.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aromatic ring. Para‑xylene is saturated with hydrogen in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney nickel, Pt/C, or Pd/C) under elevated H₂ pressure and moderate temperature (100–200 °C) to afford 1,4‑dimethylcyclohexane. The reaction is usually run in a hydrocarbon solvent such as cyclohexane or ethanol.

Oxidative coupling (thiol oxidation). Iodine oxidizes phenyl mercaptan (PhSH) to diphenyl disulfide (PhSSPh) while being reduced to hydrogen iodide (HI). Usually performed at 0–25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, carbon tetrachloride or acetonitrile; a base (e.g., pyridine or NaHCO₃) may be added to neutralize HI.

Esterification of an alcohol with an acyl chloride; acyl chloride acylation. The acetyl chloride reacts with 2‑methoxy‑1‑propanol to give the acetate ester (propylene glycol methyl ether acetate) and HCl. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) is added to scavenge the generated HCl.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Aqueous solutions of barium selenite and ammonium carbonate exchange ions, producing insoluble barium carbonate that precipitates and soluble ammonium selenite that remains in solution. The reaction is carried out at room temperature with stirring; the solid BaCO₃ is filtered off, and no catalyst is required.

Base‑mediated saponification (hydrolysis) of the acetate ester; 4‑acetyloxypentanoic acid is treated with aqueous NaOH to regenerate 4‑hydroxy‑pentanoic acid and sodium acetate. Typical conditions: 1–2 M NaOH, reflux 1–2 h, water/ethanol solvent; work‑up acidifies to isolate the acid.

Preparation of a Grignard reagent by insertion of magnesium into 1‑chlorohexane; metal insertion (organometallic formation) producing hexylmagnesium chloride. Utilized as a carbon nucleophile in subsequent C‑C bond‑forming reactions. Typical conditions: anhydrous ethereal solvent (dry diethyl ether or THF), inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), activated magnesium (iodine or sonication) and gentle reflux to initiate the reaction; no additional catalyst is required.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative cyclization (carbonylation) of an allylamine with carbon monoxide to form a five‑membered lactam (pyrrolidin‑2‑one). The reaction uses Pd(OAc)2 (often with a phosphine ligand) under CO pressure (1–10 bar) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or toluene at 80–120 °C. It provides a concise route to γ‑lactams from simple amines.

Electrophilic addition (halogenation) of chlorine across the carbon–carbon double bond of ethyl acrylate to give ethyl 2,3‑dichloropropionate, a vicinal dichloride. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to ambient temperature in a non‑nucleilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, protected from light to avoid radical side reactions.

Acid‑base neutralization (metathesis) between acetic acid and calcium methoxide. Two equivalents of acetic acid protonate the methoxide ions, yielding methanol and calcium acetate as the salt. The reaction is usually performed in methanol or a mixed solvent at ambient temperature; mild heating may be applied to drive the reaction to completion.

Zinc‑mediated reduction of a nitro aryl compound (metal reduction) in the presence of ammonium chloride.
