Zinc dust reduces the nitro group of 4‑bromo‑nitrobenzene to an amine, producing 4‑bromo‑aniline, zinc chloride, and liberating ammonia from the ammonium salt. The process is carried out in aqueous or alcoholic medium, often at reflux, with NH4Cl providing the required acidic protons.

SN2 alkylation of potassium phenylacetate with methyl iodide; nucleophilic substitution at the methyl carbon yields methyl phenylacetate; purpose is ester synthesis; typically carried out in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at reflux; potassium iodide precipitates, no catalyst required.

Borane‑mediated reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Borane (typically as BH₃·THF) reacts with isobutyric acid, delivering hydride equivalents that convert the acid to isobutanol after oxidative work‑up (e.g., H₂O₂/NaOH). The reaction is performed in dry THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; excess BH₃ is quenched after completion.

Redox / acid‑metal displacement reaction. Metallic bismuth reduces hydroiodic acid, liberating hydrogen gas and forming bismuth triiodide. Typically performed by adding Bi to aqueous HI and heating gently; no special catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Alcohol‑to‑chloride substitution (Appel‑type chlorination) using thion chloride. Primary benzylic alcohol is converted to phenethyl chloride while releasing HCl and SO₂ gases. Conducted in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, often with pyridine acting as base to trap HCl; temperature from 0 °C to reflux.

Enzymatic phosphorylation (kinase reaction); glycerol is phosphorylated by ATP to give 2,3‑dihydroxypropyl dihydrogen phosphate (lycerol‑1‑phosphate) while ATP is converted to ADP. Purpose: activation of glycerol for entry into glycolysis/gluconeogenesis. Typically catalyzed by glycerol kinase in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) with Mg²⁺ as cofactor; performed at ambient temperature in aqueous solution.

Hydrolysis of benzal chloride to benzaldehyde (nucleophilic substitution of chloride by water); carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., dilute HCl) under reflux; water acts as nucleophile, releasing hydrogen chloride as by‑product.

Esterification with formyl chloride (formyl chloride is the acyl chloride of formic acid); purpose is to synthesize allyl formate. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of allyl alcohol on the carbonyl carbon of formyl chloride, displacing chloride to give the ester and HCl. Typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C) in anhydrous dichloromethane, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine present to capture the generated HCl and prevent side reactions.

Fischer esterification of gentisic acid with methanol to afford methyl gentisate; the carboxylic acid is protonated by an acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄) and reacts with methanol, releasing water. Reflux methanol with catalytic acid for several hours; methanol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Heterocycle‑forming cyclization (synthesis of ebselen). Anthranilic acid is selenated by phenylselenyl chloride, then cyclizes in pyridine to give the 1,2‑benzisoselenazol‑3‑one (ebselen) and pyridinium chloride as by‑product. Reaction is run under reflux in dry pyridine under nitrogen; pyridine serves both solvent and base.

Alkaline hydrolysis (amide saponification). Acrylamide is attacked by hydroxide ion, cleaving the C‑N bond to afford sodium acrylate and ammonia. Carried out in aqueous NaOH solution, typically heated (50‑80 °C) until completion; water is the reaction medium, no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑metal (single‑displacement) reaction forming a potassium salt. Tartaric acid reacts with metallic potassium, releasing hydrogen gas and yielding potassium tartrate. Usually performed in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere to control the vigorous hydrogen evolution; potassium metal supplies the base, no catalyst required.

Eschweiler–Clarke reductive methylation; formaldehyde and formic acid form an iminium intermediate that is reduced by formic acid, converting the primary amine to the N‑methyl secondary amine with release of water and CO₂. Usually refluxed in a mixture of formic acid and methanol or water; no metal catalyst required.

Alcoholate‑to‑oxide sol‑gel conversion; hydrolysis of hafnium tetraisopropoxide yields hafnium dioxide and isopropanol; add controlled amount of water to a solution of Hf(OCH(CH₃)₂)₄ in anhydrous isopropanol (or other alcohol) at 0‑25 °C, optionally catalyzed by a few drops of acid (HCl) or base (NH₃); subsequent aging and drying give HfO₂ gel; solvent is the parent alcohol, catalyst optional.

Oxidation of a primary benzylic alcohol to a carboxylic acid using chromic acid (Jones oxidation). 2,4‑Dichlorobenzyl alcohol is oxidized to 2,4‑dichlorobenzoic acid while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr₂O₃. Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid with acetone as co‑solvent, temperature kept at 0–25 °C; chromic acid is the oxidant, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (acetate exchange); replaces the propargyl alkoxy group with ethoxy, yielding ethyl acetate and regenerating propargyl alcohol; run in refluxing ethanol with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid (≈1 mol %); solvent is ethanol itself; removal of ethyl acetate drives the equilibrium.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination); converts the tertiary alcohol 2‑methylpentan‑2‑ol to the corresponding alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑pentene with loss of water. Typical conditions: catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄, heating (≈130–180 °C), often the alcohol itself acts as solvent; no additional reagents required.

Peptide bond formation by thermal condensation; β‑alanine and L‑histidine lose a molecule of water to give the dipeptide carnosine. Usually performed by dry heating of the solid mixture at high temperature (≈180–200 °C) under reduced pressure or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is normally employed, though coupling reagents are more common in laboratory synthesis.

General type: double displacement precipitation (metathesis) in water; purpose: generate manganese(II) hydroxide and remove fluoride as soluble sodium fluoride; key transformation: MnF2 + NaOH → Mn(OH)2 (insoluble) + NaF (soluble); typical conditions: aqueous NaOH added to aqueous MnF2 solution at ambient temperature with stirring; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; sodium sulfate reacts with ferric nitrate to exchange anions, producing soluble sodium nitrate and iron(III) sulfate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst is required.

Catalytic dehydrogenation over Pt/Al₂O₃; propylbenzene (1‑phenylpropane) is dehydrogenated to give trans‑β‑methylstyrene and molecular hydrogen. Requires high temperature (≈450–550 °C) under an inert gas flow; platinum supported on alumina serves as the catalyst, and the reaction is typically carried out in the gas phase.

Ester aminolysis; conversion of butyl lactate to lactamide and 1‑butanol by nucleophilic attack of ammonia on the ester carbonyl with elimination of butanol; performed with excess aqueous or gaseous ammonia, heated to 100‑150 °C under reflux; often solvent‑free or in water/ethanol; no metal catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage of a C=C bond using alkaline KMnO₄; oleic acid is cleaved at the double bond to afford the C9 dicarboxylic acid azelaic acid and the C9 monocarboxylic acid nonanoic acid, with formation of KOH and MnO₂ as by‑products. Conducted in aqueous alkaline medium (KOH present) at moderate temperature (0–50 °C) followed by work‑up and acidification; potassium permanganate is the oxidant, and MnO₂ precipitates out.

O‑methylation of phenol with diazomethane; 2,3‑dichlorophenol reacts with one equivalent of diazomethane to give 2,3‑dichloroanisole and nitrogen gas. Performed in an aprotic ether (e.g., diethyl ether) at 0 °C to room temperature, often under nitrogen atmosphere; diazomethane serves both as methylating agent and source of N₂, no additional catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization of magnesium hydroxide with hydrobromic acid; the insoluble base is converted to a soluble salt. Purpose: dissolve Mg(OH)2 and generate magnesium bromide solution. Key transformation: Mg(OH)2 + 2 HBr → MgBr2 + 2 H2O. Conditions: aqueous medium, typically at ambient temperature; gentle heating may be applied to increase rate. No catalyst; solvent is water.

Metathesis (halide exchange) reaction; used to chloride ligands on cerium(III) with iodide by reacting sodium iodide with cerium(III) chloride in aqueous solution; key transformation is Na⁺I⁻ + Ce³⁺Cl₃⁻ → NaCl precipitate (or soluble) and formation of CeI₃; typically performed at reflux or moderate heating in water or polar protic solvent; common conditions include stirring under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, and filtration to isolate solid products.

Chlorination/oxide-to-chloride conversion; thionyl chloride acts as a chlorinating and dehydrating agent to convert thulium oxide to thulium(III) chloride while generating gaseous CO and SO₂; key transformation is replacement of O²⁻ by Cl⁻ with simultaneous loss of oxygen as CO and SO₂; usually carried out by heating thulium oxide directly in excess thionyl chloride (no additional solvent) under reflux, often under a dry nitrogen or argon atmosphere; gaseous by‑products are vented through a scrubber.

Nucleophilic substitution (organolithium addition) to prepare a secondary phosphine; phenyl dichlorophosphine reacts with two equivalents of methyllithium, each MeLi attacks a P–Cl bond, forming dimethylphenylphosphine and lithium chloride as by‑product; typical conditions are low temperature (‑78 °C) in dry THF or Et₂O, under inert gas (N₂ or Ar); reaction is quenched with water or ammonium chloride work‑up and the product isolated by distillation or chromatography.

Amide bond formation via acyl‑chloride coupling; the primary amine (1,3‑benzodioxol‑5‑ylmethanamine) is acylated by 2,6‑dichlorobenzoyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine, which neutralizes the HCl generated to give triethylammonium chloride; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the amine on the carbonyl carbon of the acyl chloride yielding N‑(1,3‑benzodioxol‑5‑ylmethyl)-2,6‑dichlorobenzamide; performed in an aprotic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; base is used in slight excess and the reaction mixture is washed to remove TEA·HCl.

Catalytic hydrogenation; purpose: saturate the C=C bond in the pyrrolinyl side chain of myosmine to form nornicotine; key transformation: addition of two hydrogen atoms across a C=C double bond, converting a pyrrolinyl ring to a pyrrolidine ring; typical conditions: hydrogen gas at 1–5 atm, Pd/C (or Pt/Al₂O₃) catalyst, ethanol or methanol as solvent, temperature 25–80 °C, reaction time 1–4 h.

Generation of a Wittig phosphonium ylide (methylenetriphenylphosphorane) by deprotonation of methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide with a strong non‑nucleophilic base (lithium tetramethylpiperidide, LiTMP); key transformation is removal of the acidic methyl proton to give the ylide, with lithium bromide and tetramethylpiperidine as by‑products; typically performed in dry THF at low temperature (‑78 °C to −30 °C) under an inert atmosphere; the resulting ylide is used immediately in Wittig olefination reactions.

Metallothermic reduction of boron trichloride by magnesium; elemental magnesium reduces BCl₃, forming magnesium chloride and elemental boron; key transformation is transfer chloride to magnesium and deposition of boron; carried out at high temperature (often >300 °C) in a sealed, dry, inert‑gas system; BCl₃ is introduced as a gas or liquid, and the solid Mg is added; reaction mixture is usually stirred in a quartz or steel reactor, and the boron product is collected after cooling and washing away MgCl₂.

Hydrolysis of hafnium nitrate; conversion to hafnium dioxide and release of nitric acid; dissolve Hf(NO₃)₄ in water and heat to 80‑100 °C to precipitate HfO₂; the solution remains acidic due to liberated HNO₃; no catalyst, water is the medium.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous solution of soluble barium iodide and rubidium sulfate forms insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble rubidium iodide; carried out in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Redox oxidation with concentrated nitric acid: arsenic trioxide is oxidized by HNO₃ under heating, producing arsenic acid (H₃AsO₄), nitrogen dioxide gas (NO₂) and water. Purpose is to convert insoluble As(III) oxide to soluble As(V) acid for analysis; uses concentrated HNO₃ as both oxidant and solvent, no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution of a secondary alcohol with thionyl bromide to give an alkyl bromide; converts 1-hexan-2-ol to 2-bromohexane with evolution of HBr and SO₂; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature; pyridine acts as base to scavenge HBr; no external catalyst.

Grignard carbonylation to aldehyde; ethylmagnesium bromide adds to carbon monoxide forming an acyl magnesium intermediate that on acidic work‑up yields propanal; conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under CO atmosphere at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C); quenched with dilute acid; no catalyst.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction of mercurous oxide with concentrated nitric acid; Hg₂O is oxidized to Hg(NO₃)₂ while nitric acid is reduced to NO₂ gas, producing water; performed by adding solid Hg₂O to hot concentrated HNO₃; reaction generates toxic NO₂ fumes; no catalyst.

Base‑induced E2 elimination of a tertiary alkyl chloride; aqueous NaOH (often heated or refluxed, sometimes with ethanol) abstracts a β‑hydrogen from tert‑amyl chloride, eliminating HCl and forming 2‑methyl‑2‑butene; water is formed as by‑product; no catalyst required.

Double nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1,2‑dichloroethane with dimethylamine to give N,N,N',N'-tetramethylethylenediamine (TMEDA) and HCl; typically carried out in a non‑protic solvent such as toluene or THF under reflux, with excess dimethylamine or an added base (e.g., triethylamine) to trap the liberated HCl; no additional catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; converts an organomercury bromide to the corresponding hydroxide, often used to generate a more reactive or precipitable form of the organomercury species. Conducted in aqueous sodium hydroxide solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of alkyl halides with ammonia; purpose: synthesize hexamethylenediamine; key transformation: two successive NH₃ attacks replace the two chlorine atoms of 1,6‑dichlorohexane with –NH₂ groups, producing NH₄Cl as a by‑product; typical conditions: excess aqueous or alcoholic ammonia, reflux (≈100‑120 °C) or high‑pressure NH₃ gas; common solvent/catalyst: ethanol or water (no additional catalyst required).

Geminal dihalogenation of a ketone using phosphorus pentachloride; the carbonyl carbon is converted to a gem‑dichloride while phosphorus oxychloride is formed as a by‑product. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as benzene or dichloromethane, often with gentle reflux and an inert atmosphere.

Halide exchange (metathesis) synthesis of a metal fluoride; CrCl3 reacts with anhydrous HF (or excess aqueous HF) to replace chloride with fluoride, yielding CrF3 and HCl gas. Typically carried out in a sealed tube or steel reactor at 150–300 °C under anhydrous conditions; no catalyst required; solvent is liquid HF or HF/H2O mixture.

Acid–base protonation (salt metathesis); nitric acid protonates sodium metavanadate to give soluble metavanadic acid (HVO₃) and sodium nitrate; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, typically using dilute HNO₃, no special catalyst required.

Methanolysis (transesterification) of cyclohexyl acetate; methanol attacks the ester carbonyl, exchanging the alkoxy group to produce cyclohexanol and methyl acetate; catalyzed by either a Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or a mild base (e.g., NaOMe); reflux in excess methanol, which also acts as solvent; water is removed to drive the equilibrium.

Acid‑base neutralization of a metal hydroxide with hydrogen bromide, yielding the corresponding metal tribromide and water. Conducted in aqueous solution, usually at ambient temperature or with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution of the hydroxide.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol; PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) converts 2‑pentanol to 2‑pentanone while being reduced to Cr(III) species. Conducted in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often with catalytic pyridine present to neutralize generated HCl.

N‑Methylation of a polyamine via SN2 substitution with methyl iodide in the presence of a carbonate base. The reaction replaces hydrogen atoms on the amine nitrogens with methyl groups, producing the fullyated amine, sodium iodide and water. Commonly carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, refluxing under nitrogen.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (cleavage) of anyl ether using aqueous hydrochloric acid, affording the two corresponding primary alcohols. The process involves protonation of the ether oxygen followed by C‑O bond cleavage. Typically refluxed in aqueous HCl, sometimes with a co‑solvent like ethanol or toluene to improve mixing.

Acid‑base double displacement (metathesis) reaction; nitric acid protonates bromide to generate gaseous hydrogen bromide while the ammonium cation pairs with nitrate to give ammonium nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution, often at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to minimize HBr loss; no catalyst required; typical solvent is water.

Esterification (acetylation) of a phenolic hydroxyl group with acetic anhydride, producing the corresponding phenyl acetate and acetic acid as the by‑product. Usually performed under mild heating in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base catalyst such as pyridine or DMAP to scavenge the liberated acid.

Redox oxidation of mercury selenide by hot concentrated sulfuric acid; the selenide is oxidized to selenium dioxide while mercury is converted to soluble mercury(II) sulfate, producing water as by‑product. Typically performed by refluxing HgSe in 95‑100 % H₂SO₄ at 150–200 °C; no additional solvent or catalyst is required.

Transesterification (ethanolysis) of benzyl prop-2-enoate to give ethyl acrylate and benzyl alcohol; purpose is similar cleavage of the benzyl ester to form the ethyl ester; key transformation is replacement of the benzyl alkoxy group by ethoxy; typical conditions involve excess ethanol as solvent with catalytic acid or base, refluxing for a few hours.

Palladium‑catalyzed C–O cross‑coupling (aryl ether synthesis) of 1,3‑dichlorobenzene with methanol to afford 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene. Uses Pd(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %), tri‑tert‑butylphosphine as ligand, and Cs₂CO₃ as base in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene or dioxane, heated to 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere.

Sulfonyl ester formation by reacting methanol with methanesulfonic anhydride to give methyl methanesulfonate and one equivalent of methanesulfonic acid. Usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine to scavenge the generated acid.

Acyl‑transfer esterification of benzyl alcohol with benzoic anhydride, producing benzyl benzoate and benzoic acid. Reaction proceeds under mild heating (30–60 °C) without catalyst; the acid by‑product can be removed by simple work‑up or by using a tertiary amine base (e.g., pyridine) to drive the equilibrium.

Double displacement precipitation using ammonium hydroxide; aqueous medium; lutetium(III) chloride reacts with NH4OH to precipitate lutetium(III) hydroxide and generate ammonium chloride in solution; performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Enolate acylation of γ‑butyrolactone with acetyl chloride via lithium diisopropylamide (LDA) to give 2‑acetyl‑γ‑butyrolactone. LDA is generated in THF at –78 °C, the lactone is deprotonated to form the enolate, then acetyl chloride is added; the mixture is warmed to –40 °C to 0 °C before quenching. Anhydrous conditions are essential.

Selective reduction of acetophenone to 1‑phenylethanol using sodium borohydride in methanol. The reaction is performed at 0 °C to ambient temperature, typically in MeOH as both solvent and proton source; NaBH₄ is added portion‑wise, and the product is isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation: aqueous potassium chromate and cadmium chloride are mixed, yielding soluble potassium chloride and insoluble cadmium chromate precipitate; performed at room temperature in water, no catalyst required.

N‑acetylation (acylation) of 5‑aminosalicylic acid: acetyl chloride reacts with the amine group in the presence of sodium carbonate, which neutralizes the generated HCl to NaCl and carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O), producing N‑acetyl‑5‑aminosalicylic acid; typically carried out in an anhydrous aprotic solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, base only, no catalyst.

Double displacement precipitation: aqueous sodium carbonate is added to a solution of beryllium sulfate, forming soluble sodium sulfate and sparingly soluble beryllium carbonate that precipitates; conducted at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst needed.

Esterification via acyl substitution: isobutyryl chloride reacts with sodium methoxide (generated in methanol) to give methyl 2‑methylpropanoate (methyl isobutyrate) and sodium chloride; performed in anhydrous methanol, usually 0 °C to reflux, inert atmosphere optional, no additional catalyst.

Metathesis ion exchange to form magnesium lactate: aqueous magnesium nitrate is mixed with sodium lactate, exchanging ions to afford magnesium lactate and sodium nitrate; carried out in water at room temperature, product isolated by evaporation or crystallization, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization and precipitation: hydrofluoric acid reacts with lanthanum trihydroxide to produce water and insoluble lanthanum fluoride precipitate; carried out in aqueous HF solution, typically at low temperature with PTFE equipment, no catalyst, water as solvent.

This is a chlorination of phenols using phosphorus oxychloride, a nucleophilic substitution (deoxy‑chlorination) reaction. It converts 2,4‑dinitrophenol into the corresponding aryl chloride (2,4‑dinitrophenyl chloride) while generating phosphoric acid. The reaction is typically carried out in pyridine, which acts as both solvent and base, at 0 °C to reflux temperature under an inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation; Ba(OH)2 reacts with AgNO3 in aqueous medium, forming insoluble Ag2O precipitate, soluble Ba(NO3)2 and water; often carried out with gentle heating to ensure complete precipitation; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid–base (salt‑formation) reaction; dissolution of praseodymium sesquioxide (Pr₂O₃) in aqueous nitric acid to give praseodymium nitrate (Pr(NO₃)₃) and water (Pr₂O₃ + 6 HNO₃ → 2 Pr(NO₃)₃ + 3 H₂O). Conducted at reflux temperature in water; excess acid ensures complete conversion.

Methanolysis (transesterification). Methanol attacks glycerol diacetate, converting one acetate to a methyl ester, affording glycerol monoacetate and methyl acetate. Carried out in refluxing methanol with a catalytic amount of acid (p‑TsOH) or base (NaOMe).

This is a redox (metal reduction) reaction in which hydroiodic acid reduces gold(III) chloride to gold(I) iodide, with concomitant oxidation of iodide to elemental iodine and formation of hydrogen chloride. The process is usually performed in aqueous solution, often heated gently to accelerate the reaction No external catalyst is needed; the stoichiometry provides the necessary redox equivalents.

This reaction is a nucleophilic acyl substitution where phenyl lithium adds to benzoyl chloride, giving a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to benzophenone after aqueous work‑up. It is carried out at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an aprotic ether such as THF or diethyl ether under an inert nitrogen or argon atmosphere. No catalyst is required, but careful control of temperature prevents over‑addition.

This is an oxidative cleavage of an alkene using potassium permanganate, converting the vinyl group of 2‑vinylpyridine into a carbonyl function and fully oxidizing the terminal carbon to carbon dioxide. The overall transformation yields pyridine‑2‑carboxaldehyde as the main organic product. The reaction is performed in aqueous alkaline KMnO₄ solution, typically heated to reflux; the medium is water or a water‑acetone mixture. No additional catalyst is needed.

This is an oxidation of iodobenzene to the hypervalent iodine(III) species iodosylbenzene (PhI=O) using peroxytrifluoroacetic acid as the oxidant. The reaction proceeds in a non‑protic organic solvent such as dichloromethane at low temperature (0 °C to room temperature) under an inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions. No metal catalyst is employed; the peracid supplies the oxygen atom.

This a cobalt‑catalyzed aerobic oxidation of 2,6‑dimethylpyridine to 2,6‑pyridinedicarboxylic acid (dipicolinic acid). Acetic acid serves both as solvent and as a reactant, while cobalt acetate acts as the catalyst and molecular oxygen is the oxidant. Typical conditions involve heating the reaction mixture in glacial acetic acid at 100–130 °C under an O₂ atmosphere (often at atmospheric pressure or slight overpressure). No additional oxidants are required.

Acid‑carbonate reaction where chromium(III) carbonate reacts with hydroiodic acid to yield chromium(III) iodide, carbon dioxide, and water; carried out in aqueous HI at room temperature or with slight heating, CO₂ evolution indicates completion.

Type: Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (Steglich esterification). Purpose: Convert menthol into the menthyl isovalerate ester for fragrance or flavor applications. Key transformation: The carboxylic acid (isovaleric acid) is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is then attacked by the menthol hydroxyl group; 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) catalyzes the acyl transfer. By‑product: dicyclohexylurea precipitates. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, dichloromethane (or THF) as solvent, catalytic DMAP (0.1 equiv). Reaction is usually performed under dry, nitrogen atmosphere and the mixture is stirred until completion (1–12 h).

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; cadmium bromide exchanges anions with sodium fluoride, yielding cadmium fluoride precipitate and soluble sodium bromide. Carried out in aqueous medium, room temperature, with stirring; filtration separates the solid CdF2.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); introduces a nitro group para to the biphenyl linkage to give 4‑nitrobiphenyl; H of the aromatic ring is replaced by NO2 and water is formed; carried out in a mixed acid mixture of concentrated H₂SO₄ and HNO₃, typically at 0–5 °C initially then allowed to warm to room temperature; no external solvent is required, the reaction medium itself is the sulfuric acid.

Type: Direct combination/synthesis of a metal fluoride (high‑temperature solid‑state fluorination). Purpose: Preparation of europium(III) fluoride, an inorganic salt used in phosphors and lasers. Key transformation: Oxidation of elemental europium (0) to Eu³⁺ and reduction of fluorine (F₂) to fluoride anion. No solvent; reaction is a redox process. Typical conditions: Conducted in a fluorination furnace or sealed nickel/tantalum vessel at 300–500 °C under a flow of dry F₂ gas, often with a slight excess of fluorine to ensure complete conversion. Inert handling is required to avoid moisture.

Acid–base double displacement; converts cadmium cyanide to soluble cadmium nitrate while protonating cyanide to volatile hydrogen cyanide; key transformation is CN⁻ → HCN and Cd²⁺ exchanging anion to NO₃⁻; typically carried out in aqueous solution with dilute nitric acid at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to limit HCN loss; no catalyst, water as solvent.

Type: Benzylic oxidative hydroxylation (radical oxidation of an alkyl side chain). Purpose: Introduce a hydroxyl group at the benzylic carbon to afford 1‑phenyl‑1‑propanol, a valuable intermediate in fine‑chemical synthesis. Key transformation: Hydrogen peroxide generates hydroxyl radicals (often via a metal catalyst such as Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, or Ti‑silicalite), which abstract a hydrogen from the benzylic position; subsequent recombination with HO· yields the benzylic alcohol. Typical conditions: Aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., MeCN/H₂O), catalytic amount of FeSO₄ (Fenton) or CuCl₂ (0.05–0.2 equiv), ambient to 60 °C, slow addition of 30 % H₂O₂ (1.5–2 equiv). Reaction monitored by TLC or GC; work‑up involves extraction and purification by distillation or chromatography.

Type: Reductive amination of an aldehyde. Purpose: Synthesize bufotenine (5‑hydroxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine), a psychoactive indole alkaloid. Key transformation: The aldehyde group of 5‑hydroxyindole‑3‑acetaldehyde reacts with dimethylamine to form an iminium ion, which is then reduced to the secondary amine by sodium cyanoborohydride. Typical conditions: Dimethylamine (as gas or 2 M solution in MeOH), aldehyde (1 equiv), NaCNBH₃ (1.2–1.5 equiv) in methanol or ethanol, mildly acidic pH (≈5–6) adjusted with AcOH, stirred at rt for 2–12 h. Reaction is performed under nitrogen to prevent oxidation. Final product isolated by evaporation and purification (e.g., column chromatography).

Base‑catalyzed saponification (alkaline hydrolysis) of an ethyl ester. Ethyl 3‑hydroxypentanoate is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide (often in ethanol/water) at reflux, cleaving the ethoxy group to give the sodium salt of the corresponding acid (sodium 3‑hydroxypentanoate) and ethanol. The reaction proceeds to completion under mild heating; after cooling, the product can be isolated by evaporation of ethanol and precipitation or crystallization of the sodium salt.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction: hydride ion from lithium hydride attacks methyl bromide to give methane and lithium bromide; used for dehalogenation or methane generation; key transformation CH3Br → CH4; typically performed in aprotic ether solvents (THF, diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, often under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); gaseous or aqueous ammonia reacts with hexanoic acid to form ammonium hexanoate and water. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess ammonia may be used to drive completion. No catalyst required. Purpose: generation of the ammonium carboxylate salt.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl mesylate by a secondary amine. Purpose: Generate N,N‑dimethylcyclohexylamine, a tertiary amine, while releasing methanesulfonic acid. Key transformation: The nitrogen lone pair of dimethylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon of cyclohexyl methanesulfonate, displacing methanesulfonate (mesylate) as a leaving group, which is protonated to give methanesulfonic acid. Typical conditions: Polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, excess dimethylamine (2–3 equiv), reaction heated to 50–80 °C for 4–12 h under nitrogen. The acidic by‑product may be neutralized in‑situ with a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) if desired. Product isolated by aqueous work‑up and distillation or extraction.

Acidification (protonation) of the methanesulfonate salt. Sodium methanesulfonate is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid, converting the salt back to methanesulfonic acid and forming sodium chloride in solution. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; excess HCl ensures complete protonation.

Type: Hydrolysis of a silyl ester (silyl ether cleavage). Purpose: Convert triethylsilyl benzoate into benzoic acid and recover triethylsilanol. Key transformation: Water attacks the silicon‑oxygen bond, displacing the benzoate as benzoic acid and generating the silanol. Typical conditions: Aqueous medium (often neat water or aqueous ethanol), ambient temperature or gentle heating (25–50 °C), sometimes catalyzed by a weak acid (e.g., AcOH, pH ≈ 5) to accelerate the reaction. Reaction completes within minutes to an hour; the products are isolated by extraction (benzoic acid into organic layer) and evaporation of the silanol.

Halogenolysis of trimethylaluminum with hydrogen chloride. HCl protonates a methyl group of Me3Al, releasing methane and generating dimethylaluminum chloride (Me2AlCl). The reaction proceeds under strictly anhydrous conditions, typically in non‑coordinating solvents like toluene or hexane at 0 °C to room temperature, under inert gas. It is employed to prepare mixed alkyl‑halide aluminum species used as cocatalysts in Ziegler‑Natta polymerizations.

General type: double displacement precipitation (metathesis) in aqueous medium; purpose: produce calcium fluoride and regenerate manganese(II) chloride; key transformation: MnF2 + CaCl2 → CaF2 (precipitates) + MnCl2 (soluble); typical conditions: aqueous MnF2 mixed with CaCl2 solution at ambient temperature, CaF2 precipitates; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Condensation (hydrazone formation); used to protect aldehydes or as a step toward Fischer indole synthesis; converts the carbonyl C=O of 1H‑pyrrole‑2‑carbaldehyde into a C=N‑NPh linkage yielding pyrrole‑2‑carboxaldehyde phenylhydrazone with loss of water; typically performed by refluxing the aldehyde with phenylhydrazine in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid to promote dehydration; water is removed as by‑product.

Halide exchange (double displacement) reaction; bromide from HBr replaces chloride on gold(I) chloride to give gold(I) bromide and HCl. Typically carried out in aqueous solution or polar aprotic solvent at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid–carbonate reaction; hydrogen telluride (a weak acid) reacts with zinc carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O while forming zinc telluride. Conducted in water, often under an inert atmosphere to avoid H₂Te loss; reflux may be used. No catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of sodium sesquicarbonate; heating decomposes the double salt into carbon dioxide, water vapor, and sodium carbonate. Performed by heating the solid to 200–300 °C in a dry furnace; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of bis(2‑bromoethyl) ether with sodium methoxide to afford bis(2‑methoxyethyl) ether and sodium bromide. Reaction carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, typically at reflux under inert gas; stoichiometric NaOMe acts as both nucleophile and base.

Metathesis (halide exchange) reaction between ammonium bifluoride and samarium(III) chloride, yielding samarium(III) fluoride, ammonium chloride and free hydrogen fluoride. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to promote crystallization of SmF₃; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of an acid chloride with phenol; produces phenyl 3‑chloropropionate, an ester that can be further manipulated (e.g., polymer or coupling reactions). Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as CH2Cl2 or THF with a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) at 0 °C to room temperature; HCl is scavenged by the base.

Acid–base reaction of ammonium thiocyanate with cobalt(II) hydroxide, producing cobalt(II thiocyanate, ammonia gas and water. Performed in aqueous medium at modest temperature; ammonia can be driven off; no catalyst needed.
Synthesis. Chlorination of gallium to form gallium chloride. Reacts under heat in a chlorine atmosphere; gallium melts and reacts vigorously with chlorine gas. No solvent or catalyst used.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction: aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes nickel(II) carbonate, exchanging anions to give soluble sodium carbonate and insoluble nickel(II) hydroxide precipitate. Typically carried out at ambient temperature in water with vigorous stirring; no catalyst required.

Oxidation reaction: hydrogen peroxide oxidizes p‑phenylenediamine to the corresponding p‑benzoquinone diimine, with concomitant formation of water. Usually performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media (e.g., water/acetone) at room temperature; the reaction may be acid‑ or neutral‑catalyzed but often proceeds without added catalyst.

Epoxidation (oxidation) of an alkene: hydrogen peroxide adds across the double bond of 1‑butene to give 1,2‑epoxybutane and water. Conducted with a metal catalyst (e.g., Ti‑silicalite (TS‑1), tungsten‑based complexes, or molybdenum salts) in an organic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, typically at 0–50 °C to control exotherm.

Reduction of a metal oxide by hydrogen (hydrogenation): platinum(II) oxide is reduced by hydrogen gas to metallic platinum, producing water as the only by‑product. Performed in the gas phase or in a tubular furnace under a flow of H₂ at 200–300 °C; no solvent or additional catalyst is needed.

Acid–base neutralisation forming a metal lactate: lactic acid reacts with zinc oxide to yield zinc dilactate (zinc lactate) and water. Usually carried out by heating a mixture of the acid and ZnO in a sealed vessel or under reflux in water or a minimal amount of solvent; the reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution: cerium(III) nitrate reacts with ammonium chloride, exchanging anions to afford ammonium nitrate and cerium(III) chloride. Conducted in water at room temperature or with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution; no catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation (acid‑base neutralization). Aqueous ammonium hydroxide (a weak base) reacts with soluble beryllium nitrate; the insoluble beryllium hydroxide precipitates while ammonium nitrate remains dissolved. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

General type: chemical reduction of a metal halide. Purpose: isolation of metallic ruthenium (often as a powder or nanoparticle). Key transformations: RuCl3 reduced from Ru(III) to Ru(0); NaBH4 oxidized to boric acid (B(OH)3); NaCl formed as by‑product; H2 gas evolved. Typical conditions: aqueous or ethanolic solution at 0–25 °C, NaBH4 added slowly under nitrogen or argon, stirring; occasional use of stabilizers (e.g., PVP) for nanoparticle control. No additional catalyst.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to the corresponding acid chloride using oxalyl chloride; oxalyl chloride reacts with the acid, generating CO, CO₂, and HCl gases and producing the acyl chloride; performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to activate the reagent, and the reaction is stirred until gas evolution stops.

Intramolecular lactonization (dehydrative cyclization) of o‑hydroxyphenylacetic acid to 2(3H)-benzofuranone (coumarin). Typically heated neat or in a high‑boiling polar solvent (e.g., polyphosphoric acid, POCl₃, or concentrated H₂SO₄) at 150–200 °C to promote cyclization and loss of water.

Same alkaline hydrolysis as above but using aqueous potassium hydroxide; yields 2‑chlorophenol and potassium acetate. Reaction conditions mirror those for NaOH: aqueous KOH, heating (reflux or 60‑80 °C), followed by acid work‑up to recover the phenol.

Halogenation (chlorination) of white phosphorus; elemental P₄ reacts with chlorine gas to produce phosphorus trichloride (PCl₃) when chlorine is limiting; common laboratory method: heat finely divided white phosphorus under a stream of dilute Cl₂ in an inert atmosphere (nitrogen) at 250–300 °C; reaction can be run in carbon tetrachloride or anhydrous conditions; no catalyst.

Metal‑halogen exchange to generate an organolithium reagent; purpose is to prepare hexyl lithium for use in synthesis. Key transformation: Li inserts into the C–Cl bond, forming hexyl‑Li and LiCl. Typical conditions: dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen or argon; reagents must be moisture‑free; no additional catalyst.

Electrophilic iodination of indole using N‑iodosuccinimide: NIS iodates the C‑3 position of indole, affording 3‑iodoindole and succinimide; carried out in CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN at 0‑25 °C, often under inert atmosphere to prevent over‑oxidation.

Nucleophilic methylation (esterification) using diazomethane. Diazomethane adds a methyl group to the carboxyl of acetic acid, forming methyl acetate and releasing nitrogen gas. Typically performed in anhydrous diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; the reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Oxidation of the secondary alcohol 3‑phenylbutan‑2‑ol to the corresponding ketone 3‑phenylbutan‑2‑one using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) as a mild, stoichiometric oxidant. Reaction carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, providing a clean conversion without over‑oxidation to the carboxylic acid.

Direct halogenation of elemental palladium; bromine oxidizes Pd⁰ to Pd²⁺ while Br₂ is reduced to Br⁻, producing palladium(II) bromide; usually conducted by adding Br₂ to fine Pd metal powder in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂) at room temperature or slightly warmed.

Isopropyl pentanoate + methanol → methyl pentanoate + isopropanol  
General type: transesterification (alkoxy exchange). Purpose is to replace the isopropyl alkoxy group with a methyl group, generating a different ester. Key transformation: the isopropoxy group is displaced by methoxy, yielding methyl pentanoate and releasing isopropanol. Typical conditions: reflux in excess methanol (4–10 equiv) with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid, 1–5 mol %) or base (e.g., NaOMe, 1–2 mol %). The reaction may be driven to completion by continuous removal of isopropanol. Common solvent: methanol itself acts as both reagent and solvent.

Acid–base protonation (metathesis). Concentrated nitric acid protonates ammonium phosphomolybdate, converting the ammonium salt to phosphomolybdic acid and generating soluble ammonium nitrate. Carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to ensure dissolution; no catalyst is required.

Metathesis (anion exchange) to prepare erbium(III) acetate. Erbium(III) nitrate reacts with excess acetic acid in aqueous solution, swapping nitrate for acetate to give erbium(III) acetate and liberating nitric acid. The mixture is typically heated (reflux) to drive off volatile nitric acid; water is the solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Thionation reaction; purpose is to replace the carbonyl oxygens of uracil with sulfur atoms to give thiouracil; key transformation is C=O → C=S (or C=S at one or both positions) while phosphorus pentasulfide is reduced to phosphorus pentoxide; typically carried out by heating uracil with P2S5 under reflux in a high‑boiling aprotic solvent such as pyridine or xylene, often under inert atmosphere.

SN2 alkylation of dimethylamine with ethyl iodide; more reactive iodide provides the same transformation to N,N‑dimethylethylamine and HI; usually performed in acetone or acetonitrile at low temperature (0 °C to room temperature) with excess dimethylamine or a non‑nucleophilic base to capture HI.

Double displacement and precipitation of silver oxide. Silver acetate reacts with potassium hydroxide in aqueous medium; silver oxide precipitates as a brown solid, while potassium acetate remains in solution and water is formed. Performed at room temperature or with slight heating; stirring in water suffices, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation). Lithium amide (LiNH2) attacks the carbonyl carbon of benzoyl chloride, displacing chloride to yield benzamide and lithium chloride. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether at low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base salt formation whereby 2‑aminoethanol is protonated by hydroiodic acid to give the corresponding hydroiodide salt; performed in aqueous solution, often at 0‑25 °C; purpose is to isolate the amine as a stable, water‑soluble salt.
Acid–base salt formation; bismuth oxide reacts with dilute nitric acid (aqueous, controlled pH, ambient to gentle heating) to give bismuth subnitrate and water; no special catalyst, water is solvent.

Palladium‑catalyzed C–H carboxylation (CO₂ fixation) of pyridine to form picolinic acid. Palladium acetate, reduced in situ to Pd(0) by triphenylphosphine, activates the 2‑position of pyridine; CO₂ inserts to give the carboxylate which is protonated to picolinic acid. Conducted under CO₂ pressure (1–10 atm) in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 80–120 °C; inert atmosphere (N₂) is used; PPh₃ serves as supporting ligand.

Precipitation (neutralization) reaction; iron(III) pyrophosphate reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form insoluble iron(III) hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium pyrophosphate; carried out in water, often with excess NaOH and mild heating to ensure complete precipitation; no catalyst; water is the solvent.

Neutralisation of terbium(III) hydroxide with acetic acid to give terbium(III) acetate and water; standard preparation of the acetate salt from the hydroxide precursor. Hydroxide groups are protonated, yielding the acetate and water. Conducted at ambient temperature or mild heating (30–60 °C) in aqueous or glacial acetic acid, with stirring until the solid dissolves; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization; two equivalents of gluconic acid react with one equivalent of magnesium oxide in aqueous solution (often with mild heating) to form magnesium gluconate salt and water; solvent is water, no catalyst required.

Oxidation (redox) of TEMPO; 2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine is oxidized by m‑chloroperbenzoic acid in an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, yielding the stable radical TEMPO (tetramethylpiperidine‑1‑oxyl) and reducing the peracid to m‑chlorobenzoic acid; no additional catalyst.

Hydrolysis of mixed anhydride; acetic‑formic anhydride reacts with water (usually in a dilute aqueous medium at room temperature or slight warming) to cleave the anhydride, producing equimolar acetic acid and formic acid; no catalyst needed.

Type: Acid‑induced decomposition of a metal cyanide complex (acid hydrolysis). Purpose: release hydrogen cyanide gas from ferricyanide. Key transformation: protonation of the cyanide ligands leads to liberation of HCN; the iron(III) center forms FeCl₃, and potassium is converted to KCl. Typical conditions: concentrated HCl aqueous solution, low to moderate temperature; HCN gas is evolved and captured, reaction performed in a fume hood.

Hydrolysis of a silanolate; water protonates sodium trimethylsilanolate, yielding sodium hydroxide and trimethylsilanol (Me3SiOH). This simple acid‑base process is used to generate the silanol or to quench excess silanolate. Occurs readily at ambient temperature in aqueous solution; no special reagents or catalysts required.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement) to generate silver triflate; AgNO₃ + NaOTf → AgOTf + NaNO₃; typically conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, acetonitrile orCN/H₂O) at rt; AgOTf precipitates (or remains soluble) and is isolated by filtration; purpose is preparation of a Lewis‑acidic silver salt for catalysis.

Acid‑catalyzed cleavage (hydrolysis) of vinyl ether; vinyl isobutyl ether in the presence of aqueous acid (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) and heat undergoes hydration and C–O bond cleavage to give acetaldehyde and isobutanol; solvent is water or water/organic mixture; acid acts as catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; purpose: convert nonyl acetate to 1‑nonanol and acetic acid; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon of the ester, breaking the C–O bond; typical conditions: reflux in aqueous sulfuric acid (–10 % w/w); solvent: water mixed with conc. H₂SO₄.

Aqueous ozonolysis (oxidative degradation) of caffeine yielding 1,3,7‑trimethyluric acid with molecular oxygen as by‑product. Ozone is bubbled through an aqueous caffeine solution (pH ≈ 7) at 0‑5 °C, then the mixture is stirred at ambient temperature to complete oxidation. No added catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds via formation of peroxide intermediates that decompose to O₂.

Haloform (bromoform) reaction: base‑promoted exhaustive bromination of acetone followed by cleavage to give bromoform (CHBr₃) and acetate ion, which is isolated as potassium acetate after work‑up. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH (or NaOH) solution, addition of Br₂ dropwise at 0 °C, then warming to reflux (~60 °C). The reaction is performed in water or a water/ethanol mixture; no metal catalyst is needed.

O‑methylation (alkylation) of 5‑hydroxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine using methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate; purpose: protect or modify the phenolic OH; key transformation: transfer of a methyl group from CF₃SO₂OCH₃ to the phenolate oxygen to afford O‑methylbufotenine; typical conditions: aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or acetonitrile), 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; catalyst: none (methyl triflate is a strong methylating agent).

Esterification (acylation) of a tertiary alcohol using acetic anhydride; used to form tert‑butyl acetate as a protected or functionalized ester. The hydroxyl oxygen attacks one acetyl group of acetic anhydride, displacing acetate and generating acetic acid as by‑product. Typically performed at 0 °C‑room temperature under anhydrous conditions, often with pyridine or a catalytic amount of DMAP as base/acid scavenger; common solvents are dry dichloromethane or the reaction can be run neat.

Base‑mediated methylation of N‑methylhydrazine with dimethyl sulfate; purpose: produce N,N‑dimethylhydrazine; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the hydrazine nitrogen on Me₂SO₄ displacing sulfate to give a dimethylated nitrogen; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH, 0–25 °C, water or water‑organic mixed solvent; by‑product: sodium sulfate.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction of erbium hydroxide with sodium carbonate; purpose is to convert insoluble Er(OH)3 into erbium carbonate precipitate while generating sodium hydroxide in solution; key transformation: 2 Er(OH)3 + 3 Na2CO3 → Er2(CO3)3↓ + 6 NaOH; typical conditions: aqueous medium, stirring at room temperature to ~50 °C; water as solvent; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of oleum; purpose: generate free SO₃ for subsequent sulfonations; key transformation: dissociation of the fuming sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄·SO₃) into H₂SO₄ and SO₃; typical conditions: gentle heating (50–150 °C) under reduced pressure or with a sweep gas; solvent: oleum itself; no additional catalyst required.

Selective aldehyde reduction; NaBH4 reduces 4‑methylbenzaldehyde to 4‑methylbenzyl alcohol; performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, using 1–2 equiv NaBH4, followed by quench with water and extraction.

Intramolecular dehydration (anhydride formation); converts 2‑phenylsuccinic acid into its cyclic anhydride (3‑phenyloxolane‑2,5‑dione). The reaction involves loss of one molecule of water via heating, often at 180‑200 °C, or by treatment with a dehydrating agent such as acetic anhydride or thionyl chloride in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., toluene, dichloromethane). No external catalyst is required; the reaction proceeds through intramolecular nucleophilic attack of the carboxylate on the adjacent carbonyl.

Sulfidation of neodymium oxide; purpose is to produce neodymium sulfide; Nd2O3 reacts with H2S gas, generating H2O and Nd2S3 (or NdS); carried out at 800‑1000 °C under a mixture of H2S and H2 (or inert carrier) to ensure reducing environment; solid‑gas reaction, no liquid solvent; tube furnace with gas‑tight inlet.

Copper‑catalyzed azide substitution (Ullmann‑type C–N coupling); replaces the iodine of 4‑iodopyridine with an azide to give 4azidopyridine. Typical conditions employ CuI (5–10 mol %), NaN₃ (1.2–2 equiv), and a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heated to 80–100 °C under nitrogen. The copper(I) complex activates the aryl halide and facilitates nucleophilic attack by azide.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction in aqueous solution; potassium formate exchanges anions with silver nitrate, precipitating sparingly soluble silver formate while forming soluble potassium nitrate; performed at ambient temperature, often with stirring and filtration to isolate the solid; used to prepare silver formate.

Catalytic hydrogenation reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; purpose is to convert 4‑methoxybenzoic acid into 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol while generating water. Key transformation is reduction of the –COOH group to –CH2OH. Typical conditions: hydrogen gas at 1–3 atm, 10 % Pd/C (10 wt % relative to substrate), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature from room temperature to reflux, reaction performed under inert atmosphere.

Direct combination (halogenation) of elemental arsenic with fluorine gas to afford arsenic trifluoride (AsF₃). The reaction is carried out in a fluorination apparatus at low to moderate temperatures (0–25 °C) to control the vigorous exotherm, often in a stainless‑steel or nickel reactor under a dry inert atmosphere. No solvent or catalyst is used; the stoichiometric reaction is 2 As + 3 F₂ → 2 AsF₃.

Solid‑state acid‑base reaction between a basic oxide and an acidic sulfate; yields scandium(III) oxide and calcium sulfate; 3 CaO + Sc₂(SO₄)₃ → Sc₂O₃ + 3 CaSO₄; powders are blended and heated to 800–1000 °C; calcium sulfate precipitates as a solid; performed without solvent; inert atmosphere optional.

Double‑displacement (acid‑base metathesis) between ammonium hydroxide and potassium hexafluorosilicate, yielding potassium hydroxide and ammonium hexafluorosilicate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, the reaction mixes stoichiometric amounts of NH₄OH and K₂SiF₆, allowing ion exchange: 2 NH₄OH + K₂SiF₆ → 2 KOH + (NH₄)₂SiF₆. No special catalyst is required.

Acid‑base protonation of sodium thioacetate by hydrochloric acid to generate thioacetic acid and sodium chloride. The reaction is performed in water or a mixed aqueous‑organic solvent at room temperature: HCl + NaSCOCH₃ → HSCOCH₃ + NaCl. It proceeds spontaneously; no catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base neutralization; protonates the carboxylate anion of sodium octanoate to liberate the free fatty acid, octanoic acid, while forming sodium bisulfate. Conducted in aqueous solution with dilute sulfuric acid at ambient temperature; no special solvent required.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) or copper‑catalyzed Ullmann amination converting 2‑chloropyridine to 2‑aminopyridine using gaseous ammonia. Conventional SNAr requires high temperature (180–220 °C) in a sealed tube with excess NH₃ in a polar solvent (e.g., ethanol, DMF). Alternatively, a CuI (5–10 mol %) or Pd‑based catalytic system with a ligand (e.g., L-proline) can be used at 80–120 °C under NH₃ pressure, affording the amine product efficiently.

Nucleophilic addition of an aryl lithium to trimethyl borate followed by aqueous work‑up; a typical method for preparing aryl‑boronic acids used in Suzuki‑Miyaura couplings. Performed in anhydrous THF at –78 °C to 0 °C, then quenched with water or dilute acid to give the boronic acid.

Base‑catalyzed alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of a methyl ester to the corresponding carboxylic acid. NaOH solution hydrolyzes methyl 3,4‑dimethoxybenzoate to the sodium carboxylate, which on acidification furnishes 3,4‑dimethoxybenzoic acid and methanol. Usually reflux in aqueous (or mixed aqueous/ethanol) solution.

Oxidation of a secondary benzylic alcohol to a ketone using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); mild, selective oxidation that stops at the carbonyl without over‑oxidation; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; PCC acts stoichiometrically and generates pyridinium chloride as by‑product.

Ligand substitution/hydrogenation of a metal carbonyl; purpose is to generate the iron carbonyl hydride complex FeH₂(CO)₄. Key transformation: one CO ligand is displaced by H₂, which inserts as two hydride ligands, releasing CO gas. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a sealed reactor, temperature 50–100 °C, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). Common solvent: dry tetrahydrofuran (THF) or toluene; the iron carbonyl itself acts as the reactive species, no external catalyst needed.

Acid–base condensation of sulfamic acid with aqueous ammonia to afford sulfamide (NH₂SO₂NH₂) and water. Reaction proceeds at ambient to moderate temperature in water; no catalyst required, often carried out under reflux to drive off water.

Halide metathesis (double‑replacement) between scandium trichloride and rubidium fluoride to give scandium fluoride and rubidium chloride. Typically carried out in the solid state or molten salt at elevated temperature (≈300–500 °C) to promote ion exchange; no solvent or catalyst is normally used.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an ester (butyl acetate) over palladium on carbon, reducing the C–O bond to give the corresponding primary alcohols, n‑butanol and ethanol. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a solvent such as ethanol or THF at 50–80 °C with Pd/C as the catalyst.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to the corresponding acyl chloride using oxalyl chloride; a typical acid chloride formation. Performed in dry dichloromethane (or chloroform) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to activate the reagent. By‑products are CO, CO₂ and HCl gas.

Grignard addition to an ester; used to form tertiary alcohols. Methylmagnesium bromide adds twice to ethyl propionate, the ethoxy fragment is released as ethanol and the carbonyl carbon becomes a tertiary center, giving 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol after aqueous work‑up. Conducted under inert atmosphere in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux, followed by acid quench.

Acid‑base (salt metathesis) reaction; purpose is to exchange cations between an ammonium salt and a metal carboxylate, yielding the ammonium carboxylate and sodium chloride. Typically performed by dissolving ammonium chloride and sodium valerate in water, stirring at ambient temperature, then isolating the precipitated or soluble salts.

Nucleophilic S‑alkylation with diazomethane; methylates thiophenol to give methyl phenyl sulfide while liberating N₂ gas. Reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as diethyl ether or dichloromethane, under nitrogen, with careful handling of the hazardous diazomethane.

Oxidative dehydrogenation; converts a saturated tetrahydroquinoline to the aromatic quinoline; key transformation is removal of two hydrogen atoms (formation of two C=C bonds) to achieve aromatization; typically performed with aqueous hydrogen peroxide in concentrated sulfuric acid, often at 0–25 °C or under reflux; the acid medium serves both as solvent and catalyst.

Acid–base metathesis (salt exchange); converts cadmium acetate to cadmium nitrate while liberating acetic acid; performed in aqueous solution by adding dilute nitric acid to a solution of cadmium acetate, typically at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic addition of an organolithium reagent to a carbonyl (addition of n‑propyl lithium to acetone). The n‑propyl anion attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tertiary alkoxide that is protonated on aqueous work‑up to give 3‑methyl‑3‑pentanol. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF at –78 °C to –20 °C under nitrogen or argon; the reaction is quenched with dilute NH₄Cl or water.

Chloromethane + potassium hydroxide -> methanol + potassium chloride: alkaline hydrolysis (SN2) analogous to NaOH case; purpose is preparation of methanol; key transformation is OH⁻ attack on CH3Cl yielding CH3OH and KCl; carried out in aqueous KOH (1–2 M) under reflux; water or water/ethanol mixture is used as solvent; reaction proceeds similarly to sodium hydroxide.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration) of toluene; introduces a nitro group to the aromatic ring, producing nitrotoluene (mainly ortho/para isomers) and water. Conducted with a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ (nitrating mixture) at 50–60 °C, usually in the reaction flask without additional solvent or in glacial acetic acid.

Oxidation of a primary alkyl halide; benzyl chloride is oxidized by hot aqueous potassium permanganate under reflux (often in alkaline or neutral medium) to give benzoic acid, with MnO2 precipitate formed as by‑product.

Direct solid-state synthesis; preparation of gallium(III) sulfide (Ga2S3). Gallium metal is oxidized from 0 to +3 and sulfur reduced to S2‑, forming the sulfide lattice. Conducted by grinding Ga and S together and heating in an inert atmosphere or sealed tube at 500‑700 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 3‑butylidenephthalide; saturates the exocyclic C=C bond to afford butylphthalide. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–3 atm) with a palladium on carbon (Pd/C) or PtO₂ catalyst in ethanol or methanol, at room temperature to gentle reflux until uptake ceases.

Oxidative dearomatization of phenol to para‑benzoquinone. Perbenzoic acid oxidizes phenol two electrons, forming p‑benzoquinone and benzoic acid. The reaction proceeds in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, typically at 0 °C to rt; the peracid acts as both oxidant and oxygen donor, no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a primary alkyl; purpose is to convert 1‑chlorodecane to 1‑decanol; key transformation is replacement of the chlorine atom by a hydroxyl group producing HCl as by‑product; typically carried out by heating the chloride with excess water or aqueous acid/base (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄ or NaOH) under reflux; common solvent is water or aqueous ethanol; catalyst may be a mineral acid (H₂SO₄) for acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis or base for alkaline hydrolysis.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (de‑protection) of a thioacetal back to the carbonyl compound. 4‑Methyl‑1,3‑dithiolane is hydrogenated over palladium on carbon under H₂ gas, cleaving the C‑S bonds to regenerate acetaldehyde and 1,2‑ethanedithiol. Conducted in a solvent such as ethyl acetate or methanol at room temperature and atmospheric pressure of H₂; the Pd/C catalyst is filtered off after completion.

Hydrolysis of a metal alkoxide (vanadium(V) triisopropoxide oxide); purpose is to generate vanadium(V) oxide and recover isopropanol; key transformation involves cleavage of V–O‑iPr bonds by water forming V=O (often precipitating as V₂O₅) and iPrOH; usually performed by adding measured water to a solution of the alkoxide at ambient temperature or mild reflux; solvent can be a non‑polar organic solvent such as toluene or THF; no additional catalyst required.

Knoevenagel–Doebner condensation (base‑catalyzed) of malonic acid with 2,4‑dihydroxybenzaldehyde, followed by decarboxylation to produce 2,4‑dihydroxycinnamic acid. The aldehyde and malonic acid are mixed in ethanol (or methanol) with a catalytic amount of piperidine (or pyridine) and a few drops of acetic acid; the mixture is refluxed for several hours. Decarboxylation occurs in situ, releasing CO₂ and water, yielding the cinnamic acid derivative. No metal catalyst is required.

This is a dissolution/acid‑base reaction where antimony(III) sulfide is treated with hydrochloric acid to give antimony(III) chloride in solution and hydrogen sulfide gas. The main transformation is replacement of sulfide by chloride ions, with H₂S liberated. The reaction is performed by adding solid Sb₂S₃ to concentrated or 6 M HCl, often with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to accelerate gas evolution. The system is typically set up in a fume hood or closed apparatus to capture H₂S. No catalyst is needed; water is the solvent.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an acetate ester; NaOH hydrolyzes the acetate group of 2‑bromoethyl acetate to give 2‑bromoethanol and sodium acetate. Performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) with reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h; water is the solvent and the reaction is driven to completion by excess base.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium bisulfite; purpose is to release gaseous ammonia and sulfur dioxide; key transformation is simple breakdown: NH₄HSO₃ → NH₃ + H₂O + SO₂; usually carried out by gentle heating (≈50–100 °C) in a sealed vessel or apparatus that allows gas collection; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Acidic redox reaction between sulfuric acid, ferrous sulfate and ammonium dichromate; purpose is to oxidize Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ while reducing Cr⁶⁺ to Cr³⁺; key transformations include dichromate oxidation of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, concomitant reduction of Cr⁶⁺ to Cr³⁺, and formation of ferric sulfate, chromium(III) sulfate, ammonium sulfate and water; performed in aqueous solution with excess concentrated H₂SO₄, typically heated to 80–100 °C; solvent is water; the strong acid provides the medium, no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; ethyl trifluoroacetate reacts with methanol to give methyl trifluoroacetate and ethanol; performed under reflux with catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base; excess methanol serves as solvent and removal of ethanol shifts equilibrium toward product.

Esterification via acylation of phenol with butyric anhydride; purpose is to produce phenyl butyrate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the phenoxide oxygen on one carbonyl of the anhydride, yielding the phenyl ester and liberating butyric acid; commonly carried out under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene with a base/catalyst like pyridine or DMAP to scavenge the released acid; solvent: dichloromethane (or toluene); catalyst: pyridine or DMAP.

Acid‑salt conversion (protonation). Barium metaborate reacts with hydrochloric acid to regenerate boric acid and form soluble barium chloride; conducted in aqueous HCl at room temperature, the boric acid can be removed by filtration or evaporation.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: deprotect the acetate protecting group to liberate 3,5‑dichlorophenol and generate sodium acetate as a benign by‑product. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl of 3,5‑dichlorophenyl acetate, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to give phenolate and acetate; phenolate is protonated on work‑up to phenol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) at reflux (or 60–80 °C) for 1–3 h; reaction can be run in water or a water/ethanol mixture. No special catalyst required; after completion the mixture is acidified to pH ≈ 5–6 and extracted.

Thermal or photolytic cleavage of a disilane (Si₂H₆) to generate silane (SiH₄) and a silylene (SiH₂). This is a bond‑scission reaction used to access the highly reactive divalent silicon species. Typically carried out under an inert atmosphere at 400–600 °C or by UV irradiation; no solvent is required, and silica or metal catalysts may be employed to lower the temperature.

N‑alkylation of phenothiazine with 2‑chloro‑N,N‑dimethylethylamine via an SN2 pathway followed by acid‑base neutralization with HCl to afford promethazine hydrochloride; typically carried out in ethanol or isopropanol at reflux, using a base (e.g., NaOH) to deprotonate the phenothiazine nitrogen, then treating the product with aqueous HCl; this reaction synthesizes the phenothiazine antihistamine drug.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of acenaphthene to acenaphthylene using palladium on carbon; a solid‑state oxidative dehydrogenation performed by heating (≈300 °C) under an inert atmosphere with Pd/C as the heterogeneous catalyst, often in a sealed tube without solvent; the reaction removes two hydrogens to generate the more unsaturated aromatic acenaphthylene.

Acid‑catalyzed Markovnikov hydration of 2‑pentene to give 2‑pentanol; an electrophilic addition of water in dilute sulfuric acid (5‑10 % w/w) at 60‑80 °C in aqueous medium, where the alkene is protonated, water attacks the more substituted carbocation, and deprotonation yields the secondary alcohol; the purpose is synthesis of 2‑pentanol.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein) reaction; purpose is to replace the bromine atom with iodine on a long‑chain alkyl halide; proceeds via SN2 displacement of bromide by iodide; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone (or acetonitrile) with excess KI; reflux heating drives the reaction and precipitated potassium bromide shifts the equilibrium toward 1‑iodohexadecane.

Single‑replacement acid‑metal reaction of lithium metal with dilute sulfuric acid to produce hydrogen gas and lithium sulfate; performed at 0‑25 °C in aqueous solution, adding Li gradually to 10 % H2SO4 to control vigorous gas evolution; the reaction serves as a laboratory source of H2 or to generate Li2SO4.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type) reduction of carbon tetrachloride by excess hydroiodic acid to form carbon tetraiodide and hydrochloric acid; conducted by refluxing CCl4 with concentrated HI (80‑100 °C) in an alcoholic or aqueous solvent, sometimes with a metal catalyst, under an inert atmosphere; the purpose is preparation of CI4 for further organic transformations.

Acidic cleavage of magnesium silicide using hydrochloric acid; an acid‑catalyzed reaction that yields silane gas and soluble magnesium chloride; carried out by adding solid Mg₂Si to cold dilute HCl, stirring at 0–25 °C to control gas evolution; no additional solvent beyond the aqueous acid.

Direct halogenation; elemental selenium reacts with bromine vapor to form selenium bromide (commonly SeBr₂ or SeBr₄, depending on stoichiometry); employed for synthesis of selenium‑bromine compounds; usually done by exposing finely powdered Se to Br₂ vapor at 0–25 °C in a dry, inert atmosphere; no solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination (para‑selective) of 3,5‑dimethyl phenol using N‑chlorosuccinimide as a mild Cl⁺ source; converts the phenolic OH‑activated ring to 4‑chloro‑3,5‑dimethyl phenol while generating succinimide as by‑product. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional acid catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between nickel(II) chloride and ammonium phosphate in aqueous solution; forms insoluble nickel(II) phosphate solid and soluble ammonium chloride. Usually carried out mixing aqueous solutions at ambient temperature, followed by filtration of the precipitated nickel phosphate.

Nucleophilic substitution of the secondary alcohol group of 1‑chlorobutan‑2‑ol with thionyl chloride, converting the OH to a chlorine atom to give 1,2‑dichlorobutane while releasing gaseous HCl and SO₂. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often in pyridine or dichloromethane at 0 °C→ reflux; pyridine acts as base to scavenge HCl.

Redox decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by barium manganate. Barium manganate oxidizes H₂O₂, being reduced from Mn(VI) to solid MnO₂; the reaction produces water, molecular oxygen, and barium hydroxide (in situ). Typically performed in aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH or KOH) at room temperature; the precipitated MnO₂ is filtered off.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling between 1‑fluoronaphthalene and phenylboronic acid using potassium phosphate as base. An aryl‑fluoride (a relatively inert electrophile) is activated by a palladium catalyst (e.g Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd‑N‑heterocyclic carbene) to form the C‑C bond, delivering 1‑phenyl‑naphthalene and potassium fluoride. Common conditions: 80–120 °C, dioxane/water (or toluene/ethanol) solvent, and K₃PO₄ as the base in a sealed tube under nitrogen.

Type: oxime dehydration to nitrile. Purpose: transform oxime into nitrile (furan‑2‑carbonitrile). Key transformation: (E)‑N‑(furan‑2‑ylmethylidene)hydroxylamine → furan‑2‑carbonitrile + H₂O. Typical conditions: dehydrating agents such as POCl₃, P₂O₅, Burgess reagent, or Ac₂O/TFA; solvent pyridine, DMF or toluene; temperature 50‑120 °C; reaction time 30 min‑3 h.

Leuckart‑Wallach reductive amination of 3‑methylphenylacetone with ammonia and formic acid, yielding 3‑methyl‑amphetamine together with CO₂ and H₂O. The carbonyl condenses with ammonia to form an imine, which is reduced in situ by formic acid. Heated in a sealed tube at 150‑200 °C, typically without added solvent or with a small amount of mineral oil; the reaction proceeds under acidic, high‑temperature conditions.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of bis(2‑butyl) ether to give two equivalents of 2‑butanol; performed by heating the ether with aqueous strong acid (e.g., 5–10 % H₂SO₄) at reflux, water acts as nucleophile and cleaves the C–O bonds.

Double displacement precipitation with ammonium carbonate; provides yttrium carbonate while generating ammonium nitrate in solution. Conducted in water at room temperature or gentle heating; ammonium carbonate may release CO2/NH3, aiding precipitation of Y2(CO3)3; no catalyst required.

Oxidation (peracid oxidation of a thioether); converts the sulfide functional group to a sulfoxide. Typically carried out with 1.1 equiv meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; the by‑product is meta‑chlorobenzoic acid.

Eschweiler–Clarke methylation of phenylethanolamine using formic acid and formaldehyde; the amine is converted to N‑methylphenylethanolamine via formation of an iminium intermediate, with CO₂ and water released; typically carried out at 80–100 °C in aqueous or alcoholic medium without added catalyst.

DCC‑mediated amidation of 2‑ethyl‑2‑phenylacetic acid with glutarimide to afford glutethimide; dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates the carboxyl group forming an O‑acylurea which reacts with the imide nitrogen, precipitating dicyclohexylurea; conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

SN2 substitution of 1‑bromododecane by ethylene glycol giving 2‑(dodecyloxy)ethanol and HBr; the glycol is deprotonated with a base such as NaH or K₂CO₃ and the reaction is performed in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 80–120 °C, with the base neutralizing the generated HBr.

Acid–base neutralization (saponification of a carboxylic acid); 3‑methylbutanoic acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form the sodium salt (sodium 3‑methylbutanoate) and water; performed at ambient temperature in aqueous solution, often with stirring; no special solvent beyond water is required.

SN2 alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of a carboxylate; sodium 2‑methylpentanoate reacts with methyl iodide to give the methyl ester and NaI; usually run in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone, at 0–50 °C; sodium iodide precipitates; no additional catalyst.

Type: Thermal decarboxylation of an α‑hydroxy dicarboxylic acid. Purpose: Remove one carboxyl group to generate a monocarboxylic acid. Key transformation: Dihydroxymalonic acid loses CO₂, converting the α‑hydroxy‑β‑keto acid fragment into glycolic acid (HOCH₂‑COOH). Conditions: Heating (typically 120–150 °C) in aqueous medium or melt; often performed neat or in water; no catalyst required.

Type: Multi‑functional LiAlH4 reduction (nitrile and ester to amine and alcohol). Purpose: Synthesize a β‑amino alcohol from an α‑cyano‑β‑ester precursor. Key transformation: LiAlH4 reduces the ester carbonyl to a primary alcohol and the nitrile to a primary amine in a single step, yielding 2‑amino‑1‑butanol. Typical conditions: Anhydrous ether or THF, addition of LiAlH4 at 0 °C, then reflux for 3–6 h. No additional catalyst; aqueous work‑up with dilute acid to protonate the amine and destroy excess hydride.

Direct combination (halogenation) of lanthanum metal with chlorine gas to form lanthanum(III) chloride; carried out in a dry furnace at 300–500 °C with chlorine gas passed over heated lanthanum, yielding a white solid that can be collected by sublimation.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation) of 1,1,2‑trichloropropane using hydrogen gas and palladium on carbon; one chlorine is removed as HCl producing 1,2‑dichloropropane; reaction run under 1–5 atm H₂ at 25–50 °C in ethanol or methanol, with Pd/C as the catalyst.

Hydrolysis of magnesium bromide in water. The metal halide reacts with water to give hydrobromic acid and insoluble magnesium hydroxide precip. This is an acid‑base salt hydrolysis that proceeds readily at room temperature in aqueous solution; no special catalyst is required.

Acid‑base protonation; dipotassium malate reacts with hydrochloric acid, the acid protonates the malate anion, regenerating malic acid and forming potassium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution, often at low temperature to avoid side reactions; excess HCl ensures complete conversion; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic chlorination of acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) in aqueous chlorine to afford trichloroacetaldehyde (chloral, CCl₃CHO) and hydrogen chloride. Chlorine adds sequentially at the α‑carbon, eventually yielding the gem‑trichloride. Reaction is typically performed in cold water or dilute HCl at 0–25 °C, often with a few drops of chlorine gas bubbled through the solution; the HCl generated remains in the aqueous phase.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂). (E)-But‑2‑enoic acid reacts with excess SOCl₂, usually under reflux in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a catalytic amount of pyridine or DMF to accelerate formation of the acyl‑chloride. By‑products (SO₂ and HCl) evolve as gases. Reaction time 1–2 h; the resulting (E)-but‑2‑enoyl chloride is obtained after removal of volatiles under reduced pressure.

Oxidation of o‑vanillin’s aldehyde group to the corresponding carboxylic acid (o‑vanillic acid) using hydrogen peroxide; a mild oxidation useful for preparing phenolic acids; conducted in aqueous medium, often with a basic buffer (e.g., NaOH) or a catalytic amount of transition‑metal ions (Fe²⁺, MoO₅²⁻) at ambient temperature; water is the solvent.

Appel reaction converting phenethyl alcohol to phenethyl bromide with concomitant formation of bromoform and triphenylphosphine oxide; a halogenation that replaces the hydroxyl group by bromine via activation by CBr4 and PPh3; carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane (or CHCl₃) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; stoichiometric PPh3 and CBr4 act as reagents, no external catalyst.

Alkyl‑exchange (transmetalation) between gallium trichloride and trimethylindium yielding trimethylgallium and indium trichloride; employed to prepare volatile GaMe₃ for vapor‑phase processes; performed in a dry, oxygen‑free solvent such as toluene or THF, typically under reflux and inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); reagents are used in equimolar amounts, no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of propyl bromide by sulfide anion from sodium hydrosulfide to give propyl mercaptan and sodium bromide; a straightforward method to synthesize primary thiols; executed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g DMF, DMSO) or aqueous NaSH solution, often at mild heating (30–50 °C); no catalyst required.

Transesterification (ester exchange). An alcohol diol reacts with an alkyl methacrylate ester, swapping the alkoxy groups to form a new ester (hydroxyethyl methacrylate) and liberate the corresponding alcohol (isobutanol).
