Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; converts the ester 2‑phenylethyl acetate into phenethyl alcohol while exchanging the alkoxy group for methanol to give methyl acetate; typically carried out in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) at reflux; solvent often is the methanol itself.

Type: metal insertion/organometallic synthesis (formation of dialkylzinc). Purpose: generate a nucleophilic di‑tert‑butylzinc reagent for subsequent cross‑coupling or addition reactions. Key transformation: oxidative insertion of Zn into C–Br bonds of tert‑butyl bromide forming di‑tert‑butylzinc and ZnBr₂ as by‑product. Typical conditions: dry, oxygen‑free THF or diethyl ether, reflux temperature, stoichiometric Zn (2 eq) under nitrogen or argon; reaction monitored until consumption of alkyl bromide.

Type: Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Purpose: install a benzoyl carbonyl onto chlorobenzene to afford 4‑chlorobenzophenone, a useful ketone intermediate. Key transformation: generation of the benzoyl cation by AlCl₃ activation of benzoyl chloride, electrophilic attack at the para position of chlorobenzene, loss of H⁺ (released as HCl). Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1‑1.5 eq), dry dichloromethane or carbon disulfide, cooling to 0 °C then gradual warming to reflux; reaction performed under inert atmosphere; work‑up with aqueous acid to quench excess AlCl₃.

Type: enzymatic transmethylation (biological O‑methyltransferase). Purpose: methylate the 4′‑hydroxy group of luteolin to produce diosmetin, a biologically active flavone. Key transformation: transfer of a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑Lmethionine (SAM) to the phenolic oxygen of luteolin, yielding‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine (SAH) and the 4′‑O‑methylated product. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 7–8), presence of Mg²⁺ or other divalent cations, temperature 25–37 °C, enzyme concentration dependent; reactions often run for minutes to hours.

Acid‑carbonate reaction and precipitation; phosphoric acid protonates carbonate, releasing CO₂ gas and forming barium phosphate as an insoluble solid. Performed in water, often with gentle heating to evolve CO₂; no catalyst needed.

Type: transfer hydrogenation (catalytic hydrogenation using formic acid). Purpose: saturate the heteroar isoquinoline to the fully reduced decahydroisoquinoline, a saturated nitrogen heterocycle. Key transformation: in‑situ generation of H₂ from formic acid decomposition on Pd/C surface, followed by addition of 5 equiv of hydrogen across the two double bonds of the isoquinoline ring system. Typical conditions: Pd/C (5–10 wt %), excess formic acid (2–3 eq), solvent such as ethanol or ethanol/water mixture, temperature 80–120 °C, sealed reactor or reflux condenser; reaction time 2–12 h.

Type: Staudinger reduction (azide‑to‑amine conversion). Purpose: convert the azide functional group of 2‑azidopyridine to the corresponding amine (2‑aminopyridine). Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of triphenylphosphine on the terminal nitrogen of the azide, formation of an iminophosphorane intermediate, hydrolysis to release the amine and generate triphenylphosphine oxide as the by‑product. Typical conditions: dry THF or toluene, room temperature to 50 °C, inert atmosphere; after completion, aqueous work‑up to hydrolyze the intermediate and isolate 2‑aminopyridine.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (Finkelstein‑type halogen exchange, SN2 fluorination). Purpose: replace the chlorine atom of methyl chloroacetate with fluorine to afford methyl fluoroacetate. Key transformation: fluoride ion (provided by KF) attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming the C–F bond, while 18‑crown‑6 complexes K⁺ to increase fluoride solubility in organic medium; KCl precipitates. Typical conditions: dry acetonitrile or acetone as solvent, catalytic amount of 18‑crown‑6 (0.1–0.2 eq), excess KF (2–3 eq), reflux temperature (80–85 °C), reaction time several hours to overnight; removal of solvent and filtration gives methyl fluoroacetate.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) between sodium 2,2,2‑trifluoroethoxide and 2,2,2‑trifluoroethyl tosylate, yielding bis(2,2,2‑trifluoroethyl) ether and sodium tosylate. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent (DMF, DMSO) at ambient or mild temperature under inert atmosphere. Provides a symmetrical ether from an alkoxide and a good leaving‑group alkyl halide/ tosylate.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) of tetraethylammonium bromide with potassium hydroxide, yielding tetraethylammonium hydroxide and potassium bromide; conducted at room temperature in water, product isolated by evaporation and drying.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); forms cyclopentylacetonitrile via cyanide displacement of chloride. Typically performed in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF, DMSO) under heating to enhance reactivity. No catalyst required. Key for nitrile synthesis, which can be hydrolyzed to carboxylic acids or reduced to amines.

Redox condensation reaction; forms iron(II,III) oxide (Fe3O4) from mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) hydroxides. Requires heating under basic conditions (e.g., NaOH) with controlled oxygen exclusion. Produces magnetite crystals via dehydration of Fe(OH)2 and Fe(OH)3. Purpose includes synthesis of magnetic materials.

Acid-catalyzed esterification; forms isoamyl salicylate by condensing salicylic acid and isoamyl alcohol. Commonly uses sulfuric acid or p-toluenesulfonic acid as catalyst. Conditioned with heat and water removal (e.g., Dean-Stark trap) to drive equilibrium. Produced as a fragrance/flavoring ester.

Ester hydrolysis; converts methyl 2‑anilinoacetate to 2‑anilinoacetic acid with methanol as by‑product. Typically performed under aqueous acidic (e.g., 1 M HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) conditions, heating at reflux; common solvent mixture is water/THF or water/ethanol.

Transesterification; swaps alcohol moieties between esters. Acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOMe) catalysis required. Conducted under reflux to facilitate reversible cleavage/bond formation. Purpose includes altering ester solubility or volatility in synthesis or flavor/fragrance applications.

Reduction of heptanoic acid to heptanol using lithium aluminium hydride; carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) starting at 0 °C then refluxed, followed by aqueous work‑up which generates water as a by‑product.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 O‑alkylation); sodium 4‑nitrophenolate reacts with methyl iodide to form 4‑nitroanisole, with NaI as by‑product. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or DMSO, typically under reflux. The phenoxide serves as nucleophile; no additional catalyst is needed.

Lewis‑acid mediated esterification forming a borate ester; purpose is preparation of cyclohexyl borate, a reagent for organic synthesis or polymer chemistry; key transformation is replacement of a B–Cl bond by a B–O‑cyclohexyl bond with release of HCl gas; carried out under anhydrous conditions, inert atmosphere, at 0 °C to room temperature in non‑protic solvents like dichloromethane or toluene; HCl is removed or trapped; no additional catalyst.

Solid-state redox oxidation; elemental oxygen oxidizes iron(II) oxide to mixed-valence iron(II,III) oxide (magnetite). Typically carried out at elevated temperatures (300‑600 °C) in a furnace under an O₂ atmosphere; no solvent, may be done in the presence of inert support.

Salt metathesis (ion‑exchange) between lithium bromide and sodium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide, yielding sodium bromide and lithium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide. Performed in anhydrous ethereal solvents such as THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to rt; inert atmosphere (N₂) is common to avoid moisture.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of normorphine with allyl bromide to give nalorphine (N‑allyl morphine) and hydrogen bromide. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF or DMSO) with a mild base (triethylamine or NaH) at 0 °C to reflux to deprotonate the phenolic amine and drive substitution.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic addition (Markovnikov hydration) of 3‑methyl‑1‑butene to 3‑methyl‑2‑butanol. Performed in aqueous sulfuric acid (≈1–5 % H₂SO₄) at 50–80 °C; water acts as nucleophile, sulfate provides the proton source.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of 2‑phenylethyl propionate with NaOH to afford sodium propionate and 2‑phenylethanol; carried out in aqueous NaOH (often with MeOH as co‑solvent) at room temperature or under reflux; the reaction mixture may be acidified after completion to isolate the free acid if needed.

Catalytic dehydrogenation to a trans‑internal alkene; butane converts to trans‑2‑butene and hydrogen; performed under similar high‑temperature conditions (500–600 °C) with metal catalysts (Pt, Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃) that thermodynamically favor the trans isomer; gas‑phase, solvent‑free.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis (partial, stopping at amide) of 4‑hydroxybutanenitrile to 4‑hydroxybutanamide. Conducted in aqueous H₂SO₄ (conc. or dilute) with heating (80–120 °C); water supplies the nucleophile, acid protonates the nitrile to facilitate addition.

Aerobic oxidation (redox) of ferrous citrate to ferric citrate by molecular oxygen, producing water as by‑product. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mildly elevated temperature (20–40 °C) with stirring and excess O₂ (air or O₂ balloon); citrate chelates iron and stabilizes the Fe(III) product.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde; purpose: reduce octanal to 1‑octanol; key transformation: H₂ adds across the C=O bond in the presence of Pd/C, yielding the corresponding alcohol after proton transfer; typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, 5 % Pd on carbon catalyst, solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–50 °C, often under an inert atmosphere.

Base‑catalyzed benzilic acid rearrangement; converts a 1,2‑diketone into an α‑hydroxycarboxylic acid. Phenyl migration from one carbonyl to the adjacent carbon gives benzilic acid as the potassium salt, which upon acid work‑up affords the free acid. Typical conditions: excess KOH (often 10 M) in aqueous ethanol, reflux 1–2 h; then acidification. No special catalyst required.

N‑Alkylation of succinimide (SN2). Ethyl bromide alkylates the imide nitrogen of succinimide to give N‑ethylsuccinimide, with concomitant formation of HBr. The reaction is usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or dimethyl sulfoxide, using a mild base (e.g., K2CO3, NaHCO3, or Na₂CO₃) to neutralize the generated HBr. Conditions: 0‑25 °C to reflux for several hours, inert atmosphere optional, followed by aqueous work‑up and crystallization of the N‑alkyl product.

Chromium(VI) oxidative side‑chain oxidation; phenylacetic acid is oxidized to benzoic acid while the benzylic carbon is removed as carbon dioxide. Sodium dichromate in concentrated H₂SO₄ provides the Cr(VI) oxidant; reaction is carried out under reflux in aqueous medium. Water is the solvent; the by‑products are Cr³⁺ (as chromium(III) sulfate) and water.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of methyl heptanoate with ethanol, yielding ethyl heptanoate and methanol. Typical conditions employ either a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid or sodium methoxide in refluxing ethanol; excess ethanol shifts the equilibrium toward the ethyl ester. Removal of methanol (e.g., by distillation) drives the reaction to completion.

Thionyl chloride conversion of a phenol to an aryl chloride; the hydroxyl group of picric acid is replaced by chlorine to give picryl chloride. The reaction proceeds via formation of a chlorosulfite intermediate and liberates HCl and SO₂ gases. Conducted neat with thionyl chloride, often with a base such as pyridine to scavenge HCl; reflux for 1–2 h under anhydrous conditions.

Thermal decomposition (calcination); solid iron(III) nitrate is heated, decomposing to iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃), nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen; used to obtain Fe₂O₃ and to release gaseous NO₂; heating typically at 300–400 °C in a furnace under air; no solvent or catalyst, solid‑state reaction.

Hydrolysis of an alkyl nitrite; ethyl nitrite reacts with water to regenerate ethanol and nitrous acid. The process is a simple ester‑hydrolysis under neutral or mildly acidic conditions, typically at room temperature or gentle heating. Water is both reactant and solvent; no catalyst is required.

Dimerization of thioformaldehyde to a four‑membered heterocycle; two molecules undergo a [2+2] cycloaddition forming 1,2‑dithietane. This reaction is observed under low‑temperature gas‑phase or matrix‑isolation conditions; it may be initiated by photolysis or by cooling a neat vapor. No solvent or catalyst is generally used; the reaction is driven by concentration and temperature control.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (acetalization) of acetaldehyde with ethylene glycol to give 1,3‑dioxolane. The aldehyde carbonyl reacts with the diol, followed by loss of water to generate a five‑membered cyclic acetal, used as a protecting group. Typical conditions: catalytic p‑TsOH or H₂SO₄ (0.1–1 mol %), reflux in a Dean‑Stark apparatus using a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or benzene to continuously remove water; reaction time 1–3 h.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of a diamine; p‑phenylenediamine is di‑alkylated with sec‑butyl bromide in the presence of potassium carbonate, yielding N,N′‑di‑sec‑butyl‑p‑phenylenediamine. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or acetonitrile), K₂CO₃ as base, reflux (80–110 °C) for several hours; potassium bromide precipitates out. No additional catalyst is needed.

Thionation of a carboxylic acid; P₂S₅ converts benzoic acid to thiobenzoic acid by replacing the carbonyl oxygen with sulfur; typically performed under reflux in anhydrous pyridine or carbon disulfide, inert atmosphere, stoichiometric P₂S₅.

Alcoholysis of an ester (ethanolysis); analogous to the methanol case but using ethanol; ethanol attacks the ester carbonyl, producing cinnamyl alcohol and ethyl acetate; the reaction is typically run in refluxing ethanol with a catalytic acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid or a few drops of conc. H₂SO₄) for 2–6 h.

Oxidation of a primary benzylic alcohol; KMnO₄ oxidizes 2‑chlorobenzyl alcohol to 2‑chlorobenzoic acid, usually in aqueous alkaline solution with heating (reflux) and subsequent acid work‑up to isolate the acid.

Schiff‑base condensation; butanal reacts with aniline to give butylideneaniline (an imine) under mild acidic or neutral conditions, often in toluene with a Dean‑Stark trap or in the presence of molecular sieves to remove water.

Condensation (esterification) of two salicylic acid molecules; heating salicylic acid with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) drives dehydration to form salsalate and water, usually performed at 180–200 °C under reduced pressure or with azeotropic removal of water.

Solid‑state redox synthesis; direct combination of elemental tantalum with selenium dioxide to afford tantalum selenide (likely TaSe₂) while releasing O₂. Typically performed by grinding the reagents together, sealing in an evacuated quartz tube, and heating to 600–1000 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis; cleavage of 2‑methoxy‑1,3‑dioxane protecting group to give ethylene glycol and methoxyacetaldehyde. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 0.5–1 M HCl) at reflux (≈100 °C). Water serves as both solvent and reactant; acid catalyst is essential.

Conversion of an alcohol to a chloroformate using triphosgene (phosgene surrogate); ethanol reacts to form ethyl chloroformate with liberation of HCl. Performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, in the presence of a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl. Triphosgene is used stoichiometrically (1 equiv per 3 equiv alcohol).

Salt metathesis (double displacement) in aqueous solution; copper(II) bromide exchanges anions with potassium benzoate to give copper(II) benzoate and potassium bromide. Usually carried out by dissolving both salts in water and stirring at ambient temperature; the reaction may be driven to completion by precipitation or removal of the more soluble product.

Ligand exchange/acid‑base metathesis; aluminum chloride reacts with sodium lactate to form aluminum lactate complex and sodium chloride. Conducted in water or an alcohol medium (e.g., methanol) with gentle heating to ensure dissolution; acidic AlCl₃ hydrolyzes, so the reaction is typically kept slightly acidic to maintain Al³⁺ solubility.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; cyanide attacks cyclohexyl methanesulfonate displacing methanesulfonate to give cyclohexyl cyanide; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0–50 °C; no catalyst required.

Type: oxidative acid digestion (redox). Purpose: converts cadmium phosphide into soluble cadmium nitrate while oxidizing phosphorus to phosphoric acid; nitrogen dioxide is released as a by‑product. Key transformation: metal phosphide is oxidized by concentrated HNO₃, forming Cd(NO₃)₂, H₃PO₄ and NO₂ gas. Typical conditions: excess conc. HNO₃, reflux 60–80 °C, careful control of gas evolution. Solvent/catalyst: aqueous nitric acid; no added catalyst required.

Double displacement/acid‑base reaction using ammonium hydroxide; zinc oxalate reacts with NH₄OH to give soluble ammonium oxalate and precipitated zinc hydroxide. Key transformation: ZnC₂O₄(s) + 2 NH₄OH → (NH₄)₂C₂O₄(aq) + Zn(OH)₂(s). Performed in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Type: acid‑catalyzed esterification (formation of alkyl hydrogen sulfate). Purpose: prepares decyl hydrogen sulfate, a surfactant or intermediate, from decyl alcohol. Key transformation: the hydroxyl of decyl alcohol is replaced by a hydrogen sulfate group, yielding water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: dropwise addition of conc. H₂SO₄ to decyl alcohol at 0–50 °C, stirring under inert atmosphere to avoid dehydration to alkene. Solvent/catalyst: concentrated H₂SO₄ itself acts as both reagent and catalyst; the alcohol often serves as the reaction medium.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification; purpose: generate sodium 2‑hydroxypropanoate (sodium lactate) and liberate 1‑butanol. OH⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon of butyl lactate, forming the carboxylate salt and releasing butanol. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (10–20 % w/w), temperature 50–80 °C, water or aqueous ethanol as solvent; reaction proceeds to completion as butanol is removed or drives equilibrium.

Type: acid‑base salt formation (hydrochloride generation). Purpose: converts the free base 1‑(3‑chlorophenyl)biguanide into its more stable, water‑soluble hydrochloride salt for pharmaceutical or analytical use. Key transformation: protonation of the biguanide nitrogen by HCl to give the hydrochloride. Typical conditions: dissolve the biguanide in a minimal amount of ethanol or water, add aqueous HCl at ambient temperature, stir until dissolution is complete, then evaporate or precipitate the salt. Solvent/catalyst: aqueous HCl; no additional catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of octan‑2‑yl acetate with sodium hydroxide; provides 2‑octanol and sodium acetate; conducted in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (≈80 °C) for 1–2 h, then acidified to liberate the alcohol.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) / acid‑base neutralization. Purpose: generates aluminum phosphate precipitate and releases acetic acid; useful for phosphate precipitation or removal of aluminum ions. Key transformation: exchange of acetate and phosphate ions between aluminum acetate and phosphoric acid, forming insoluble AlPO₄ and liberating AcOH. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions mixed at room temperature or mild heating (≤60 °C), vigorous stirring, followed by filtration of the AlPO₄ solid. Solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst required.

Type: metathesis/precipitation (metal‑soap formation). Purpose: prepares zinc stearate, an insoluble metal soap used as a lubricant, stabilizer or pigment; sodium chloride remains in solution. Key transformation: exchange of chloride for stearate ions, yielding Zn(C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂ solid and NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous or ethanolic solutions of ZnCl₂ and NaSt (sodium stearate) mixed at ambient temperature, stirred until precipitate forms, then filtered and washed. Solvent/catalyst: water or dilute ethanol; no catalyst needed.

Free‑radical bromination of 2‑methylhexane directed toward the secondary carbon (C‑3) to afford 3‑bromo‑2‑methylhexane; the mechanism is the same radical chain (Br2 → 2 Br·, H‑abstraction, radical recombination); because the secondary C‑3 radical is more stable than a primary radical, this product is the major component; conditions as above (UV light or peroxide, dilute Br2, CCl4 or CHCl3 as solvent), temperature 60–80 °C; product typically isolated by distillation.

Type: nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S_NAr). Purpose: replaces one fluorine of hexafluorobenzene with a hydroxyl group to give pentafluorophenol, while generating fluoride ion as sodium fluoride. Key transformation: OH⁻ attacks the electron‑deficient aromatic ring, displacing F⁻. Typical conditions: suspension of hexafluorobenzene in polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMSO or DMF) with excess NaOH or NaOCH₃, heated 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere, then work‑up to isolate pentafluorophenol and NaF. Solvent/catalyst: polar aprotic solvent; base acts as nucleophile; no additional catalyst required.

Type: Rosenmund‑von Braun cyanation (nucleophilic aromatic substitution). Purpose: convert aryl bromides to aryl nitriles. Key transformation: each bromine on 1,3‑dibromobenzene is replaced by a cyano group, forming 1,3‑dicyanobenzene and copper(I) bromide as by‑product. Typical conditions: heating 1,3‑dibromobenzene with excess CuCN in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry dimethylformamide (DMF) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) under inert atmosphere; reaction temperatures 120–180 °C. No additional catalyst required.

Type: Thermal decarboxylation of an α‑amino acid. Purpose: generate a primary amine from the corresponding amino acid while releasing CO₂. Key transformation: the carboxyl group of α‑aminobutyric acid is removed carbon dioxide, yielding propylamine. Typical conditions: heating the amino acid alone or in the presence of a mild acid/base (e.g., pyridoxal‑phosphate enzyme in biosynthesis, or strong heat >200 °C in the laboratory). No solvent is strictly required, but high‑boiling solvents such as o‑xylene can be used.

Oxidative dissolution of cerium metal in hot dilute nitric acid; Ce(0) is oxidized to cerium(III) nitrate while nitrate is reduced to nitric oxide, producing water; carried out in aqueous HNO₃ at about 60–80 °C; no additional reagents needed.

Double‑displacement (acid‑base neutralization) precipitation; aqueous iron(III) chloride reacts with sodium hydroxide to form insoluble iron(III) hydroxide and soluble sodium chloride; FeCl3 + 3 NaOH → Fe(OH)3↓ + 3 NaCl; carried out in water at room temperature with vigorous stirring; precipitate is filtered or washed.

Halide exchange (fluorination) reaction; purpose is to convert hafnium tetrachloride into hafnium tetrafluoride for further processing; key transformation: hafnium tetrachloride reacts with excess hydrofluoric acid to replace chloride ligands with fluoride, producing hafnium tetrafluoride and hydrogen chloride; usually conducted in anhydrous HF as both solvent and reagent at elevated temperatures (≈150–200 °C) in a sealed PTFE or nickel vessel; no additional catalyst is employed.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange between nickel(II) acetate and hydrobromic acid; replaces acetate with bromide to give nickel(II) bromide and acetic acid; conducted in aqueous solution, normally at room temperature or with slight heating.

Acid–base neutralization/precipitation (double‑replacement); thorium nitrate reacts with aqueous NaOH, Th⁴⁺ precipitates as insoluble thorium hydroxide while sodium nitrate remains in solution; carried out in water at moderate temperature, excess NaOH often used.

Type: Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification. Purpose: exchange the ethoxy group of ethyl acrylate with a hydroxyl group of ethylene glycol to generate a hydroxy‑functional acrylate monomer. Key transformation: one hydroxyl of ethylene glycol attacks the carbonyl of ethyl acrylate, displacing ethanol and forming 2‑hydroxyethyl acrylate. Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous solvent (toluene or cyclohexane) with catalytic amount of acid (p‑TsOH) or base (NaOMe); removal of ethanol by azeotropic distillation drives the equilibrium toward product. No special metal catalyst required.

Type: Friedel‑Crafts condensation (electrophilic aromatic substitution) leading to phenolphthalein synthesis. Purpose: couple two equivalents of phenol with phthalic anhydride to produce pH‑indicator phenolphthalein. Key transformation: AlCl₃ activates phthalic anhydride, generating an acylium ion that alkylates phenol at the para position; subsequent intramolecular cyclization and dehydration give phenolphthalein and water. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1–2 equiv) in dry carbon disulfide or chloroform, reflux under nitrogen, temperature ≈80–100 °C. Reaction is moisture‑sensitive.

Type: Oxid of a saturated hydrocarbon with hydrogen peroxide (hydroperoxide‑mediated oxidation). Purpose: convert cyclohexane to cyclohexanol (and often cyclohexanone) using H₂O₂ as oxidant. Key transformation: hydrogen peroxide, activated by a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺ in Fenton system, or Ti‑silsesquioxane, or tungsten‑based complexes), abstracts a hydrogen atom from cyclohexane to form a cyclohexyl radical, which reacts with •OH give cyclohexyl hydroperoxide that is subsequently reduced to cyclohexanol water is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂O₂ (30 %), catalyst loading 0.1–5 mol %, temperature 25–80 °C, often in mixed organic/aqueous solvent (e.g., acetonitrile/water).

0.‑chlorination of a secondary amine using tert‑butyl hypochlorite electrophilic chlorination at nitrogen forms 1‑chloropiperidine while tert‑butanol is released as the leaving group. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; no additional catalyst required.

Reductive conversion of an ortho‑quinone to a catechol; sodium dithionite reduces cyclohexa‑3,5‑diene‑1,2‑dione (ortho‑benzoquinone) to catechol (1,2‑dihydroxybenzene). Performed in water (or aqueous buffer) at ambient temperature, often under nitrogen, with Na₂S₂O₄ (excess) serving as the reducing agent; sodium sulfite is formed as a by‑product.

Williamson ether synthesis via SN2 substitution. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates methanol to give methoxide, which attacks allyl chloride, displacing chloride to afford allyl methyl ether; NaCl and water are formed. Commonly carried out in excess methanol (solvent) at 0–50 °C, using aqueous NaOH; the reaction may be performed in a biphasic system to improve phase contact.

Oxidation of dimethyl sulfoxide to dimethyl sulfone with a peracid (peracetic acid). The peracid transfers an oxygen atom to the sulfoxide, generating acetic acid as the by‑product. Conducted at 0 °C to 25 °C in aprotic solvents like dichloromethane or acetone; stoichiometric peracid is used, no metal catalyst.

General type: thermal decomposition (calcination). Purpose: preparation of gadolinium oxide, a high‑temperature ceramic material. Key transformation: Gd2(CO3)3 → Gd2O3 + 3 CO2 (solid‑phase decarbonation). Typical conditions: heating the carbonate to 600–800 °C in air or an inert atmosphere; the solid is ground to increase surface area. No solvent; the reaction proceeds without catalysts.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification of diethyl adipate with methanol to give dimethyl adipate and ethanol. Sulfuric acid protonates the ester carbonyl to facilitate exchange; reaction is performed under reflux (≈65 °C) with excess methanol as solvent and a catalytic amount of H₂SO₄ (≈1–5 mol %). Removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium.

High‑temperature solid‑state reaction between cadmium sulfide and elemental antimony producing cadmium antimonide (CdSb) and elemental sulfur. Typical conditions involve heating the powdered mixture to 800–1000 °C under an inert atmosphere (argon) or vacuum for several hours; no solvents or catalysts are used, only thorough mixing of the solids.

Acid‑base neutralization of isovaleric acid with sodium bicarbonate yielding sodium isovalerate, carbon dioxide and water. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously without catalyst, often used for CO₂ evolution tests.

Hydrolytic cleavage of N‑hydroxysuccinimide in water to give succinimide and hydroxylamine. The reaction is a nucleophilic hydrolysis of the N‑O bond, proceeding faster under mild acidic (pH ≈ 4‑5) or basic (pH ≈ 9‑10) conditions and gentle heating (30‑60 °C). No external catalyst is required; water acts as both solvent and nucleophile.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; thioacetate anion displaces the tosylate of methyl tosylate to give methyl thioacetate and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at room temperature to 60 °C; no catalyst required. Used for preparation of thioesters from alkyl sulfonates.

Nucleophilic silylation (formation of a silyl ether) via substitution of chloride; potassium tert‑butoxide attacks trimethylsilyl chloride, producing tert‑butyl trimethylsilyl ether and KCl. Performed in dry, aprotic solvents such as THF or DMF under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C to rt; the base itself acts as the nucleophile, no extra catalyst.

Metal‑mediated reduction of a nitro aromatic to an amine (Zn/NH4Cl reduction, also called Béchamp reduction). Zinc dust reacts with ammonium chloride to generate HCl in situ, reducing 2‑nitrotoluene to 2‑methylaniline while evolving H2 gas and forming ZnCl2. Conducted in refluxing ethanol (or ethanol/water) with excess Zn; purpose is conversion of nitro groups to anilines.

Oxime formation (condensation of a ketone with hydroxylamine). Hydroxylamine adds to heptan‑2‑one, followed by loss of water to afford heptan‑2‑one oxime. Usually performed in ethanol or ethanol/water at 50‑80 °C, often in the presence of a weak acid catalyst (e.g., acetic acid) or pyridine to promote dehydration. Provides a protected carbonyl functionality useful for subsequent transformations.

Hydrolysis of a nitrate ester; methyl nitrate reacts with water to cleave the O–NO2 bond, yielding methanol and nitric acid; generally acid‑catalyzed or neutral hydrolysis at ambient to mildly elevated temperature (25–80 °C) in aqueous medium; purpose is decomposition or detoxification of methyl nitrate.

Double‑displacement/metathesis with acid‑base character; strontium formate reacts with ammonium carbonate to precipitateontium carbonate and liberate ammonia gas and formic acid; performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to drive off NH₃; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed cross‑aldol condensation (Claisen‑Schmidt condensation). Calcium hydroxide deprotonates acetone, generating an enolate that attacks benzaldehyde; subsequent dehydration yields the conjugated diketone dibenzylideneacetone and water. Conducted in refluxing ethanol with solid Ca(OH)2 (or CaO) as base; water removal (by azeotropic distillation or drying agents) drives the reaction forward. Used to synthesize α,β‑unsaturated ketones and pigments.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; aryl bromide (1‑bromo‑3‑phenylbenzene) couples with phenylboronic acid to afford 1,3‑diphenylbenzene; uses a Pd(0) catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(dppf)Cl₂), a base (K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃), in a mixed solvent such as dioxane/water or toluene/ethanol, heated to 80–100 °C under inert atmosphere.

Double‑displacement precipitation/acid‑base reaction; AgNO₃ reacts with aqueous HBr to precipitate AgBr while generating nitric acid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst.

General type: hydrogenolysis/reduction of a metal nitride. Purpose: generates ammonia and recovers metallic zinc from zinc nitride. Key transformation: Zn3N2 + 3 H2 → 3 Zn + 2 NH3 (cleavage of N‑Zn bonds, formation of N‑H). Typical conditions: solid‑state reaction at elevated temperature (300–500 °C) under a pressure of H2 gas (often several atmospheres). Common solvent/catal: none; reaction performed in the gas‑phase or in a sealed tube.

General type: acid–base neutralization / salt formation. Purpose: generate the soluble sodium phenylboronate for use in cross‑coupling or analytical applications. Key transformation: deprotonation of phenylboronic acid by hydroxide to give the boronate anion and water. Typical conditions: add aqueous NaOH (1 equiv) to phenylboronic acid at rt, stirring briefly. Common solvents/catalysts: water or water/ethanol; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of 2,3,5,6‑tetrachlorophenol to tetrachloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone using Oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate); peroxymonosulfate oxidizes the phenol, yielding water and potassium bisulfate; commonly done in aqueous acetone or water at 0–25 °C; Oxone is the sole oxidant, no metal catalyst needed.

General type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction in aqueous solution. Purpose: swaps counter‑ions to precipitate insoluble manganese carbonate while forming soluble potassium sulfate. Key transformation: K2CO3 + MnSO4 → MnCO3(s) + K2SO4(aq). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating, vigorous stirring to promote nucleation. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst needed.

General type: oxidation of a sulfoxide to a sulfone using hydrogen peroxide. Purpose: converts methylsulfinylmethylbenzene (phenyl‑CH2‑SO‑CH3) to the corresponding sulfone (phenyl‑CH2‑SO2‑CH3). Key transformation: addition of an oxygen atom to the sulfur center, raising the oxidation state from +4 (sulfoxide) to +6 (sulfone), with water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic medium (e.g., methanol, acetonitrile) at 0–25 °C to 50 °C; sometimes a small amount of acid (e.g., acetic acid) or a metal catalyst (e.g., Na2WO4, Ti‑syringe) to enhance rate. Common solvent/catalyst: methanol or acetonitrile; hydrogen peroxide (30 % aq.) as oxidant, optional catalytic acid or transition‑metal catalyst.

General type: nitrosation of a secondary amine. Purpose: forms N‑methyl‑N‑propyl‑nitrosamine, a common step in nitrosamine synthesis or in analytical of amines. Key transformation: nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO2/HCl) reacts with the lone pair on nitrogen, producing the N‑nitroso group and releasing water. Typical conditions: cold aqueous acidic media (0–5 °C) to control reaction rate and avoid over‑oxidation; nitrous acid generated freshly and added slowly to a solution of the amine. Common solvent/catalyst: dilute aqueous HCl with NaNO2; temperature control is critical.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of methyl chloride by sulfide anion from sodium sulfide to generate sodium methanethiolate and sodium chloride. Used to prepare thiolate salts from primary alkyl halides. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0‑50 °C under an inert atmosphere.

Reductive amination of indole‑3‑acetaldehyde with ethylpropylamine using sodium cyanoborohydride. Forms the secondary amine ethylpropyltryptamine in a single step. Reaction proceeds in mild acid (pH 5‑6) in methanol or dichloromethane at 0‑25 °C; NaBH₃CN is the reducing agent that selectively reduces the imine intermediate.

Transesterification of methyl salicylate with 3,3,5‑trimethylcyclohexanol to afford homosalate and methanol. Employed to prepare the UV‑filter ester homosalate. Catalyzed by an acid such as p‑toluenesulfonic acid or by a base (e.g., NaOMe) and performed under reflux in toluene or xylene with azeotropic removal of methanol.

This is an alcoholysis (transesterification) of a metal alkoxide; titanium tetra‑ethyl ether reacts with methanol to exchange ligands, yielding titanium tetramethoxide and ethanol; performed by refluxing the reactants in methanol (or a mixed solvent) often under inert atmosphere, sometimes catalyzed by a small amount of acid or base.

Hydrolysis of triphenyl phosphate with water to give phenol and phosphoric acid. Represents acid‑ or neutral‑catalyzed cleavage of a phosphate ester. Typically heated in aqueous solution (often with dilute HCl) at reflux; the reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of water on the phosphorus center.

Acid hydrolysis (leaching) of a silicate mineral; aqueous HCl protonates and cleaves the Si–O–Mg bonds of magnesium orthosilicate, yielding soluble magnesium chloride and silicic acid (Si(OH)₄). Typically performed by refluxing the solid in concentrated HCl solution (water as solvent) at temperatures of 80–120 °C.

Alpha‑halogenation of acetaldehyde with chlorine gas to form chloroacetaldehyde and hydrogen chloride. Electrophilic substitution at the α‑carbon via enol intermediate. Performed at 0‑25 °C in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) or aqueous medium, with controlled addition of Cl₂ to avoid over‑chlorination.

Acid‑base neutralization and salt metathesis; aqueous NaOH deprotonates ammonium chromate, liberating NH₃ gas and water while forming soluble sodium chromate. Usually performed in water at ambient temperature; excess NaOH helps drive off NH₃.

Catalytic dehydrogenation (alkane to alkene); removal of H₂ from 2‑methylhexane to give 2‑methylhex‑1‑ene. Conducted at high temperature (≈500–600 °C) over metal oxide or precious‑metal catalysts (e.g., Pt, Cr₂O₃) possibly with steam; inert gas atmosphere; no solvent needed.

Single‑displacement redox (metal displacement): magnesium metal reduces Cu²⁺ from copper(II) sulfate to elemental copper while being oxidized to Mg²⁺, forming magnesium sulfate in solution. Conducted in aqueous copper(II) sulfate at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Halogenolysis/oxidative cleavage of trisulfane with Cl₂; chlorine attacks the S–S bonds, producing hydrogen chloride, sulfur dichloride (SCl₂) and elemental sulfur as by‑products. Typically carried out at low temperature (0–5 °C) in a dry, inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane under anhydrous conditions.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ester; H₂ adds across the C=C double bond of benzyl prop‑2‑enoate to afford saturated benzyl propanoate. Standard conditions use H₂ (1–5 atm) with Pd/C (or Pt) in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) at 25–50 °C.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between nickel(II) acetate and silver, exchanging counter‑ions to give soluble nickel(II) nitrate and silver acetate. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special reagents or catalysts required.

Sequence of Grignard addition followed by catalytic hydrogenation; 4‑methoxyphenylmagnesium bromide adds twice to the carbonyl of trichloroacetaldehyde (chloral) to give the bis‑(p‑methoxyphenyl)carbinol intermediate, which is then reduced with H₂/Pd‑C to replace the hydroxyl group by hydrogen, affording methoxychlor. Common conditions: anhydrous ether or THF at –78 °C to 0 °C for the Grignard step, then work‑up and hydrogenation in ethanol or EtOAc at pressure and room temperature with 5–10 % Pd on carbon.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation) where calcium carbonate reacts with the sulfonic acid N‑acetylhomotaurine. The carbonate is protonated, releasing CO₂ and H₂O, while the calcium cation forms the calcium acetylhomotaurinate salt. Typical conditions: aqueous suspension, mild heating, stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Metal chalcogenide synthesis via organometallic transmetallation. Dimethylcadmium transfers a methyl group to hydrogen telluride, generating methane and cadmium telluride. Conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at 80–150 °C in dry, oxygen‑free solvents such as THF or toluene; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an acetaldehyde semicarbazone. Dilute HCl protonates the C=N bond, water attacks, and the semicarbazone breaks down to regenerate acetaldehyde and free semicarbazide. Usually carried out in aqueous HCl (0.1–1 M) at 40–80 °C for 30 min to 2 h; no external catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution using an activated acetyl phosphate. Dimethylamine attacks the acetyl carbonyl of trisodium acetyl phosphate, displacing phosphate to form N,N‑dimethylacetamide and sodium phosphate. Reaction proceeds in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic medium at ambient temperature or mild heating (20–50 °C); the phosphate acts as leaving group, no extra catalyst needed.

DCC‑mediated Steglich esterification to form dimethocaine. 4‑Aminobenzoic acid is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide, which forms an O‑acylurea intermediate that reacts with 2‑dimethylaminoethanol to give the ester dimethocaine; dicyclohexylurea precipitates as by‑product. Conducted in dry dichloromethane (or CHCl₃) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen, often with catalytic DMAP to speed acyl transfer.

Williamson ether synthesis; alkoxide formed from diethylene glycol monoethyl ether by NaOH attacks bromoethane to give diethylene glycol diethyl ether; typically performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution under reflux, NaOH as base, no additional catalyst.

Oxidative disulfide formation – Iodine oxidatively couples two molecules of 2‑mercaptopyridine to give 2,2'‑dipyridyl disulfide while generating hydrogen iodide. Typically run in an aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂, MeCN, or EtOAc at room temperature; stoichiometric I₂ is used, and the reaction is finished by aqueous work‑up to remove HI.

Acid‑carbonate reaction of magnesium carbonate with hydrobromic acid; produces magnesium bromide, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Carried out in aqueous HBr, usually at room temperature with observable effervescence; heating can be applied to drive completion, no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization to form a metal soap; two equivalents of stearic acid react with zinc hydroxide to produce zinc stearate and water; carried out in water or ethanol with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution and precipitation of the insoluble zinc stearate.

Hydroboration‑oxidation (anti‑Markovnikov hydration); BH₃·THF adds across the cyclopentene double bond to give the organoborane, which is then oxidized with H₂O₂/NaOH to afford cyclopentanol; reaction carried out in THF at 0 °C to rt for hydroboration, followed by aqueous H₂O₂/alkaline work‑up at 0‑25 °C.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination (para‑bromination). Bromine is added to a solution of N‑methyl‑aniline in glacial acetic acid; the generated bromonium electrophile substitutes at the para position, affording N‑methyl‑4‑bromoaniline and HBr as by‑product. Temperature kept low (0‑20 °C) to control rate and avoid poly‑bromination. Reaction proceeds in 30‑60 min; work‑up involves quenching excess Br₂ with aqueous Na₂SO₃, then extraction with dichloromethane. No additional catalyst is needed.

Fischer esterification of an aminooxy acid; aminooxyacetic acid reacts with methanol in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄) to give methyl 2‑(hydroxyamino)acetate and water; reflux in methanol with removal of water drives the equilibrium.

Conversion of a primary alcohol to the bromide using phosphorus tribromide; 4‑chlorobenzyl alcohol reacts with PBr₃ to give 4‑chlorobenzyl bromide (and H₃PO₃ as by‑product); carried out in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or ether at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to convert 4‑fluorobenzoic acid into its methyl ester. The carboxylic acid reacts with methanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid, forming methyl 4‑fluorobenzoate and water. Typical conditions are reflux in excess methanol with a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄; methanol serves as both reactant and solvent, and removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium forward.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide; aqueous NaOH attacks 1‑bromoheptane to replace Br with OH, yielding 1‑heptanol and NaBr; typically performed by refluxing the substrate in a NaOH solution (often 1‑2 M) possibly with a co‑solvent such as ethanol; temperature 60‑80 °C; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ether synthesis (Fischer etherification). Purpose: convert 2‑butanol to the corresponding ether with methanol. Key transformation: protonation of the secondary alcohol, loss of water to give a carbocation, nucleophilic attack by methanol and formation of 2‑methoxybutane; water is generated as by‑product. Typical conditions: concentrated H2SO4, reflux (~140 °C), often the alcohols act as solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Deoxy‑chlorination of phenols with phosphorus oxychloride. Purpose: replace the phenolic OH of 1‑naphthol by chlorine to afford 1‑chloronaphthalene. Key transformation: formation of a phosphorodichloridate intermediate from POCl3 and the phenol, followed by chloride transfer to the aromatic carbon and release of phosphoric acid. Typical conditions: POCl3 used neat or in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane), with a base such as pyridine to scavenge HCl, mild heating (0–80 °C) under nitrogen.

Acid–base dissociation (generation of TFA); heating ammonium trifluoroacetate releases volatile ammonia and leaves behind trifluoroacetic acid; can be done by gentle distillation under reduced pressure to remove NH3; no solvent or catalyst needed; temperature around 80–100 °C.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of 2‑bromopropane by acetate ion to give isopropyl acetate; usually run in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, refluxed, sometimes with excess sodium acetate.
Acid fluorination of silica; HF attacks SiO₂ to generate volatile SiF₄ gas and water. Performed in aqueous or anhydrous HF, often at 0‑100 °C; no catalyst needed.

Ammonolysis/condensation of alloxan to give murexide. Purpose: analytical preparation of the dye murexide (ammonium purpurate) used in colorimetric tests. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of ammonia on the carbonyl groups of alloxan, cyclization and loss of water to generate the heterocyclic murexide salt. Typical conditions: gaseous NH3 bubbled through an aqueous solution of alloxan, gentle heating (40–60 °C); the reaction proceeds in water without additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: synthesis of insoluble silver telluride, a semiconductor material. Key transformation: exchange of anions between Na2Te and AgF to produce NaF (soluble) and Ag2Te (precipitate). Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as THF or acetonitrile, inert atmosphere (argon) to avoid oxidation of telluride, ambient to mildly heated temperature; the solid Ag2Te is filtered off.

Silane‑mediated reduction of pyridine N‑oxide (oxygen‑atom transfer). Purpose: regenerate pyridine and form the corresponding silanol. Key transformation: transfer of the oxygen atom from the N‑oxide to triethylsilane, yielding pyridine and triethylsilanol. Typical conditions: stoichiometric triethylsilane, often in dichloromethane or toluene, at room temperature to reflux; the reaction can be accelerated by a Lewis acid catalyst such as BF3·OEt2, under nitrogen.

Photocatalytic hydrolysis of an organophosphate fluoridate on TiO2. Purpose: detoxify the nerve‑agent analogue O‑isopropyl methylphosphonofluoridate, producing non‑toxic residues. Key transformation: UV‑excited TiO2 generates surface hydroxyl radicals that cleave the P‑F bond, yielding methylphosphonic acid, isopropanol (from the O‑isopropyl group) and hydrogen fluoride. Typical conditions: suspension of TiO2 (e.g., P25) in water or mixed solvent, irradiation with UV light (λ ≈ 350 nm), ambient temperature, stirring under air or nitrogen.

N‑alkylation (nucleophilic substitution, SN2) of p‑phenylenediamine; the amine nitrogens act as nucleophiles toward ethyl bromide in the presence of the mild inorganic base potassium carbonate, which deprotonates the amine and scavenges HBr. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMS), 0 °C to reflux, stoichiometric K₂CO₃, and excess ethyl bromide; the reaction yields N,N‑diethyl‑p‑phenylenediamine and potassium bromide as a solid by‑product.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 1,1‑diphenylethylene; molecular hydrogen adds across the C=C double bond to give the saturated alkane 1,1‑diphenylethane. Usually performed with a transition‑metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, at 1–5 atm H₂ and ambient to moderate temperature (25–80 °C). The reaction cleanly reduces the alkene without affecting the phenyl groups.

Decarboxylation of acetolactate to acetoin plus CO₂; the α‑keto‑acid loses its carboxyl group, forming the vicinal diol (acetoin) and carbon dioxide. Can proceed enzymatically (acetolactate decarboxylase) under near‑physiological pH, or chemically by heating the sodium or potassium salt of acetolactate in aqueous solution (80–120 °C) sometimes with a weak acid catalyst. No external reagents are required besides heat.

Hydrolysis (SN2 displacement) of octyl bromide with aqueous potassium carbonate to give 1‑octanol; the carbonate ion provides a basic aqueous medium that generates alkoxide/OH⁻ which attacks the primary bromide, displacing bromide and forming the alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous K₂CO₃ (10 % w/v) at reflux (≈100 °C) for several hours, often in a mixed water/ethanol solvent to improve solubility. Carbonic acid is transiently formed from CO₂ dissolution and decomposes to CO₂ + H₂O; the net solid product is potassium bromide.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 2,3‑butanediol to give but‑2‑ene and water; protonation of a hydroxyl group facilitates loss of water, followed by elimination to form the internal alkene. Commonly with concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ at 120–180 °C, sometimes in a toluene or xylene solvent to azeotropically remove water. The reaction yields a mixture of cis‑ and trans‑2‑butene; the water produced is removed with the azeotrope.

Fischer esterification; condensation of pent‑4‑en‑1‑ol with acetic acid to form pent‑4‑enyl acetate and water. Conducted under reflux (≈80 °C) with a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid (5–10 % v/v) or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, often employing a Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water to drive equilibrium toward ester formation.

Swern oxidation of 3‑pentanol to 3‑pentanone. Oxalyl chloride activates DMSO at –78 °C in dichloromethane forming a chlorodimethyl‑sulfonium intermediate; addition of the alcohol gives an alkoxysulfonium species, which upon treatment with triethylamine eliminates to the ketone, producing dimethyl sulfide, CO, CO₂ and triethylammonium chloride as by‑products. Typical conditions: dry DCM, –78 °C (dry ice/acetone bath) for activation and addition steps, then gradual warming to 0 °C; excess TEA used. Purpose: mild oxidation of secondary alcohols without over‑oxidation.

Fischer esterification of acetic acid with 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol to produce 2‑methylbutyl acetate and water; the carboxylic acid and alcohol are equilibrated in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., 5–10 % H₂SO₄, p‑toluenesulfonic acid, or HCl). The mixture is refluxed (≈80 °C) in a solvent such as toluene or benzene, often using a Dean‑Stark trap to continuously remove water and drive the equilibrium toward ester formation. The final product is isolated by extraction and purification (distillation).

SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate (Williamson-type ester synthesis); converts benzoate anion into ethyl benzoate while displacing bromide as NaBr. Used to prepare esters. Typically run in dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, refluxing with excess ethyl bromide under anhydrous conditions; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a pyridine ring; methoxide replaces the chlorine ortho to the nitrogen to give 2‑methoxy‑6‑chloropyridine and NaCl. Employed for introducing alkoxy groups on activated heteroaromatics. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO) at elevated temperature (80‑150 °C) with excess NaOMe; no additional catalyst needed.

Type: Alcohol‑to‑chloride substitution using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂). Purpose: Install a chloride in place of the hydroxyl group. Key transformation: 3‑pentanol reacts with SOCl₂, forming the chlorosulfite intermediate that collapses to 3‑chloropentane, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or pyridine as solvent, 0 °C to rt, often with a base (pyridine) to scavenge HCl. No metal catalyst.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) N‑alkylation of a primary amine. Purpose: methylate the nitrogen of 2‑(1H‑pyrrol‑2‑yl)ethanamine to give the N‑methyl derivative. Key transformation: the lone pair on nitrogen attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide and forming an N‑Me bond while generating HI as by‑product. Typical conditions: methyl iodide (1.1–1.5 equiv) in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF, MeCN, or THF, with a base (e.g., triethylamine, NaHCO₃, or K₂CO₃) to neutralize HI; reaction carried out at 0 °C to rt for 1–4 h.

Direct fluorination/dehydration of sulfur trioxide with hydrogen fluoride to form sulfuryl fluoride (SO₂F₂) and water. Generates a useful V‑VI fluorinating agent. Performed by bubbling anhydrous HF gas through gaseous or liquid SO₃ at 0‑50 °C, often under pressure; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2); ethoxide ion from sodium ethoxide attacks ethyl iodide to give diethyl ether and NaI; carried out in dry ethanol or another polar aprotic solvent, often under reflux; no added catalyst.

High‑temperature metallothermic reduction; magnesium reduces niobium(V) oxide (Nb₂O₅) to niobium(IV) oxide (NbO₂) while being oxidized to MgO. Provides lower‑valent niobium oxides for ceramic or catalytic applications. Carried out in a furnace at ~1000 °C in a sealed crucible or inert atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Swern oxidation of a primary alcohol; dimethyl sulfoxide activated by oxalyl chloride is reduced by triethylamine while oxidizing 3‑nitrobenzyl alcohol to 3‑nitrobenzaldehyde. Gives aldehydes under mild, non‑acidic conditions. Conducted at –78 °C to 0 °C in dry dichloromethane or THF; reagents added sequentially (oxalyl chloride to DMSO, then alcohol, then TEA). No metal catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation) of 1‑methylindole; chlorine electrophile attacks the activated C‑3 position of the indole ring, yielding 3‑chloro‑1‑methylindole and HCl. Used to install chloro substituents on indole scaffolds. Typically carried out in an inert solvent such as chloroform or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to rt; often proceeds without added Lewis acid due to the high nucleophilicity of indole.

Copper‑mediated Ullmann ether synthesis; replaces the bromine on an aryl ring with a methoxy group to afford 2‑methoxynaphthalene. The aryl bromide reacts with sodium methoxide in the presence of CuI, typically under reflux in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO. The purpose is to form an aryl ether via nucleophilic aromatic substitution.

Acid‑base neutralization of a carbonate with sulfuric acid; magnesium carbonate reacts with H₂SO₄ to release CO₂ gas and H₂O while forming magnesium hydrogen sulfate (or magnesium sulfate). The reaction is performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with stirring to promote gas evolution. It is used to generate CO₂ and soluble magnesium sulfate salts.

Thionyl chloride conversion (acid → acid chloride); transformation of 3,5‑dichlorobenzoic acid into 3,5‑dichlorobenzoyl chloride with evolution of SO₂ and HCl gases; excess SOCl₂ (3–4 eq) added to the acid, refluxed (≈70 °C) for 30 min to 1 h, often in the absence of solvent or in dry dichloromethane; excess SOCl₂ removed under reduced pressure, product purified by distillation or chromatography.

Skeletal isomerization of 2‑methylhexane to 3‑methylhexane; purpose is to shift the methyl substituent from C‑2 to C‑3, often employed in catalytic reforming or hydrocracking streams to improve fuel octane; typically carried out over solid acid catalysts such as zeolites (e.g., H‑ZSM‑5) or metal‑oxide acids (e.g., Pt/Al2O3 with HCl), at 300–450 °C and moderate pressure (1–5 atm); hydrogen may be co‑fed to suppress coke; the key transformation is a carbocation rearrangement (1,2‑alkyl shift) that moves the methyl group.

Direct halogenation synthesis of a metal halide; elemental terbium reacts with bromine vapor to give terbium tribromide (TbBr₃). The combination is usually performed in a sealed tube or under an inert atmosphere at elevated temperatures (150–300 °C) to ensure complete reaction. The purpose is preparation of the inorganic bromide salt for further use.

TiO₂‑catalyzed photooxidative conversion of a benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid; 2,4‑dichlorotoluene is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide under UV illumination in the presence of titanium dioxide. The reaction proceeds in a mixed aqueous‑organic suspension (e.g., water/acetone) at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, generating 2,4‑dichlorobenzoic acid and water. It is used for environmentally friendly oxidation of alkylbenzenes.

Formation of a Grignard reagent (metal‑halogen exchange); magnesium inserts into 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane to generate tert‑butylmagnesium bromide; performed in dry ether or THF, often with a catalytic amount of iodine or a brief reflux to initiate; reaction kept under nitrogen or argon, temperature reflux; purpose is preparation of a tert‑butyl nucleophile for subsequent organometallic reactions.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to cleave the ester into a carboxylate salt and the corresponding alcohol. Key transformation: 2‑methylpropyl benzoate + OH⁻ → benzoate anion + 2‑methylpropanol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–3 h, often in water/ethanol mixture. No special catalyst required; work‑up with acid gives sodium benzoate.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduction of the C=C bond in cis‑2‑decenoic acid to give the saturated fatty acid decanoic acid. Conducted with H2 gas (1–5 atm) over a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO2, or Raney Ni, in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or methanol) or ethyl acetate, at room temperature to mild reflux. The reaction selectively saturates the alkene without affecting the carboxyl group.

Base‑induced neutralization of fulminic acid; potassium hydroxide deprotonates fulminic acid to afford potassium fulminate and water. The reaction is carried out in cold aqueous solution to minimize decomposition of the unstable fulminate ion. It serves to prepare the fulminate salt, which is a known primary explosive.

Oxidation (N‑oxide formation). Quinoline is oxidized to its N‑oxide (1‑oxidoquinolin‑1‑ium) using peracetic acid generated in situ from acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide. The reaction proceeds under mild acidic conditions, typically at 0 °C to room temperature in a mixture of glacial acetic acid and water. No external catalyst is required; the peracid itself is the oxidant.

Chlorination/activation of sulfonate. Potassium p‑toluenesulfonate reacts with thionyl chloride to give p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride (tosyl chloride) while liberating HCl, SO₂ and KCl. The transformation is a typical SOCl₂‑mediated conversion of a sulfonate salt to the corresponding sulfonyl chloride. It is usually performed under anhydrous conditions, refluxing in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with pyridine or triethylamine present to trap the evolved HCl.

Electrophilic aromatic alkylation (Friedel‑Crafts alkylation). Catechol (1,2‑dihydroxybenzene) undergoes para‑tert‑butylation with isobutylene in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid, affording 4‑tert‑butylbenzene‑1,2‑diol and water. The strong acid protonates isobutylene to generate the tert‑butyl cation, which attacks the activated aromatic ring. Reaction is carried out at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) in bulk sulfuric acid or a sulfuric‑acid–water mixture; no metal catalyst is needed.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation of p‑xylene to terephthalic acid; a high‑temperature, high‑pressure oxidation (the Amoco or BP process) that converts the aromatic methyl groups to carboxyl groups, producing terephthalic acid for PET manufacture; typical conditions: 175–225 °C, 15–30 atm O₂ (air), acetic acid solvent, Co/Mn bromide catalyst system (0.1–0.5 % Co, 0.1–0.5 % Mn, bromine promoter).

Enzymatic N‑methyl transfer; L‑histidine receives a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to form 1‑methyl‑L‑histidine, while SAM is converted to S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Catalyzed by a histidine N‑methyltransferase in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at physiological temperature (≈37 °C); no synthetic reagents required.

Acyl‑chloride esterification. Ethanol reacts with valeryl chloride to form ethyl valerate and HCl. This is a nucleophilic acyl substitution where the alcohol attacks the acyl chloride. The reaction is typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, with a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or NaHCO₃) added to neutralize the generated HCl and drive the reaction to completion.

Redox single‑displacement reaction; copper metal reduces mercuric ion to elemental mercury while being oxidized to copper(II) chloride; solid Cu added to an aqueous HgCl2 solution yields CuCl2 and liquid Hg; typically conducted in water, sometimes with mild heating to accelerate, under neutral or slightly acidic conditions; no external catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene. Vinyl acetate (CH₂=CH‑OAc) is reduced with molecular hydrogen to give ethyl acetate (CH₃CH₂‑OAc). The process uses a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni, or similar) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature (20–50 °C) in a solvent such as ethanol, ethyl acetate, or THF. The reaction selectively saturates the C=C bond without affecting the ester functionality.

Transamination (enzymatic aminotransferase reaction). 3‑Hydroxykynurenine transfers its amino group to α‑ketoglutaric acid, yielding xanthurenic acid and L‑glutamic acid. This reaction is catalyzed by a pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate (PLP)‑dependent aminotransferase under physiological conditions (pH 7–8, aqueous buffer, 37 °C). No additional reagents are required beyond the enzyme and cofactor.

Metathesis/acid–base exchange; converts cadmium selenite to soluble cadmium sulfate while liberating selenous acid. Performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Heterogeneous catalytic oxidation; TiO₂ under UV irradiation oxidizes 2‑methylpyridine (2‑picoline) with molecular oxygen to give pyridine‑2‑carboxaldehyde. Typical conditions: O₂ atmosphere, TiO₂ suspension in acetonitrile or water, UV light, ambient to moderate temperature; no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidation to amine N‑oxide using a hypervalent iodine oxidant; iodosylbenzene (PhIO) transfers an oxygen atom to N,N‑dimethyldodecylamine, forming the N‑oxide and iodobenzene as by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt; is usually stoichiometric, no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition; heating solid bismuth nitrate causes it to break down to bismuth oxide, nitrogen dioxide gas and oxygen; typically performed by heating to 300‑400 °C in a furnace; no solvent or catalyst needed, solid‑state reaction.

Double‑replacement/acid‑base reaction; ammonium thiocyanate reacts with nickel(II) hydroxide in water to produce nickel(II) thiocyanate, releasing ammonia gas and water. Conducted in aqueous medium, mild heating may be applied to drive off NH₃; no catalyst needed.

Copper‑catalyzed cyanation (SN2 displacement of bromide by cyanide). CuCN provides cyanide that attacks the carbon bearing bromine of 2‑bromoacetonitrile, affording malononitrile and CuBr. Typically run in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 120–150 °C under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric CuCN is used, no additional catalyst.

Gas‑solid reduction; hydrogen reduces iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃) to mixed‑valence iron(II,III) oxide (Fe₃O₄) with formation of water. Carried out at elevated temperatures (≈300–500 °C) under a flow of H₂ (often diluted with inert gas); solid‑state, no solvent or catalyst besides the iron oxide itself.

Acylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution); acetic anhydride acetylates the amino group of 2‑nitroaniline to give N‑(2‑nitrophenyl)acetamide, generating acetic acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux in pyridine or a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with possible catalytic DMAP; reaction proceeds at rt to reflux, no metal catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization and salt metathesis; base deprotonates the 2‑H‑triazol‑1‑ium cation to liberate free 1,2,3‑triazole while the tetrafluoroborate anion pairs with sodium; usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with stirring; water is both solvent and product, no additional catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) with concurrent carbonate decomposition; sodium carbonate reacts with aluminum nitrate to precipitate aluminum hydroxide and liberate carbon dioxide while forming sodium nitrate in solution; performed in aqueous medium, typically with gentle heating to promote CO2 evolution; no special catalyst needed.

Aqueous double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction between copper(II) sulfate and sodium arsenite; the sulfate and arsenite ions exchange partners to precipitate copper(II) arsenite (generally insoluble) while sodium sulfate remains in solution. Performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid copper arsenite is filtered off and washed.

Double displacement precipitation (metathesis) forming lead sulfite solid and soluble ammonium nitrate; lead nitrate reacts with ammonium sulfite in aqueous solution, precipitating lead sulfite while ammonium nitrate remains in the filtrate; typically carried out at ambient temperature with stirring; filtration separates the precipitate; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation) of N,N‑dimethylhydrazine with acetic anhydride to form N,N‑dimethylacetohydrazide and acetic acid as by‑product; usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature to control exotherm; pyridine also acts as base to scavenge the generated acetic acid; no metal catalyst required.

This is a cyclization reaction. It synthesizes a substituted pyrazine via condensation of an α-diketone with an aminoketone. The reaction forms a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing two nitrogen atoms, releasing water and hydrochloric acid. Occurs under mild heating with acidic conditions (e.g., ethanol or water as solvent).

Redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction; elemental chlorine oxidizes selenide ion to elemental selenium while being reduced to chloride ion, yielding sodium chloride as the ionic by‑product; commonly carried out in aqueous solution or polar aprotic solvent under cold conditions to avoid over‑oxidation; stoichiometric amounts of Cl₂ are bubbled through the Na₂Se solution; no additional catalyst is necessary.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of a 4‑chloro heteroaryl; replaces chlorine with an amino group to afford 4‑aminopyridine; key transformation: NH3 attacks the electron‑deficient pyridine ring and displaces Cl⁻; usually performed with aqueous or alcoholic ammonia (e.g., NH3 in ethanol) under reflux (80‑120 °C); excess ammonia acts as both nucleophile and acid scavenger; no metal catalyst needed.

Oxidation of nitroethane with potassium permanganate; alkaline aqueous KMnO4 oxidizes the nitroalkane to nitroacetic acid, producing water and insoluble MnO2; typically performed by refluxing the substrate in aqueous potassium carbonate or NaOH solution; purpose is to convert a primary nitroalkane into an α‑nitro carboxylic acid; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of cycloheptanone to cycloheptane; the carbonyl group is fully reduced to a C–H bond using H₂ and a metal catalyst (Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂). Typical conditions are 3–10 atm H₂, solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol, temperature 50–100 °C.

Fischer esterification with methanol; purpose: convert crotonic acid into methyl crotonate; key transformation: formation of a methyl ester with loss of water; typical conditions: excess methanol, catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, reflux 60–80 °C, methanol serves as both reagent and solvent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (aminolysis) of benzyl chloroformate with ammonia; ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing chloride and forming benzyl carbamate while releasing HCl. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to 25 °C, often in the presence of a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to neutralize the generated HCl.

Condensation/heterocyclization of urea with ethylene oxide to form oxazolidin‑2‑one; the nucleophilic nitrogen of urea attacks the strained epoxide, ring‑opens and cyclizes with loss of water; usually carried out in water or a polar protic solvent (e.g., methanol) at 80–120 °C under reflux, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid or base to speed up epoxide opening; purpose is the preparation of a cyclic carbamate protecting group.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling between 4‑bromonitrobenzene and phenylboronic acid; K2CO3 serves as base, Pd(PPh3)4 as catalyst, effecting transmetallation and reductive elimination to afford 4‑nitro‑1,1′‑biphenyl with potassium bromide as by‑product; typical conditions are reflux in a mixed polar aprotic solvent such as dioxane/water or toluene/ethanol under nitrogen atmosphere; purpose is construction of a biaryl linkage.

α‑Bromination of hexadecanoic acid via in‑situ formation of the acyl bromide with phosphorus tribromide followed by N‑bromosuccinimide; PBr3 converts the fatty acid to the more reactive acyl bromide, which undergoes bromination at the α‑position by NBS, giving 2‑bromohexadecanoic acid while releasing HBr and succinimide; normally performed in dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0–25 °C, often with a radical initiator or light; purpose is introduction of a bromine atom for subsequent functionalization.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a Weinreb amide. Purpose: cleave N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide to give the parentylic acid and release methanol and methylamine. Key transformation: amide C–N bonds are hydrolyzed in the presence of aqueous HCl, yielding acetic acid, methanol, and methylamine. Typical conditions: excess aqueous HCl (≈6 M) heated under reflux for several hours, often in water or water/MeOH mixture; the acid acts as catalyst, water is the solvent.

Redox reduction of selenious acid by sulfite ion; two equivalents of sodium sulfite oxidize to sodium sulfate while selenious acid is reduced to elemental selenium, with water formed; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, generally under mildly acidic to neutral pH; no catalyst is required; purpose is precipitation or recovery of elemental selenium.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of β‑propiolactone by sodium azide to give3‑azidopropionic acid; azide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of the lactone, opening the four‑membered ring and forming the azido‑substituted carboxylic acid; typically carried out in water or a water‑acetone mixture at 50–80 °C, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst to improve azide solubility; purpose is synthesis of an azide‑functionalized acid for click‑chemistry applications.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis) to free the free amine from its hydrochloride salt; carbonate ion abstracts the HCl from two equivalents of 3‑chloropropan‑1‑amine·HCl, generating carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O) and two equivalents of potassium chloride while liberating the neutral 3‑chloropropan‑1‑amine. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solution, typically with heating to evolve CO₂; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a pyridine ring where hydroxide replaces the chlorine atom of 2‑chloropyridine to give 2‑hydroxypyridine and sodium chloride. Usually performed in aqueous NaOH or NaOH/ethanol mixture under reflux (100–150 °C); polar protic solvent facilitates the reaction; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed ring‑opening hydrolysis of a strained aziridine, converting 2‑ethylaziridine and water into the β‑amino alcohol 2‑amino‑1‑butanol. Reaction proceeds in aqueous medium, often with dilute HCl or NaOH to accelerate nucleophilic attack; temperature ranging from room temperature to gentle heating; no additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of trichlorosilane (SiHCl₃) where water attacks the Si‑Cl bonds, producing orthosilicic acid (Si(OH)₄) and releasing hydrogen chloride gas. Performed by slow addition of water to SiHCl₃ under cooling (0–5 °C) to control exotherm and HCl evolution; typically in an inert organic solvent (e.g., toluene) or with the reaction carried out in a vented system; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement metathesis that forms a copper(II) dimethyldithiocarbamate coordination complex and sodium sulfate from copper(II) sulfate and sodium dimethyl dithiocarbamate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the copper complex often precipitates as a dark solid; no additional catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation). Lauric acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, generating carbon dioxide gas, water and the sodium salt (sodium dodecanoate). No catalyst required; typical solvent is water.

Base‑catalyzed transester (alcoholysis of an ester). Cis‑vaccenyl acetate is treated with excess methanol in the presence of a base such as sodium methoxide (or an acid catalyst like H₂SO₄) under reflux. The acetate group is transferred to methanol, producing methyl acetate and cis‑11‑octadecenol. Common solvent: methanol (also acts as reactant).

N‑acylation (amide formation) of an amine. Serotonin’s primary amine is acylated with acetyl bromide in the presence of triethylamine, which scavenges the generated HBr. Reaction is usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C room temperature. The product is N‑acetylserotonin and triethylammonium bromide.

Selective carbonyl reduction of an α,β‑unsaturated ketone. Isophorone is reduced with sodium borohydride, which adds hydride to the carbonyl carbon while leaving the C=C double bond intact, yielding 3,5,5‑trimethyl‑2‑cyclohexen‑1‑ol. Typical conditions: NaBH₄ in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus (azidation). Sodium azide attacks the phosphorus center of O,O‑diphenyl phosphorochloridate, displacing chloride to give diphenyl azidophosphate and sodium chloride. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetone or DMF, often at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Acid–base neutralization to form a bisphosphonate salt. Ibandronic acid is treated with sodium bicarbonate in aqueous medium; the acid is deprotonated, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and producing the anhydrous sodium ibandronate salt. Reaction proceeds at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). NaOH attacks the carbonyl of ethyl acetate, yielding ethanol and acetate ion which pairs with Na⁺ to give sodium acetate. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol as co‑solvent) and refluxed (~80 °C) for 1–2 h; no additional catalyst.

Oxidation to the quinone (anthracene‑9,10‑dione); peracid generated from formic acid and H₂O₂ (performic acid) oxidizes the central double bond to a diketone; usually performed by heating the substrate in neat formic acid or a formic‑acid/water mixture at reflux; no external metal catalyst required.

Strong hydride reduction of a ketone; LiAlH4 delivers a hydride to the carbonyl of 3‑methylpentan‑2‑one producing the secondary alcohol 3‑methyl‑2‑pentanol. Typically performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen at  °C to reflux, followed by careful aqueous work‑up to quench excess reagent.

Haloform (iodoform) reaction; I2/NaOH oxidizes the methyl ketone moiety of acetylacetone, yielding yellow iodoform (CHI3) and sodium acetate as the carboxylate fragment. Conducted in aqueous NaOH at ambient to gently heated temperature; iodine is added portionwise and the mixture is stirred until precipitation stops.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acid chloride with potassium hydrosulfide; KSH attacks acetyl chloride to give thioacetic acid and KCl. Usually carried out in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or water at 0 °C to room temperature, with stoichiometric KSH and without additional catalyst.

Transmetallation (organomercury formation); 2‑furyl lithium reacts with HgCl2 to exchange lithium for mercury, affording 2‑furyl‑mercury chloride and LiCl. Conducted in dry THF (or ether) at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; the reaction proceeds rapidly without added catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (ester exchange); isobutanol attacks methyl acetate, producing isobutyl acetate and methanol. Performed under reflux with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H2SO4) or solid acid resin; removal of methanol (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium toward product. Solvent can be the reacting ester itself or a high‑boiling inert solvent such as toluene.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution using an acid fluoride; dimethylamine attacks trifluoroacetyl fluoride, forming N,N‑dimethyltrifluoroacetamide and releasing HF. Typically run in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) present to scavenge the generated HF.

This is a decarboxylation reaction. The purpose is the metabolic conversion of L-alpha-methyldopa to alpha-methyldopamine in the body. Key transformation involves the removal of a carboxyl group (-COOH) as carbon dioxide. Reaction occurs under physiological conditions, requiring the enzyme aromatic amino acid decarboxylase and the coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate (PLP). No explicit solvent, as it occurs in aqueous cellular environments.

This is a coordination complex formation reaction. The purpose is to synthesize the tri(oxalato(2-))diholmium complex. Key transformation involves the coordination of oxalate ligands to Holmium(III) ions. Reaction conditions include aqueous solution, with potassium oxalate and Holmium(III) chloride dissolved in water. The complex may precipitate out of solution. No additional catalysts are required.

This is an acid-base reaction. The purpose is to produce scandium trichloride from scandium oxide nanopowder. Key transformation involves the reaction of a metal oxide with hydrochloric acid to form a salt (ScCl3) and water. Typical conditions include heating and aqueous hydrochloric acid. No explicit catalysts are mentioned, but the nanopowder increases reactivity.

This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction. The purpose is to form 2,5-dichloroanisole via methylation of a phenoxide. Key transformation involves phenoxide acting as a nucleophile attacking methyl iodide, displacing iodide. Conditions include a polar aprotic solvent like DMF or a biphasic system with a phase-transfer catalyst. A base (here, sodium phenoxide itself) maintains the phenoxide ion.
