Selective ester reduction with diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H); purpose is to convert ethyl benzoate to benzaldehyde without over‑reduction to the alcohol; key transformation is hydride delivery to the carbonyl carbon forming an aluminum alkoxide intermediate that on work‑up gives aldehyde and ethanol; conditions: –78 °C to –20 °C, dry inert solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, 1.0–1.2 equiv DIBAL‑H, quench with aqueous ammonium chloride; no additional catalyst.

Oxidative coupling; thiophenol is oxidized by FeCl3 to form diphenyl disulfide while Fe(III) is reduced to Fe(II). Used to generate aryl disulfides. Typically performed in anhydrous organic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at room temperature; stoichiometric FeCl3 acts as oxidant, producing HCl as by‑product.

Redox oxidation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes iron(II) selenide, converting Fe2+ to Fe3+ oxide (Fe2O3) and reducing Se– to elemental selenium. Conducted in aqueous H2O2 solution, often at moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to control rapid oxidation; excess H2O2 may be added.

Carbothermic reduction; solid calcium sulfate is reduced by carbon at high temperature to give calcium sulfide and carbon monoxide. Employed in metallurgical processes for sulfide production. Requires furnace temperatures of 1300–1500 °C in an inert or reducing atmosphere; reactants are mixed powders without solvent.

Double‑displacement (athesis) acid–salt exchange; aqueous hydroic acid swaps anions with thallium nitrate, yielding thallium iodide and nitric acid. Performed in dilute aqueous solution at ambient temperature; products remain in solution or precipitate depending on solubility, and no catalyst is needed.

Acid‑metal reaction; magnesium metal reacts with lactic acid, liberating hydrogen gas and forming magnesium lactate salt. Carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., water or dilute ethanol) with gentle heating or stirring to accelerate gas evolution; typical lab scale at room temperature to 50 °C.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). The β‑hydroxy ester (ethyl 3‑hydroxybutanoate) is oxidized to the corresponding β‑keto ester (ethyl acetoacetate) with water as the only by‑product. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; PCC is used in slight excess. No additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation; full saturation of the aromatic ring of 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydronaphthalene to give decalin; adds six hydrogen atoms across the remaining double bonds; typically performed with H2 (3 equiv) under severalpheres pressure using a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO2, or Raney Ni in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at 50‑100 °C.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); NaOH attacks the acetate carbonyl, yielding the corresponding primary alcohol and sodium acetate; performed in aqueous NaOH (or NaOH/EtOH) at reflux, typically 60–100 °C.

Nitrile reduction; LiAlH4 reduces 2,6‑dimethylbenzonitrile to the corresponding primary amine, 2,6‑dimethylbenzylamine, by delivering hydride to the carbon of the C≡N group; performed in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to reflux, with careful quench of excess LiAlH4.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination); concentrated H2SO4 protonates 3‑methylpentan‑2‑ol, leading to loss of water and formation of the more substituted alkene 3‑methyl‑2‑pentene; reaction is heated (80‑120 °C) in the presence of excess sulfuric acid, often using the alcohol itself as the reaction medium.

Oxidative leaching/acid digestion; hot concentrated HNO3 oxidizes europium sulfide, converting sulfide to sulfur dioxide gas while forming soluble europium nitrate and water; typically carried out under reflux in a glass reactor with stoichiometric excess nitric acid; vigorous gas evolution requires proper venting.

Type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction). Purpose: convert N‑hydroxylamine to a primary amine by cleaving the N‑O bond. Key transformation: N‑O bond is reduced; H₂ adds across N‑O, yielding hexylamine and water. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure (1–10 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C or PtO₂, usually in ethanol or methanol at 25–100 °C.

Dehydrative cyclization to a 1,2,3‑oxadiazolone; carbonyldiimidazole activates N‑hydroxyurea, promoting intramolecular attack of the hydroxyl nitrogen on the carbonyl carbon and expelling imidazole, yielding 1,2,3‑oxadiazol‑5(2H)‑one; performed in an aprotic solvent such as CH2Cl2 or THF at room temperature or mild heating; imidazole is formed as the by‑product.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; used to exchange anions and prepare cadmium cyanide. In aqueous solution, sodium cyanide solution is mixed with cadmium acetate solution at ambient temperature with stirring, yielding insoluble cadmium cyanide precipitate and sodium acetate in the filtrate. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Base‑promoted ether cleavage (alkoxide exchange); converts dimethyl ether into methanol and sodium methoxide. Typically carried out by adding gaseous dimethyl ether to a suspension of solid NaOH in a polar protic solvent such as methanol or aqueous ethanol and heating under pressure (100–150 °C). The reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Acidification of a sodium salt (reverse neutralization); disodium 2‑aminopentanedioate is treated with aqueous HCl to regenerate L‑glutamic acid and form NaCl; done by slowly adding dilute HCl (≈1 M) to the aqueous salt solution while monitoring pH (≈2–3); the free amino acid may precipitate upon cooling; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (DCC coupling); forms ethyl benzoate from benzoic acid and ethanol while generating dicyclohexylurea as a precipitated by‑product. Conducted in dry dichloromethane (or CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP. No external catalyst beyond DCC; the reaction is performed under an inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a hydroperoxide to an alcohol; reduces cyclohexyl hydroperoxide to cyclohexanol while forming water. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5 % Pd/C (or Raney Ni) as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or methanol 25–60 °C. Reaction proceeds to completion under; catalyst is filtered off after the reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of isopropylamine with ethyl bromide; furnishes N‑ethyl‑2‑propanamine and hydrogen bromide. Usually performed by refluxing ethyl bromide in excess isopropylamine (which acts as solvent and base) in a sealed tube or under nitrogen, temperature 80–100 °C. No additional catalyst; the generated HBr is neutralized by the excess amine.

Transcarbamoylation (carbamate exchange) between ethanol and methyl carbamate; produces ethyl carbamate and methanol. Conducted under reflux in anhydrous toluene or benzene with catalytic acid (e.g., p‑OH) or base (e.g., NaOMe), and the liberated methanol is removed by azeotropic distillation (Dean–Stark trap) to drive the equilibrium forward. No metal catalyst required.

Dehydration (thermal loss of water) of calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate to give anhydrous calcium hydrogen phosphate; typically achieved by gentle heating (≈150–200 °C) under reduced pressure or dry air; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst required.

Halide exchange of silver fluoride with hydroiodic acid. Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction. Purpose: preparation of silver iodide precipitate and recovery of HF. Key transformation: AgF + HI → AgI↓ + HF. Typical conditions: aqueous HI at ambient temperature; driven by the very low solubility of AgI. Common solvents/catalysts: water; no catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction between aqueous ammonium hydroxide and terbium triiodide forming insoluble terbium(III) hydroxide and soluble ammonium iodide; carried out in water at ambient temperature; purpose is isolation of Tb(OH)₃; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of 2‑bromobutanal to 2‑bromobutanoic acid using potassium permanganate in alkaline aqueous solution; KMnO₄ acts as oxidant, reduced to insoluble MnO₂ precipitate; typically performed at warm temperature (50–80 °C) with stirring; purpose is conversion of aldehyde to carboxylic acid.

Metallothermic reduction of silicon tetrachloride by sodium metal to produce elemental silicon and sodium chloride; conducted in dry, oxygen‑free conditions, often in a sealed tube or under inert atmosphere at elevated temperature; no solvent; purpose is preparation of silicon metal.

Mitsunobu coupling of 4‑aminobenzoic acid with 2‑dimethylaminoethanol to afford dimeth reagents triphenylphosphine and diisopyl azodicarboxylate (DIAD) activate the carboxylic acid for nucleophilic substitution; performed in anhydrous THF (or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; by‑products are triphenylphosphine oxide and diisopropyl hydrazodicarboxylate.

Acid–base conversion (salt metathesis); lithium sulfide is protonated by hydrochloric acid, releasing hydrogen sulfide gas and forming soluble lithium chloride; carried out in aqueous solution, typically at low temperature to control H₂S evolution; water as solvent.

Reduction of 2‑methylphenylacetonitrile to 2‑methylphenethylamine using lithium aluminium hydride; carried out in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) at low temperature during addition, followed by reflux; purpose is conversion of a nitrile to a primary amine; no additional catalyst required.

N‑nitramination (nitration) of a secondary amine; dimethylamine reacts with fuming nitric acid to give dimethylnitramine and water. This is an electrophilic nitrogen nitration. Typically performed at 0‑5 °C in concentrated nitric acid, sometimes with a small amount of sulfuric acid as a catalyst; no separate solvent is required. The reaction converts an amine N‑H to an N‑NO₂ group.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (Finkelstein‑type) where iodide ion from sodium iodide in acetone displaces chloride in chloroacetone to give 1‑iodopropan‑2‑one and sodium chloride precipitate. Conducted in dry acetone at reflux; sodium chloride precipitates, driving the equilibrium; no additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride to the carbon–carbon double bond of methacrylic acid (Markovnikov addition), yielding 2‑chloro‑2‑methylpropionic acid. Typically performed in aqueous HCl or an inert solvent at room temperature; the acid supplies both H⁺ and Cl⁻; no catalyst required.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: converts lead sulfate to the less soluble lead carbonate, often for purification or further processing. Key transformation: exchange of cations and anions between sodium carbonate and lead sulfate to give insoluble lead carbonate precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient temperature, may be warmed to improve precipitation. Common solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Gas‑phase redox reaction of bromine monoxide with nitric oxide; BrO + NO → Br + NO2. Bromine monoxide is reduced to bromine and nitric oxide is oxidized to nitrogen dioxide. Relevant to atmospheric chemistry; proceeds at ambient pressure and temperature in the gas phase, often under sunlight; no added catalyst.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of copper(II) acetate. Upon heating (≈200 °C), copper(II) acetate breaks down to give copper(II) oxide solid, acetone vapor, and carbon dioxide gas. No solvent or catalyst; performed in a crucible or tube furnace, often under an inert atmosphere to avoid further oxidation.

Hydrolysis of a silyl isothiocyanate; water cleaves the Si‑NCS bond of isothiocyanatotrimethylsilane producing trimethylsilanol and isothiocyanic acid; performed at room temperature in water or an aqueous organic solvent (e.g., THF); neutral or mildly acidic conditions; no catalyst required.

General type: hydrolysis of a binary halide. Purpose: conversion of selenium tetrafluoride to a more stable oxide and generation of hydrogen fluoride. Key transformation: replacement of four fluorine atoms by two oxygen atoms, yielding selenium dioxide (SeO2) and HF. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient to reflux temperature; reaction proceeds readily with water, often under controlled temperature to manage HF evolution. Common solvents/catalysts: pure water; no catalyst required, though acid media may be used to trap HF.

Double‑replacement metathesis between aqueous lead nitrate and calcium bromide, producing insoluble lead bromide precipitate and soluble calcium nitrate. Carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; the formation of the lead bromide solid drives the reaction forward.

Acid‑base salt formation (protonation) of a tertiary phosphine; purpose is to generate the trimethylphosphonium bromide salt used as a phase‑transfer catalyst or Wittig reagent precursor. The lone pair on trimethylphosphine accepts a proton from hydrogen bromide, yielding the phosphonium cation [Me₃P‑H]⁺ and Br⁻. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dry ether, dichloromethane, or acetonitrile; gaseous or aqueous HBr can be used, with the solvent kept anhydrous.

Lithiation‑formylation (directed metalation) of furan‑2‑carboxaldehyde using LDA to generate a C‑5 carbanion, which is then electrophilically formylated with DMF; low temperature (‑78 °C) in THF under inert atmosphere, aqueous work‑up gives 2,5‑furandicarboxaldehyde.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a C–Cl bond: hydrogen gas reduces hexachloroethane to pentachloroethane with concurrent formation of HCl; typically performed with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni or Pt under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in an organic solvent (e.g., ethanol or THF) at elevated temperature (50–100 °C).

Redox oxidation; formic acid is oxidized by hypochlorite, which is reduced to chloride. Key transformation: HCOOH → CO2 + H2O, NaOCl → NaCl. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; pH maintained slightly alkaline to keep hypochlorite stable. No special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalysed nitrosation of cyanamide: NaNO₂ + HCl forms nitrous acid, which nitrosates the amino group of cyanamide to give N‑nitrosocyanamide; carried out in aqueous HCl at 0–5 °C to control side reactions, no additional catalyst required.

O‑Methylation of 5‑hydroxypsoralen using methyl triflate: triethylamine acts as base to neutralise the generated triflic acid while the phenoxide attacks MeOTf in an aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN) at 0 °C to rt, affording 5‑methoxypsoralen.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling: DCC activates 2,6‑dimethoxybenzoic acid to an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is attacked by 2‑(dimethylamino)ethylamine to form trimethobenzamide; dicyclohexylurea precipitates as by‑product. Reaction is performed in dry dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to rt, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP to accelerate acyl transfer.

Thermal decomposition of zinc sulfate to zinc oxide and sulfur trioxide; occurs on strong heating (>500 °C) of the solid salt in the absence of water; no solvent or catalyst required; used for preparation of ZnO or SO₃.

Oxidative conversion of anthracene to anthraquinone using concentrated nitric acid; nitric acid acts as oxidant, being reduced to nitrogen dioxide and water; performed by refluxing anthracene in excess conc. HNO₃ at 80‑100 °C; purpose is synthesis of anthraquinone; no additional solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization forming nickel(II) iodide; hydroiodic acid reacts with nickel(II) hydroxide in aqueous solution to give NiI₂ and water; carried out at room temperature in water; simple salt‑formation reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution/condensation forming secnidazole from 5‑nitro‑2‑methylimidazole and 2‑chloro‑2‑methyl‑1‑propanol; the alkyl halide undergoes SN2 attack by the imidazole nitrogen, releasing HCl; typically performed in anhydrous ethanol or DMF with a base (e.g., NaH, K₂CO₃) at reflux; purpose is preparation of the antiprotozoal drug secnidazole.

Redox reduction; high‑temperature solid‑state reduction of TiO2 by CO to lower‑valent Ti2O3, releasing CO2. Typically carried out in a furnace at 800–1000 °C under flowing CO or CO/N2 gas; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Oxidation of emodin anthrone to emodin using silver(I) oxide; Ag₂O oxidizes the anthrone carbonyl to the quinone, producing water and metallic silver; usually carried out in dry ethanol or acetic acid at 50‑80 °C; provides a mild oxidation method for converting anthrones to anthraquinones.

Carbothermic reduction of lanthanum sesquioxide to metallic lanthanum; carbon serves as reducing agent, converting La₂O₃ to La metal and CO gas; reaction performed at very high temperature (≈2000 °C) in a graphite or electric‑arc furnace under an inert atmosphere; used for production of lanthanum metal.

Fischer esterification of acetonedicarboxylic acid with ethanol; acid‑catalyzed equilibrium condensation forming ethyl acetonedicarboxylate and water. Typical conditions: catalytic H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, reflux in excess ethanol, removal of water (Dean‑Stark or azeotropic distillation) to drive to completion.

Peracid epoxidation; peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to ethylene, producing ethylene oxide and acetic acid as by‑product; usually run in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) at 0–25 °C; can be catalyzed by silver or titanium salts but often proceeds without added catalyst.

Oxidation–reduction reaction; phenol is oxidized to a quinone while Cu(II) is reduced to Cu(I). Key transformation: 2,3,5,6‑tetrachlorophenol loses two electrons to become tetrachloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone; copperII) acetate transfers an acetate to acetic acid and is reduced to copper(I) acetate. Typical conditions: reflux in acetic acid or a polar protic solvent, often under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric Cu(II) acetate acts as oxidant. No additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ring‑opening of a cyclic ether; HCl protonates tetrahydrofuran and the resulting oxonium ion is attacked by chloride to give 4‑chloro‑1‑butanol. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O bond of THF with addition of H and Cl across the ring. Typical conditions: aqueous or gaseous HCl, reflux temperature (≈80 °C), sometimes in a mixed organic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂. Reaction is usually performed without added catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization of iron(III) hydroxide with sulfuric acid; Fe(OH)3 reacts with H2SO4 to form iron(III) sulfate (Fe2(SO4)3) and water. Performed in aqueous solution, typically with stoichiometric or slight excess H2SO4 and gentle heating to aid dissolution. Purpose: preparation of iron(III) sulfate for use in analytical or synthetic applications.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis (double decomposition). Calcium oxide exchanges anions with aluminium molybdate to form calcium molybdate and aluminium oxide. Key transformation: exchange of Ca²⁺ and Al³⁺ between oxide lattices. Typical conditions: calcination at 800–1000 °C in a furnace, dry solid reagents, no solvent. Often performed in a crucible with intermittent grinding.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) salt exchange; conversion of indium(III) chloride to indium(III) acetate. An aqueous or alcoholic solution of NaOAc is mixed with an aqueous solution of InCl₃, and the mixture is stirred and gently warmed. NaCl precipitates (or remains soluble) and Indium acetate stays in solution and can be isolated by evaporation or crystallisation. Typical solvent: water or ethanol; no catalyst.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of a linear alkane. Nonadecane loses two hydrogen atoms to give nonadecene plus molecular hydrogen. Key transformation: removal of H₂ from adjacent carbon atoms to form a C=C double bond. Typical conditions: 500–700 °C, low pressure of H₂, over metal catalysts such as Pt/Al₂O₃, Pd/C, Cr₂O₃, or zeolite‑based systems. Inert carrier gas (N₂ or Ar) is used; no solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (formation of a sulfonate ester). Methanol attacks the sulfur of p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride, displacing chloride and generating methyl p‑toluenesulfonate; HCl is released. Key transformation: conversion of a sulfonyl chloride to a sulfonate ester. Typical conditions: anhydrous pyridine orethylamine as base to scavenge HCl, 0 °C to room temperature, inert solvent such as dichloromethane. Reaction performed under dry, inert atmosphere.

Metal‑hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid. Lithium aluminium hydride reduces 4‑isopropylbenzoic acid to the corresponding primary alcohol, 4‑isopropylbenzyl alcohol. Key transformation: conversion of –CO₂H to –CH₂OH with consumption of LiAlH₄. Typical conditions: dry ether (THF or diethyl ether), 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, careful quench with water or dilute acid after completion. No additional catalyst required.

O‑acylation (esterification) of meta‑resol with acetic anhydride; phenolic OH attacks the anhydride to give 3‑methyl phenyl acetate and acetic acid; typically performed at 50‑80 °C in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base catalyst such as pyridine or DMAP to scavenge the liberated acid.

Oxidation of fenbendazole to oxfendazole using hydrogen peroxide in acetic acid; the sulfur atom of fenbendazole is oxidized to the sulfoxide (or sulfone) functional group, yielding oxfendazole and water; commonly carried out by adding 30 % H₂O₂ dropwise to a solution of fenbendazole in glacial acetic acid at 0‑25 °C, often with a catalytic amount of acid, and stirring for 1‑2 h.

Acid–base (deprotonation) reaction; NaH deprotonates methanol to give sodium methoxide and hydrogen gas; NaOMe is a common strong base and nucleophile for transesterifications, Williamson ether synthesis, and deprotonations; the reaction is performed in dry, aprotic solvents (THF, DME, DMF) under inert atmosphere, usually at 0 °C to room temperature; H2 is evolved.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation of two acrylamide molecules with formaldehyde to form N,N′‑methylenebisacrylamide and water; formaldehyde bridges the amide nitrogens via a methylene linkage; performed in aqueous HCl (1‑2 M) at 0‑5 °C initially, then warmed to 40‑60 °C for several hours, with pH controlled to prevent premature polymerization.

Acid‑base (salt metathesis) reaction; concentrated sulfuric acid protonates fluoride to volatile HF while forming iron(II) sulfate; usually done by adding solid FeF₂ to cold concentrated H₂SO₄ (≤50 °C) to control HF evolution; no additional solvent or catalyst needed.

Ligand‑exchange complexation (cyanide complex formation); used in gold refining and plating to generate soluble tetracyanoaurate(III); AuCl3 reacts with excess KCN in aqueous solution to give K[Au(CN)4] and KCl; the reaction is carried out at 20–50 °C in neutral to slightly alkaline water, often with a slight excess of CN⁻ to drive the equilibrium; no catalyst is needed, but the mixture must be handled with appropriate safety measures for cyanide.

Free‑radical chlorination of cyclopropane with chlorine gas; homolytic cleavage of Cl₂ under UV light generates Cl· radicals that abstract hydrogen from cyclopropane, forming HCl and a cyclopropyl radical that combines with Cl· to give chlorocyclopropane; carried out by bubbling Cl₂ through cyclopropane in an inert solvent (e.g., CCl₄) under UV irradiation (≈254 nm) or mild heating (≈70 °C).

Metathesis (double‑displacement) between tetramethylammonium bromide and potassium formate; Br⁻ exchanges with HCOO⁻ to produce tetramethylammonium formate and potassium bromide; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; products are isolated by evaporation or crystallization, no catalyst required.

Protonation of a carboxylate (acid‑base exchange); aqueous HCl protonates lithium 2‑methylpropanoate to regenerate 2‑methylpropionic acid and produce LiCl. Done in water at room temperature; purpose is to recover the free acid from its lithium salt.

Acid‑chloride exchange between tin(IV) chloride and concentrated sulfuric acid, generating hydrogen chloride gas and tin(IV) sulfate; the four chloride ligands are protonated by H₂SO₄, releasing HCl, while SO₄²⁻ coordinates to Sn⁴⁺; carried out by adding anhydrous H₂SO₄ dropwise to SnCl₄ at 0‑10 °C in a dry apparatus, with HCl collected over a gas‑washing bottle.

Thermal dehydration (decomposition) of iron(II) hydroxide; yields iron(II) oxide (wüstite) plus water vapor; used to prepare FeO or to remove hydroxide groups before further processing; requires heating the solid to 300–400 °C in a furnace, often under inert (N2) or reducing atmosphere to prevent oxidation to Fe3+; no solvent; solid-state reaction.

Second SN2 substitution of the remaining chloride by cyanide; is to convert the mono‑nitrile into the dinitrile adiponitrile. 5‑Chloropentanenitrile reacts with NaCN, replacing the chloride with a second –CN group, yielding adiponitrile and NaCl. Same typical conditions as reaction 1: DMF or DMSO, 80–120 °C, excess NaCN.

Amide coupling (carbodiimide‑mediated peptide bond formation). The carboxylic acid group of 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzoic acid is activated by N,N′‑dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate, which is then attacked by the amino group of 3‑aminopyridine to give the desired amide (Tyrphostin A46). Dicyclohexylurea precipitates as the by‑product. Typical conditions: DCM or DMF as solvent, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; often catalytic DMAP is added to accelerate acyl transfer.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: convert the halo‑acid to its sodium salt for easier handling or subsequent reactions. Key transformation: proton transfer from the carboxylic acid to bicarbonate, yielding sodium 2‑chloro‑2,2‑difluoroacetate, carbon dioxide and water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, stirring; excess NaHCO3 may be used.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile (meta‑methoxy substrate); purpose is conversion of 3‑methoxybenzonitrile to the corresponding primary amine. Same mechanistic pathway as reaction 2: H₂/Pd‑C adds hydrogen across the C≡N to give 3‑methoxybenzylamine. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5–10 % Pd/C, ethanol or methanol as solvent, 40–80 °C, stirred under inert atmosphere before hydrogen introduction.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling (aryl‑vinyl coupling). Phenylboronic acid couples with the vinyl halide crotyl chloride in the presence of palladium(II) acetate as the precatalyst and potassium carbonate as base, producing (E)‑1‑phenyl‑2‑butene. The reaction also generates potassium chloride and boric acid as inorganic by‑products. Typical conditions: mixed organic/aqueous solvent (toluene/ethanol/water or dioxane/water), 80–100 °C, nitrogen atmosphere, 2–24 h.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed saponification). Methyl 2‑methylbutanoate reacts with water to give 2‑methylbutanoic acid and methanol. In practice the reaction is performed with aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or aqueous base (e.g., NaOH) and heated under reflux. After completion, acidification of the basic hydrolysate (if base used) yields the free carboxylic acid.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution) reaction; installs an acetyl group para to the methyl group on toluene; key transformation: toluene reacts with acetyl chloride in the presence of aluminum chloride to give p‑methylacetophenone and hydrochloric acid; carried out anhydrous in a non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide, at 0 °C to reflux; aluminum chloride acts as the Lewis‑acid catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (transesterification) of the thioester S‑phenyl ethanethioate with ethanol; ethanol attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing phenyl‑thiolate which protonates to give thiophenol and forming ethyl acetate. Usually performed by refluxing the substrate in excess ethanol (often the solvent) and may be accelerated with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOEt).

SuFEx (sulfur‑fluoride exchange) sulfonamide formation. Benzenesulfonyl fluoride undergoes nucleophilic substitution by n‑butylamine to afford N‑butylbenzenesulfonamide. Triethylamine scavenges the released HF, acting as a base. Typical conditions: aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, ambient temperature, inert atmosphere; reaction is usually complete within a few hours.

Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon. 4‑Methylnonane reacts with molecular oxygen under high‑temperature flame conditions, oxidizing fully to carbon dioxide and water. Requires excess O₂, ignition source, and temperatures generally above 500 °C; the process is exothermic and proceeds rapidly.

Diazo‑methylation of a phenol (C‑1 transfer). Diazomethane reacts with 2,4,5‑trichlorophenol to replace phenolic hydrogen with a methyl group, forming 2,4,5‑trichloroanisole and releasing nitrogen gas. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert, aprotic solvent such as ether or dichloromethane, under a nitrogen blanket, with careful control due to the toxicity and explosiveness of diazomethane.

Electrophilic nitration of a polyol to form nitrate esters; purpose is synthesis of the high‑explosive PETN. Four hydroxyl groups of pentaerythritol are converted to nitrate groups by nitronium tetrafluoroborate, generating hydrogen tetrafluoroborate as a by‑product. Typical conditions: dry, low temperature (0‑25 °C), inert solvent such as acetonitrile or dry dichloromethane, stoichiometric nitronium salt, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation; the benzylic methyl groups of p‑xylene are oxidized to carboxylic acids. Key transformation: –CH3 → –COOH forming p‑toluic acid, with O2 reduced to H2O. Conducted at 150–250 °C and 5–10 atm O2 in the presence of metal catalysts such as Co‑Mo, Mn‑Br or Pt on carbon. Solvent often a high‑boiling hydrocarbon (e.g., diphenyl ether) or solvent‑free gas‑phase flow.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of β‑chloroglycerol with ammonia; purpose is preparation of 3‑amino‑1,2‑propanediol. Ammonia replaces the chlorine atom, forming the amino‑diol and ammonium chloride as a by‑product. Typical conditions: excess aqueous NH₃ or NH₄OH, 50‑80 °C, water or aqueous ethanol as solvent, stirring; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of ethyl 2‑nitropropionate; purpose is to obtain 2‑nitropropionic acid. Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl, cleaving the ethoxy group to give ethanol and the nitro‑propionate anion, which is acidified to the free acid. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1‑2 M), reflux 60‑80 °C, followed by acidification with dilute HCl; no special catalyst required.

Alkylation of piperazine with benzyl iodide in the presence of potassium carbonate; purpose is synthesis of N,N'‑dibenzylpiperazine. The carbonate deprotonates the piperazine nitrogens, allowing two SN2 attacks on benzyl iodide; HI formed is scavenged as potassium iodide. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (acetone, acetonitrile, DMF), reflux 50‑80 °C, excess benzyl iodide, inert; no additional catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous solution of silver nitrate and sodium carbonate; silver(I) carbonate precipitates while sodium nitrate remains dissolved; typically performed at room temperature in water, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (cleavage) of allyl ethyl ether; purpose is to separate the ether into ethanol and allyl alcohol. Concentrated sulfuric acid protonates the ether oxygen, water attacks, and the C–O bond cleaves to give the two alcohols. Typical conditions: conc. H₂SO₄ (≈90 %), aqueous medium, heating 80‑120 °C for 1‑2 h; no other catalyst required.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; used to introduce additional nitroso groups onto the piperazine ring; the N‑H of N‑nitrosopiperazine is attacked by nitrous acid (HNO2) to form N,N′‑dinitrosopiperazine with release of water; typically carried out in aqueous acidic solution (often 0–5 °C) with HNO2 generated in situ from NaNO2/HCl; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Oxidative leaching (acid‑mine‑drainage type) of iron disulfide; purpose is to convert pyritic FeS₂ into soluble iron(II) sulfate and sulfuric acid; O₂ oxidizes FeS₂ in the presence of water, yielding Fe²⁺, SO₄²⁻ and H⁺ which combine to give FeSO₄ and H₂SO₄; performed at ambient to elevated temperatures (often 25–80 °C) in aqueous media, sometimes under aeration; no special catalyst, just dissolved O₂.

α‑Methylation of acetophenone using LDA to generate the kinetic enolate followed by carbon alkylation with methyl triflate, affording 2‑methylacetophenone. Performed at –78 °C to –20 °C in dry THF under inert atmosphere; lithium triflate is formed as the counter‑ion.

Acidification of potassium acetate with hydrochloric acid; purpose: regenerate acetic acid from its potassium salt; key transformation: protonation of acetate ion to give acetic acid while chloride forms potassium chloride; typical conditions: aqueous medium, 0 °C to rt, HCl added slowly to control heat; solvent: water.

Carbothermal reduction/synthesis of zirconium diboride; purpose is to produce ZrB₂ ceramic material; carbon reduces ZrO₂ and B₂O₃, producing CO₂ and ZrB₂ as the solid product; carried out at very high temperatures (≥1500 °C) in an inert (Ar or N₂) atmosphere; reactants are mixed powders, no liquid solvent, and often a graphite crucible is used.

Type: hydrolysis (acid‑base). Description: Lithium tetrafluoroborate reacts with water, hydrolyzing the BF4‑ anion to produce lithium fluoride, boric acid (B(OH)3) and hydrofluoric acid (HF). The reaction proceeds at room temperature or with gentle heating in aqueous solution. Common solvent is water; pH may be adjusted to control HF release.

Hydrolytic decomposition of a mixed carbonate; cyclohexyl methyl carbonate is cleaved by water to regenerate cyclohexanol, methanol, and carbon dioxide. The reaction proceeds under acidic (e.g., dilute HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) aqueous conditions, typically refluxed for several hours. No special catalyst beyond the acid or base.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (inversion) of sucrose; sucrose reacts with water to cleave the glycosidic bond, yielding equimolar D‑glucose and D‑fructose; performed in aqueous solution with a dilute mineral acid (e.g., HCl) or by the enzyme invertase at 60–80 °C; water is the solvent, acid or enzyme serves as catalyst.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (acylation) of 2‑ethylphenol; purpose is to prepare 2‑ethylphenyl acetate; the phenolic O attacks acetyl chloride forming the acetate ester and liberating HCl; pyridine acts as both solvent and base to scavenge HCl; reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol. PCC converts trifluoro-substituted 2-propanol to the ketone (trifluoroacetone). Non-aqueous solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2), room temperature. Trifluoromethyl group stabilizes the product.

Double‑displacement/precipitation of lead selenide; purpose is to obtain insoluble PbSe as a semiconductor material; H₂Se (acid) reacts with lead(II) acetate, swapping anions to give PbSe solid and acetic acid in solution; performed in aqueous medium at room temperature, often under an inert gas to avoid oxidation of H₂Se; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange) between hydrochloric acid and tetramethylammonium acetate; purpose is to generate tetramethylammonium chloride and acetic acid; H⁺ exchanges with CH₃COO⁻ the corresponding acid and chloride salt; typically carried out in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization with hydrofluoric acid; purpose is to obtain indium(III) fluoride. Indium(III) hydroxide is suspended in water and treated with aqueous HF (typically 1–5 M) at 0–25 °C. The OH groups are protonated and replaced by fluoride, yielding InF3 and water. Reaction is performed in aqueous solution; careful handling of HF is required, but no additional catalyst is needed.

Fluorination/halogen exchange. Selenium dioxide reacts with hydrogen fluoride to give selenium tetrafluoride and water. Key step is replacement of oxygen by fluorine. Typically carried out in glass or Teflon apparatus with excess gaseous HF at low temperature (‑10 to 0 °C) to control exotherm; the reaction is moisture‑sensitive, so dry HF is used and the product SeF₄ is distilled from the mixture.

Intramolecular nucleophilic substitution (cyclization) forming a thiirane; Na2S supplies sulfide anion that displaces one chloride of 1,2‑dichloropropane and then intramolecularly attacks the second carbon to give propylene sulfide with NaCl as by‑product; typically performed in polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at reflux (80‑120 °C).

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid (Jones oxidation); chromic acid (generated from Na2Cr2O7/H2SO) oxidizes 2‑oxyethanol to 2‑methoxyacetic acid, reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III); carried out in aqueous acetone or water at 0‑25 °C then warmed, with Na2SO4 to keep medium acidic.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration (meta‑directed) of 3‑nitrobenzamide; mixed concentrated HNO3/H2SO4 supplies the nitronium ion that adds a second nitro group to give 3,5‑dinitrobenzamide, releasing water; reaction conducted at low temperature (0‑5 °C) then slowly warmed, using the acid mixture as both solvent and nitrating medium.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination of 4‑nitroaniline using alkaline hypochlorite; NaOCl generates Cl2/HOCl in NaOH, which chlorinates the ortho position relative to the amino group to afford 2‑chloro‑4‑nitroaniline, with NaCl and water as by‑products; performed in aqueous NaOH at 0‑25 °C.

Direct combination (synthesis) of tin(IV) chloride; elemental chlorine gas oxidizes metallic tin to SnCl4; the reaction is carried out in a dry, inert atmosphere, often by passing Cl2 over heated tin (≈200 °C) under anhydrous conditions, no solvent required.

Oxidation of the aldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid using potassium permanganate; KMnO4 (2–3 equiv) in aqueous solution (often alkaline, NaOH or Na2CO3) at room temperature to gentle heating; acidic work‑up gives 4‑nitrobenzoic acid.

Redox reaction where 2‑iodoxybenzoic acid (a hypervalent iodine(V) oxidant) is reduced to 2‑iodobenzoic acid while sodium sulfite is oxidized to sulfate; typically run in aqueous solution (often mildly acidic) at room temperature, producing sodium sulfate and the iodo‑benzoic acid as products.

The reaction is a Fischer indole synthesis, a cyclocondensation reaction used to form indole nuclei from aryl hydrazones. The key transformation involves the cyclization of the phenylhydrazone of acetophenone under acidic conditions to yield 2-phenylindole. Typical conditions include acidic catalysis, often using strong acids like sulfuric acid, and heating. Ethanol or acetic acid may serve as solvents.

This is an acid-base reaction where the phenolic hydroxy group of methylparaben is deprotonated by sodium ethoxide, forming sodium methylparaben. The purpose is to deprotonate the acidic hydrogen, yielding ethanol as a byproduct. The reaction typically occurs in ethanol as a solvent.

This reaction is an oxidation of a primary alcohol (arachidyl alcohol) to a carboxylic acid (eicosanoic acid) using chromic acid as the oxidizing agent. Key transformations include sequential oxidation steps (alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid). Conditions require strong acidic media (concentrated sulfuric acid) and elevated temperatures. A catalytic amount of H2SO4 is often used.

This reaction is an acid-catalyzed condensation of acetone with hydrogen peroxide to form triacetone triperoxide (TATP), a sensitive peroxide-based explosive. Sulfuric acid serves as the catalyst, and the reaction typically proceeds under low temperature conditions to mitigate decomposition. Water is a byproduct, and the solvent system includes sulfuric acid or aqueous solutions.

Alpha‑halogenation (chlorination) of a ketone; acetone forms an enolate that reacts with hypochlorite to give chloroacetone. Key transformation: CH3COCH3 → CH3COCH2Cl, with NaOCl reduced to NaOH. Performed in aqueous NaOCl (household bleach) at 0–25 °C, pH 8–10, often in a mixed water/acetone medium. No additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed Markovnikov hydration of isobutylene; dilute sulfuric acid in water adds water across the double bond to give tert‑butyl alcohol; typically performed at 0‑30 °C in aqueous medium, product isolated by distillation.

N‑bromination of an amide; acetamide reacts with hypobromite to install a bromine on nitrogen. Key transformation: CH3CONH2 → CH3CONHBr, with NaOBr converted to NaOH. Carried out in aqueous NaOBr solution (generated in‑situ from NaClO/NaBr) at 0–5 °C, neutral to slightly basic pH. No further catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; purpose is to saturate the carbon‑carbon double bond of 2,4‑dimethyl‑2‑pentene to give 2,4‑dimethylpentane. Key transformation: C=C → C–C by addition of H₂. Typically performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, in a solvent like ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to moderate heating (25‑80 °C).

Acidic oxidative oxidation of a primary alcoholJones oxidation); converts pentan‑1‑ol to pentanoic acid while reducing Na₂Cr₂O₇⁺⁶ to Cr³⁺ and generating sulfate. Key steps: primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; dichromate acts as oxidant in sulfuric acid. Conducted in aqueous H₂SO₄ (≈1 M) with Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O at 0 °C to reflux (≈60 °C), often in acetone/water mixture. Sodium sulfate is formed as by‑product.

Direct fluorination/oxidation of sulfur tetrafluoride; yields sulfur hexafluoride, a highly inert gas. Reaction: SF₄ + F₂ → SF₆. Performed under dry, inert atmosphere, usually at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) to control exotherm, in a non‑reactive solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or perfluorinated solvents. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a tetrafluoroborate salt; fluoroboric acid reacts with tetramethylammonium hydroxide to give water and tetramethylammonium tetrafluoroborate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often in methanol or water as solvent; stoichiometric amounts give quantitative salt precipitation upon cooling.

Halide exchange (nucleophilic substitution, F‑for‑Cl). Benzoyl chloride reacts with potassium fluoride to give benzoyl fluoride and potassium chloride. Usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile, DMF, or acetone, under gentle heating (50‑80 °C); excess KF is used and crown ethers (e.g., 18‑crown‑6) can be added to increase fluoride solubility. No additional catalyst is necessary.

Catalytic alkane isomerization; purpose to convert linear n‑hexane into branched 2‑methylpentane for higher octane rating; key transformation is skeletal rearrangement of C‑C bonds under hydrogen; typical conditions: Pt supported on Al₂O₃, H₂ pressure 1–30 atm, temperature 150–300 °C; reaction carried out in the gas phase, no solvent.

Reductive amination of isobutyraldehyde with ammonia; purpose to produce primary isobutylamine; key steps: condensation of aldehyde with NH₃ to form an imine followed by catalytic hydrogenation to amine while water is eliminated; typical conditions: H₂ pressure 30–50 bar, 80–120 °C, Pd/C or Raney Ni catalyst; solvent commonly ethanol or methanol.

Metathesis/precipitation double‑displacement; purpose to prepare cobalt(II) stearate, a metal fatty‑acid salt used as lubricant or soap; key transformation: exchange of nitrate and stearate anions forming insoluble cobalt stearate; typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient or mild heat until precipitation; solvent water (optional ethanol to aid dissolution).

Complete combustion; converts 2‑methylpropane (isobutane) to CO2 and H2O, releasing heat. Occurs in the gas phase with excess O2, initiated by a spark or flame at high temperature (≈500‑800 °C). No solvent; simply oxygen gas.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification; purpose to synthesize ethyl 2‑aminobenzoate (ethyl anthranilate); key transformation: protonation of the carboxyl group of 2‑aminobenzoic acid, nucleophilic attack by ethanol, loss of water to give the ethyl ester; typical conditions: excess ethanol, catalytic H₂SO₄, reflux (≈78 °C) for several hours; removal of water by azeotropic distillation improves yield.

Reductive amination of 2‑indanone with methylamine; purpose to obtain secondary N‑methyl‑2‑indanamine; key transformation: formation of an imine between ketone and methylamine then selective reduction by sodium cyanoborohydride to the amine; typical conditions: methanol or dichloromethane solvent, pH 5–6 (buffered with acetic acid), ambient temperature to 40 °C, NaCNBH₃ (1–2 equiv).

Oxidation of a primary allylic alcohol to an α,β‑unsaturated carboxylic acid; potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes allyl alcohol to acrylic acid while being reduced to manganese dioxide; typically performed at 0–25 °C in water with excess KMnO4, no additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; purpose to produce 4‑nitropyrazole, a precursor for energetic or pharmaceutical compounds; key transformation: generation of NO₂⁺ from concentrated HNO₃ (often with H₂SO₄) which attacks the 4‑position of pyrazole, releasing water; typical conditions: mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ at 0–5 °C, slow addition of pyrazole, reaction in an inert solvent such as glacial acetic acid or dichloromethane; work‑up includes quench with ice and extraction.

Catalytic dehydrogenation; converts a saturated C18 hydrocarbon (octadecane) the corresponding terminal alkene (1‑octadecene) with liberation of H₂ gas. Typically carried out at 500–600 °C in the gas phase over supported metal catalysts such as Pt, Pd or Ni, under an inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen) to avoid combustion.

Acid‑base double‑replacement (salt metathesis); lead(II) oxalate reacts with excess perchloric acid to give soluble lead(II) perchlorate and free oxalic acid. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring ensures complete dissolution. No special catalyst required; the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon mixing.

Redox (oxide‑fluoride) reaction; water reduces cobalt(III) fluoride to cobalt(II) fluoride while being oxidized to molecular oxygen, simultaneously generating hydrogen fluoride. Usually performed in a sealed high‑pressure reactor at 200–300 °C to drive the equilibrium toward O₂ evolution. The solid CoF₃ is reduced in situ; no external catalyst is needed, but corrosion‑resistant materials are required due to formation.

Neutralization and decomposition; ammonium nitrite in the presence of calcium hydroxide yields ammonia gas, water, and calcium nitrite. The reaction proceeds at room temperature in aqueous suspension; the liberated NH₃ is collected by gas washing. No catalyst is required; the base shifts the equilibrium away from nitrous decomposition (N₂O) toward nitrite formation.

reaction type: hydrogenation (reduction); purpose: saturate unsaturated diacid; transformation: hydrogen addition to C=C double bond; conditions: H2 (atmospheric pressure), Pd/C catalyst; solvents: ethanol or water.

Complete combustion of methylcyclohexane; reaction with excess dioxygen under ignition conditions produces carbon dioxide and water. Highly exothermic; carried out in open air or a combustion chamber at high temperature (flame) with sufficient O₂ supply.

Double‑displacement precipitation with ammonium base; magnesium chloride hexahydrate reacts with ammonium hydroxide to give insoluble magnesium hydroxide and soluble ammonium chloride; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature, excess NH₄OH ensures complete precipitation, no catalyst.

Oxidative leaching (acidic oxidation); copper arsenide is attacked by concentrated nitric acid, oxidizing arsenic to arsenic acid (H₃AsO₄), copper to copper(II) nitrate, and reducing nitrate to nitrogen dioxide gas. Carried out at 30–60 °C in reflux apparatus to control NO₂ evolution; excess HNO₃ is used to ensure complete dissolution. No additional catalyst; the reaction is driven by the strong oxidizing power of nitric acid.

Lewis acid‑base adduct formation; borane (often as BH₃·THF) coordinates to triethylamine yielding the stable triethylamine‑borane complex; carried out at room temperature in inert solvents such as THF or diethyl ether; stoichiometric mixing, no catalyst required.

Fluorination/acid‑base displacement; antimony pentoxide reacts with fluorosulfuric acid to replace oxygen with fluorine, producing antimony pentafluoride (a powerful Lewis acid) and regenerating sulfuric acid. Performed at low temperature0 °C to –20 °C) in anhydrous conditions, often in a fluorinated solvent such as liquid SO₂F₂ or in the gas phase. No catalyst; careful handling required due to corrosive HF‑type species.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); introduces a nitro group meta to the ester on the benzene ring. Mixed acid (conc. HNO3/H2SO4) generates the nitronium ion; reaction is kept cold (0‑5 °C) and then allowed to warm to 40‑50 °C. Water is formed as by‑product; sulfuric acid acts as the catalyst and solvent.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; aqueous exchange of cyanide and thiocyanate anions to precipitate sparingly soluble silver cyanide while forming soluble sodium thiyanate; typically performed in water at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

N‑alkylation of 5‑methoxytryptamine via deprotonation with sodium hydride followed by SN2 substitution with allyl bromide, repeated to give the N,N‑diallyl product; carried out in dry aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or DMF) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C room temperature; sodium bromide is the only by‑product.

Diazonium‑mediated deamination of 3‑aminophenol: nitrous acid generated in situ (NaNO₂/HCl, 0–5 °C) converts the amine to a diazonium salt which loses N₂ and hydrolyzes to give resorcinol (1,3‑dihydroxybenzene); aqueous acidic conditions, low temperature, no catalyst needed.

Hydrazinolysis of maleic anhydride (ring‑opening amidation) to produce maleic hydrazide; acetic acid serves as solvent and catalyst. Key transformation: anhydride carbonyls are attacked by hydrazine, forming a hydrazide and releasing water. Typical conditions: reflux maleic anhydride with excess hydrazine monohydrate in glacial acetic acid (≈100 °C) for 2–4 h; product precipitates on cooling and is isolated by filtration, water removed as by‑product.

Electrophilic silylation (protecting) of acetylene: trimethylsilyl trifluoromethanesulfonate transfers two trimethylsilyl groups to acetylene in the presence of the sterically hindered base 2,6‑lutidine; conducted in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; no catalyst beyond the silyl donor.

Reaction type: double displacement (metathesis). Purpose: selective anion exchange. Key transformation: bromide and chloride ions are exchanged between tetraethylammonium and silver salts. Conditions: occurs under aqueous or solid-state conditions. Silver bromide precipitates due to low solubility, driving the reaction. No catalyst required.

Reaction type: halogen addition (electrophilic addition). Purpose: formation of dibromide. Key transformation: bromine adds across the cyclooctene double bond, yielding 1,2-dibromocyclooctane. Conditions: bromine in inert solvents (e.g., CCl4) or neat. No catalyst required.

Carboxylation (nucleophilic addition) of methyllithium to carbon dioxide; the methyl anion attacks CO₂ to form lithium acetate; typically carried out in dry THF or ether at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) under nitrogen or argon, then quenched with water if needed.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Purpose: N-methylation of imidazole. Key transformation: imidazole attacks the electrophilic methyl carbon in methyl p-toluenesulfonate, displacing p-toluenesulfonic acid. Conditions: polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF) at elevated temperatures.

Precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction regenerating benzoic acid; purpose: recover benzoic acid and form insoluble AgCl. Key transformation: chloride ion replaces the benzoate on silver, yielding AgCl precipitate and free benzoic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (or dilute HCl solution) added to a suspension of silver benzoate at room temperature; immediate formation of white AgCl solid; filtration isolates the product.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an alkyl chloride; Pd/C catalyzes cleavage of the C–Cl bond under hydrogen gas, yielding the dehalogenated alkane (heptane). Typical conditions: H₂ pressure (1–5 atm), Pd/C (5–10 wt %), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, ambient to mild temperature (25–50 °C).

Reaction type: thermal decomposition. Purpose: breakdown into metal oxide and acidic oxide. Key transformation: samarium phosphate decomposes into samarium(III) oxide and phosphorus pentoxide. Conditions: high-temperature heating (solid-state reaction), no solvent or catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; used to exchange anions and isolate insoluble silver bromide. Aqueous solutions of silver nitrite and sodium bromide are mixed at room temperature, resulting in the formation of a white precipitate of AgBr and soluble NaNO₂. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Metal‑halogen exchange; preparation of a primary organolithium reagent. Lithium metal inserts into the C–Br bond of bromomethane, yielding methyllithium and lithium bromide. Performed under anhydrous, oxygen‑free conditions in dry ether or THF, typically at 0 °C to reflux, using excess lithium; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride (hydrohalogenation, Markovnikov). Purpose: convert the alkene into a tertiary chloride. Key transformation: protonation of the double bond to generate a carbocation at C‑3 followed by capture of Cl⁻, yielding 3‑chloro‑3‑methylheptane. Typical conditions: gaseous or aqueous HCl (1 M), often in a non‑protic solvent (CH2Cl2, THF), 0 °C to ambient temperature; can be catalyzed by a Lewis acid (e.g., ZnCl2) for increased rate.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) followed by hydrolysis; replaces the 6‑chloro substituent of purine with a mercapto group to give 6‑mercaptopurine. Potassium thioacetate acts as the nucleophile, attacking the electron‑deficient purine ring to give an acetyl‑thio intermediate, which is hydrolyzed by water to liberate acetic acid and the mercapto product. Typically carried out in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol/water mixture, heated under reflux. No additional catalyst is needed; K⁺ balances charge.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); 2‑ethylbutyl acetate reacts with NaOH to give sodium acetate and 2‑ethylbutanol. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) with heating (60–100 °C) until completion. No extra catalyst needed; the hydroxide ion serves as nucleophile. Solvent: water.

Grignard formation and formylation using DMF; converts 4‑methoxyphenyl bromide to 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde. Magnesium turnings react with the aryl bromide in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere to generate the arylmagnesium bromide. The Grignard reagent then adds to the carbonyl carbon of dimethylformamide, and upon aqueous acidic work‑up the intermediate collapses to the aldehyde. Conditions: anhydrous ether/THF, 0 °C to reflux for Grignard formation, followed by addition of DMF at low temperature, then quench with dilute acid. No catalyst required.

Redox oxidation of arsenous acid (As(III)) to arsenic acid (As(V)) by chlorine gas. Chlorine acts as the oxidizing agent, being reduced to chloride that protonates to give HCl. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution, often at low to moderate temperature to control gas evolution. No catalyst; the medium is water.

High‑temperature gas‑phase reduction of indium(III) chloride and antimony(III) chloride with hydrogen to synthesize indium antimonide (InSb). Hydrogen reduces the metal chlorides, producing hydrogen chloride gas and the binary semiconductor InSb as a solid. Conducted in a tubular furnace or reactor at 800–1000 °C under a flowing H₂ atmosphere. No solvent; gaseous reagents only.

Fischer esterification of a pyridine‑2‑carboxylic acid. Methanol and an acid catalyst (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) convert 2‑chloronicotinic acid to methyl 2‑chloro‑3‑pyridinecarboxylate, releasing water. Reaction is performed by refluxing the acid in excess methanol (≈65 °C) with catalytic acid; removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark) favors product formation.

Electrolytic decomposition (electrolysis) of water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. An external electric current is passed through an aqueous electrolyte (e.g., dilute acid, NaOH, or K₂SO₄) using inert electrodes (commonly Pt or Ni). The overall reaction yields 2 H₂ and O₂, requiring a minimum cell voltage of about 1.23 V plus overpotential. Catalysts such as Pt for the hydrogen evolution reaction and IrO₂ or RuO₂ for the oxygen evolution reaction improve efficiency.

Acid‑base double displacement (ion‑exchange) reaction; used to prepare tetrabutylammonium hydroxide, a phase‑transfer catalyst. Sodium hydroxide neutralizes tetrabutylammonium hydrogen sulfate, yielding sodium hydrogen sulfate and tetrabutylammonium hydroxide. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Gas‑ redox recombination/disproation reaction; combines nitric oxide (NO, a reductant) with dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄, an oxidized NO₂ dimer) to give dinitrogen trioxide (N₂O₃) and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂). Reaction is favored at low temperatures (often below 20 °C) to stabilize the labile N₂O₃; performed in a sealed gas vessel or inert solvent (e.g., dry acetonitrile) without additional catalyst.

Hydrolysis of an acyl cyanide to the corresponding carboxylic acid with release of hydrogen cyanide; converts benzoyl cyanide into benzoic acid and HCN; generally carried out in aqueous medium, either neutral or mildly acidic, at room temperature to gentle reflux; water acts as the nucleophile, and the reaction proceeds via addition of water to the nitrile carbon followed by tautomerization.

Lewis acid–base adduct formation (complexation); generates fluoroboric acid (HBF4), a strong non‑oxidizing acid and source of BF4⁻ anion. Anhydrous HF is mixed with BF3, often in a dry aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or directly in excess HF, at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

DCC‑mediated Steglich esterification; benzyl alcohol and acrylic acid are activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to give benzyl acrylate and dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Often performed in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt with catalytic DMAP; the reaction is mild and avoids strong acids or bases.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (aminolysis of an ester); ammonia attacks ethyl valerate, displacing ethanol and forming valeric acid amide (valeramide). The reaction is performed under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as ethanol or toluene, often in a sealed tube or pressure vessel to retain ammonia, at 80–120 °C. Excess ammonia drives the equilibrium; no catalyst is necessary.

Intramolecular base‑induced SN2 reaction; purpose is to convert a β‑halo‑alcohol into an epoxide. The hydroxyl is deprotonated by NaOH to give an alkoxide which attacks the adjacent carbon bearing bromine, forming a three‑membered epoxy ring and releasing NaBr and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH, reflux or 50–80 °C, often in water or water/ethanol mixture; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ketalization (formation of a cyclic thioacetal); butan‑2‑one reacts with ethane‑1,2‑dithiol to give a 1,3‑dithiolane ring (2‑ethyl‑4‑methyl‑1,3‑dithiolane) with loss of water. Typical conditions employ a catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid or another strong acid in a dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, often with a Dean–Stark trap to remove water. Reaction temperature ranges from room temperature to reflux (~40–110 °C).

High‑temperature solid‑state carbothermic reduction; hafnium tetrachloride reacts with carbon (graphite) at 1700–2000 °C under an inert (argon) atmosphere to produce hafnium carbide (HfC) and liberate chlorine gas. No solvent is used; the reaction proceeds in a furnace or electric arc furnace. The chlorine evolves and is typically captured or vented safely.

Dehydration condensation; purpose: preparation of formic anhydride by removal of water from formic acid. Key transformation: two molecules of formic acid lose one molecule of water to form the anhydride (HCO-O-COH). Typical conditions: reaction performed under anhydrous conditions using phosphorus pentoxide (P₂O₅) as a strong dehydrating agent, often at 0–50 °C under nitrogen or argon. The mixture may be stirred in a dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dry dichloromethane, chloroform or diethyl ether; excess P₂O₅ scavenges the generated water. No additional catalyst is required.

Reaction type: nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S_NAr) on a heteroaryl chloride. Purpose: install a piperazine substituent onto the pyrimidine ring to afford a basic heterocycle useful in medicinal chemistry. Key transformation: the secondary amine of piperazine attacks the C‑2 carbon of 2‑chloropyrimidine, displacing chloride and forming 1‑(pyrimidin‑2‑yl)piperazine; HCl is released. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., N,N‑dimethylformamide or isopropanol) with 2–3 eq of a tertiary base (triethylamine, DIPEA) to neutralise HCl; reaction time 4–12 h. Alternative: use piperazine as the solvent (excess) at 120 °C in a sealed tube.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: synthesis of insoluble iron(II) molybdate and removal of iron(II) sulfate from solution. Key transformation: Fe²⁺ exchanges counter‑ions with MoO₄²⁻ to form FeMoO₄ (iron(II) molybdate) which precipitates, while Na⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to give soluble Na₂SO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of FeSO₄·7H₂O and Na₂MoO₄·2H₂O mixed at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring. The precipitate is filtered, washed with cold water and dried. No catalyst needed.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: isolation of barium oxalate from soluble salts. Key transformation: Ba²⁺ combines with C₂O₄²⁻ to give BaC₂O₄ (barium oxalate) which precipitates, while Na⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to form NaCl in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of Na₂C₂O₄ and BaCl₂ mixed at room temperature; the mixture may be cooled to enhance precipitation. The solid is filtered, washed with cold water and dried. No catalyst required.

Alcoholysis (transesterification) of an aryl acetate with methanol. Purpose: exchange the acetyl group from the phenoxy oxygen to methanol, producing 3,5‑dichlorophenol and methyl acetate. Key transformation: methanol acts as nucleophile on the carbonyl, displacing phenolate; phenolate is protonated to phenol. Typical conditions: excess methanol (10–20 equiv) with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid, 5 mol %) or base (NaOMe, 5 mol %). Reaction temperature 50–80 °C for 2–6 h, often in a sealed tube. Solvent is methanol itself; no additional solvent needed.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis of an acid chloride; purpose: conversion of oxalyl chloride to the corresponding potassium salt while generating hydrochloric acid. Key transformation: each carbonyl‑chloride bond is attacked by hydroxide, producing potassium oxalate (K₂C₂O₄) and releasing two equivalents of HCl. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic KOH solution (often 1 M) added dropwise to oxalyl chloride kept cold (0 °C) to control vigorous HCl evolution, then allowed to warm to ambient temperature. The reaction mixture is stirred for 30 min to 1 h. No additional catalyst; the reaction is exothermic.

SN2 alkylation (carboxylate methylation); purpose is to convert the sodium pyridine‑4‑carboxylate salt into the methyl ester of nicotinic acid. The carboxylate oxygen attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide to give methyl pyridine‑4‑carboxylate and NaI. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, acetone or MeCN), 0 °C to reflux, sometimes a phase‑transfer catalyst; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide; purpose: synthesis of 4‑methyl‑1‑pentanol from the corresponding bromide. Key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the primary carbon bearing bromine, displacing Br⁻ and forming the primary alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH (or KOH in ethanol) heated under reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours. The reaction may be carried out in a mixed water/ethanol solvent to improve solubility of the organic bromide. After completion, the mixture is extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., diethyl ether), the organic layer dried, and the alcohol purified by distillation. No catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation (acid‑base exchange); purpose is to prepare insoluble indium(III) phosphate. Indium(III) acetate in aqueous solution is mixed with phosphoric acid; acetate ions exchange with phosphate, forming indium(III) phosphate as a precipitate and releasing acetic acid into solution. Reaction is carried out in water, often with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to improve crystallization.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amidation (DCC coupling). Propionic acid is activated by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC) to form an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is then attacked by dibutylamine to afford N,N‑dibutylpropanamide. Dicyclohexylurea (DCU) precipitates and is removed by filtration. Typical conditions: 0 °C addition of DCC to a solution of the acid in dry dichloromethane (or DMF), followed by addition of dibutylamine (often with catalytic DMAP) and stirring at rt for several hours. The reaction is performed under inert atmosphere to prevent moisture.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (sulfonation); purpose: introduction of a sulfonic acid group onto the aromatic ring of toluene to give toluenesulfonic acid (mainly para‑isomer). Key transformation: sulfur trioxide generated in situ from concentrated H₂SO₄ attacks the aromatic ring, forming a σ‑complex that loses a proton to give the sulfonated product; water is a by‑product. Typical conditions: excess concentrated H₂SO₄ (≥ 98 %) used as reactant and solvent; the mixture is heated to 140–160 °C (often in a sealed tube or oil bath) for 1–3 h. The reaction is performed under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation. After cooling, the mixture is poured onto ice, the solid toluenesulfonic acid is collected, washed, and dried. No additional catalyst is required.

Amide formation (acid–hydrazide condensation); oxalic acid reacts with hydrazine hydrate to give oxalyl dihydrazide, a di‑hydrazide, with elimination of water. The two carboxyl groups of oxalic acid are each converted into hydrazide groups via nucleophilic attack of hydrazine and loss of water. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solution by heating under reflux, often with an excess of hydrazine to push the equilibrium forward. No external catalyst is required; the reaction is driven by removal of water (e.g., by azeotropic distillation). Common solvent: water or mixture of water/ethanol.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; converts 2‑(2‑methylphenyl)acetonitrile to the corresponding carboxylic acid. The nitrile is protonated by aqueous HCl, then water attacks, giving an amide intermediate that further hydrolyzes to 2‑(2‑methylphenyl)acetic acid while ammonia is protonated to NH₄Cl. Conducted by refluxing the nitrile in concentrated HCl (≈6 M) at 80‑120 °C for several hours; the reaction medium is aqueous HCl, no external catalyst needed.

Esterification (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of methanol with bromodifluoroacetyl chloride to give methyl bromodifluoroacetate and HCl; typically performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) at 0 °C to rt with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HCl.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of the two bromide groups in bis(2‑bromoethyl) ether by cyanide ions from NaCN, producing bis(2‑cyanoethyl) ether and NaBr; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at moderate temperature (0–50 °C); excess NaCN often used to drive the reaction to completion.

Thermal oxidative decomposition (solid‑propellant combustion) of 1,3,5‑trioxane mixed with ammonium perchlorate, yielding gaseous CO2, HCl, N2 and H2O; initiated by ignition and sustained at high temperature (several hundred °C) under pressure; no solvent or catalyst required.

Oxidation/hydrolysis; excess borane is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to give boric acid and water; performed in aqueous medium, usually ice‑cold to control exotherm, with dilute H₂O₂ added slowly; no catalyst needed.

Halide metathesis (double‑displacement) in aqueous acid where MnF2 reacts with excess hydroiodic acid to form MnI2 and liberate hydrogen fluoride; typically performed in water with heating (reflux) to ensure complete exchange; no special catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of butyl acetate with water in the presence of concentrated H2SO4, giving acetic acid and n‑butanol; reflux in a biphasic mixture or in excess water, sulfuric acid acts as both catalyst and dehydrating agent; temperature around 80–100 °C.

Jones oxidation (chromic‑acid oxidation) of 2‑pentafluorobenzyl alcohol to pentafluorobenzoic acid, with water as by‑product; carried out in aqueous H2SO4/Na2Cr2O7 (or CrO3) in acetone at 0 °C to room temperature; the chromium(VI) species functions as the oxidant.

Type: hydride reduction of a silicon halide. Purpose: conversion of a silyl chloride to the corresponding hydrosilane. Key transformation: transfer of a hydride from diisobutylaluminum hydride to triisopropylsilyl chloride, forming diisobutylaluminum chloride and triisopropsilane (Si–Cl → Si–H). Typical conditions: inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) to control reactivity; reaction run in dry, aprotic solvents such as toluene or THF. No additional catalyst required.

The general type is a gas-liquid double displacement (metathesis) reaction. Purpose is to precipitate copper(II) sulfide. Key transformation involves hydrogen sulfide gas providing sulfide ions to react with copper ions. Conditions occur in aqueous solution with hydrogen sulfide gas bubbled through the system at ambient temperature. Solvent is water, and no catalyst is required.

Type: acid‑base neutralization / salt formation. Purpose: preparation of copper(II) acetate from inexpensive reagents. Key transformation: the basic oxide CuO reacts with two equivalents of acetic acid, yielding copper(II) acetate and water (CuO + 2 HOAc → Cu(OAc)₂ + H₂O). Typical conditions: refluxing aqueous or ethanolic solution of acetic acid with solid CuO; stirring until gas evolution ceases. Solvent: water or a mixture of water/ethanol.

Type: free‑radical chlorination (substitution). Purpose: synthesis of a trichlorinated ethane derivative. Key transformation: one hydrogen atom on 1,2‑dichloroethane is replaced by chlorine, producing 1,1,2‑trichloroethane and generating HCl as a by‑product (C₂H₄Cl₂ + Cl₂ → C₂H₃Cl₃ + HCl). Typical conditions: UV irradiation or thermal initiation (Δ ≈ 80–120 °C) in an inert, non‑protic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; radical initiator (e.g., benzoyl peroxide) can be used. No metal catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution of ethyl chloride with hydrogen sulfide to produce ethyl mercaptan and HCl. Due to the poorer leaving ability of chloride, the reaction requires stronger conditions such as higher temperature, excess H2S, and often a basic medium (e.g., NaHS or K2S) to trap the released HCl.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction. Purpose: preparation of cobalt(II) bromide and sodium nitrate salts. Key transformation: exchange of anions between cobalt(II) nitrate and sodium bromide, yielding cobalt(II) bromide and sodium nitrate (Co(NO₃)₂ + 2 NaBr → CoBr₂ + 2 NaNO₃). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; complete dissolution and stirring until equilibrium is reached. No special catalyst; optional gentle heating to improve solubility.

Nucleophilic substitution (rolysis) of a primary alkyl halide; water acts as nucleophile, displacing chloride and yielding cyclopropanol with formation of HCl; generally conducted in warm aqueous solution, sometimes with a polar solvent such as ethanol to improve solubility.

Type: Hofmann rearrangement (oxidative decarboxylation of an amide). Purpose: conversion of 3,4‑dimethoxyphenylacetamide to the corresponding primary amine (homoveratrylamine) with loss of the carbonyl carbon as CO₂. Key transformation: NaOBr oxidatively converts the amide into an isocyanate intermediate, which hydrolyzes to give the amine while releasing CO₂ and NaBr (Ar‑CH₂‑CONH₂ + NaOBr → Ar‑CH₂NH₂ + CO₂ + NaBr). Typical conditions: aqueous sodium hydroxide solution with in‑situ generated hypobromite (NaOBr) at 0–25 °C; reaction is kept mildly basic (pH ≈ 9–10). No metal catalyst; the bromine source (NaOBr) acts as oxidant.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a metal oxalate salt; oxalic acid protonates the basic beryllium oxide to give water and soluble beryllium oxalate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating; water acts as solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

SN2 O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of phenol with allyl bromide; potassium carbonate deprotonates phenol to generate phenoxide, which attacks the allyl bromide, producing allyl phenyl ether and potassium bromide. Usually performed at 50‑80 °C in the ionic liquid 1‑butyl‑3‑methylimidazolium tetraoroborate, which serves as both solvent and phase‑transfer medium; no metal catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) of phosphate salts in aqueous solution; sodium hydrogen phosphate exchanges cations with calcium dihydrogen phosphate, yielding calcium hydrogen phosphate (often precipitated) and sodium dihydrogen phosphate in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst is required, and the reaction may be driven by differences in solubility.

Base‑ or‑catalyzed transesterification between isopropyl alcohol and tert‑butyl butanoate; the alkoxy group of the ester is exchanged with the incoming alcohol, producing tert‑butyl alcohol and isopropyl butanoate. Typical conditions involve refluxing the mixture (80‑120 °C) with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid or sodium methoxide, using excess alcohol as solvent; removal of the formed alcohol drives the equilibrium forward.

Precipitation (double‑replacement) reaction of lead(II) acetate with sodium selenide; lead(II) ions combine with selenide to form insoluble lead selenide (PbSe) while sodium acetate remains in solution. Performed in aqueous solution under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of selenide; ambient temperature is sufficient and no additional catalyst is required.

Carbonation (acid‑base) of yttrium hydroxide with carbon dioxide; CO₂ reacts with Y(OH)₃ to generate yttrium carbonate and water. Usually done by bubbling CO₂ through an aqueous suspension of Y(OH)₃ at room temperature to 60 °C, sometimes under slight pressure to increase solubility; water is the solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Decarboxylation of barbituric acid to uracil; a thermal/acid‑catalyzed decarboxation where the 2‑pyrimidinone ring loses the C‑5 carboxyl group as CO₂, yielding uracil (pyrimidine‑2,4‑dione). Typical conditions: heating barbituric acid (150‑200 °C) in the presence of dilute acid (e.g., HCl) or solid acid catalysts; solvent often absent or minimal (dry melt).

Oxidation of iodide to iodate by hydrogen peroxide in alkaline medium; a redox reaction where NaI is oxidized by H₂O₂ under basic conditions (NaOH) to give NaIO₃ and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess NaOH ensures the reaction stays in the iodide/iodate redox couple. No special catalyst required.

Ester reduction with lithium aluminium hydride: methyl 2‑(thiophen‑2‑yl)acetate is reduced to 2‑(thiophen‑2‑yl)ethanol. LAH reduces the ester to the primary alcohol via a hydride attack on the carbonyl. Conditions mirror reaction 3: LAH (1.5 equiv) added to a solution of the ester in dry THF or ether at 0 °C, then stirred at rt for 1–3 h. Work‑up with careful quench (water, then dilute acid) affords the alcohol after extraction and purification. No additional catalyst required.

Acid dissolution / salt formation; vanadium(III) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to give soluble vanadium(III) chloride and water; performed in dilute HCl, often refluxed or gently warmed to aid dissolution, aqueous medium, no additional catalyst.

General type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2′) of a propargylic halide by azide ion. Purpose: convert the iodide leaving group into an azide, yielding 1‑azidoprop‑1‑yne, a versatile synthetic intermediate. Key transformation: azide anion attacks the sp‑hybridized carbon bearing iodine, displacing I⁻ and forming the carbon‑azide bond. Typical conditions: dissolve sodium azide and 1‑iodoprop‑1‑yne in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO; stir at 0 °C to 50 °C under nitrogen; reaction is complete in 1–4 h; sodium iodide remains in solution.

Electrophilic chloromethylation of benzene (Blanc reaction); formaldehyde and HCl generate the electrophilic chloromethyl cation which undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution on benzene, producing benzyl chloride and water. Typical conditions: ZnCl₂ or FeCl₃ as Lewis‑acid catalyst, aqueous HCl, paraformaldehyde or aqueous formaldehyde, solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform or nitrobenzene, temperature 0–50 °C.

Markovnikov hydrohalogenation of ethyl methacrylate; HBr adds across the C=C double bond of the methacrylate ester, delivering ethyl 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropanoate Usually performed in an inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to reflux; HBr can be introduced as gaseous HBr or aqueous HBr solution; no catalyst needed for the normal addition.

Halogen exchange (Swarts reaction) converting chloroacetone to fluoroacetone using antimony trifluoride; SbF₃ acts as a fluorinating agent, replacing the chlorine atom with fluorine while generating SbCl₃ as by‑product. Conducted under anhydrous conditions, often refluxing in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; temperature typically 80‑120 °C.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Lactic acid reacts with basic aluminum oxide to produce aluminum lactate and water. Purpose: preparation of the metal lactate salt, which can serve as a catalyst or polymer additive. Key transformation: deprotonation of the carboxyl groups and coordination of Al³⁺ to form the lactate anion, with release of water. Typical conditions: heating the mixture (90–150 °C) to drive off water, often in an aqueous suspension or with minimal solvent. Common solvent: water or ethanol; solid‑state grinding can also be used.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide by a thiolate. Methanethiol is deprotonated (commonly with a mild base such as NaH, K₂CO₃, or Na₂CO₃) to generate the methanethiolate nucleophile, which displaces bromide on 3‑bromopropanamide to give 3‑(methylthio)propanamide and HBr. Purpose: introduction of a thioether functionality. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at 0 °C to reflux; stoichiometric base to neutralize the generated HBr.

Type: Aryl diazonium hydrolysis (phenol formation). Purpose: Convert a para‑methoxy aryl diazonium into the corresponding phenol. Key transformation: loss of N₂ gas and replacement of the diazonium group by OH, yielding 4‑methoxyphenol and HCl.
